title: As summer heat waves intensify, North Carolina advocates push for farmworker protection
description: When the heat index tops 105°F, as it has this week in central North Carolina, the National Weather Service issues a heat advisory. Meteorologists warn people to limit their time in the sun and advise that hot temperatures and high humidity may cause heat-related illness. But for many workers, taking a break from summer’s extreme […]
text:
Farmworkers tend to young seedlings during a sweltering summer day. (Photo: Getty Images) When the heat index tops 105°F, as it has this week in central North Carolina, the National Weather Service issues a heat advisory. Meteorologists warn people to limit their time in the sun and advise that hot temperatures and high humidity may cause heat-related illness.
But for many workers, taking a break from summer’s extreme conditions is not an option.
Andressia Ramirez, an advocacy and civic engagement manager at Casa Azul de Wilson, said farmworkers in North Carolina are expected to work long hours even in triple-digit conditions.
Ramirez was joined by a group of Latine agricultural workers at the state capitol Thursday to highlight the contributions of immigrant farmworkers and the workplace dangers they face.
Ramirez, who grew up in rural Wilson County, said she was recently visiting a farmworker camp when she noticed a young man sitting alone on a bucket underneath a tree.
The man told Ramirez he had a fever. He should have been resting inside the mobile home, but the coolest place he could find on the 95-degree day was outdoors underneath a tree.
In North Carolina, farmworker housing is still not required to have air conditioning.
“This isn’t just about one young man. It is about the conditions we have allowed to become normal,” said Ramirez.
Esmeralda Juarez, Xitlali Gomez, and Andressia Ramirez highlight the need for better workplace conditions for workers in agriculture and construction. (Photo: Alanna Joyner/Progress NC)
The federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration offers guidelines for prevention of heat illness, but it has not yet implemented any specific heat standards for workers apart from its general duty clause.
Seven states have enacted their own specific occupational heat safety standards designed to protect workers when temperatures become hazardous. North Carolina is not among those states. State lawmakers have said requiring farmers to follow heat safety rules would hurt them economically.
The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH), which is under the CDC, recommends limiting worker heat stress, enforcing work-rest cycles, rotating tasks, and encouraging hydration during moderate work, but those are not legal requirements.
Esmeralda Juarez was never offered those protections.
Juarez, who works for the Kinston nonprofit NC Field, told reporters Thursday that she began working in the tobacco fields at age 13.
“My head would hurt, my stomach ached, and I would feel so nauseated that I’d want to throw up,” Juarez said.
Juarez said many farmworker families endure pain and unbearable heat without complaint out of need.
“Many people would tell me, if you don’t feel well, don’t go,” said Juarez. “But poverty does not give families that kind of choice.”
Juarez said agriculture is one of the most dangerous industries in the U.S. and North Carolina lawmakers must do more to protect farmworkers and child laborers from extreme conditions.
Farmworkers sue over Trump’s low wages for foreign guest workers

“Water alone is not enough. Workers need shade. We need training that we can actually understand, and time to adjust to extreme heat,” said Juarez.
Immigrant workers make up 12% of North Carolina’s workforce, and by conservative estimates contribute $60 billion annually to the state’s economy, according to the left-leaning N.C. Budget and Tax Center.
Ramirez said she often hears lawmakers talk about struggles that farmers are facing, with higher input costs, tariffs, and this summer’s punishing drought.
“I agree, our farmers deserve support, but why must one lose for the other to gain?” Ramirez said. “We can support our farmers without sacrificing the people who work in their fields.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas firefighters union advocating for staffing increase alleges government violated free speech
description: TOPEKA — A Kansas firefighters union and county government are “at loggerheads with each other,” a federal judge said Wednesday, complaining they threw the case at him to solve after months of conflict. The Kansas City, Kansas Professional Firefighters Association’s lawsuit against the Unified Government of Wyandotte County was filed against the backdrop of[...]
text:
The International Association of Fire Fighters Local 64 is suing the Unified Government of Wyandotte County over alleged free speech violations rooted in understaffing issues at the Kansas City, Kansas, Fire Department. Attorneys for the union and the government appeared on Aug. 12, 2026, at a Kansas federal courthouse, which appears here in April 2025 in Topeka. (Photo by Grace Hills/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A Kansas firefighters union and county government are “at loggerheads with each other,” a federal judge said Wednesday, complaining they threw the case at him to solve after months of conflict.
The Kansas City, Kansas Professional Firefighters Association’s lawsuit against the Unified Government of Wyandotte County was filed against the backdrop of a December fire that left four firefighters with second- and third-degree burns. A federal agency investigated the incident, finding that one of the factors that contributed to the injuries was understaffing. 
The union said its members had been trying to speak about inadequate staffing levels with the Unified Government’s board of commissioners, which was also named in the Aug. 4 lawsuit, and public safety committee, but the Unified Government “repeatedly quashed these requests, falsely claiming that state law forbids the union from speaking to elected officials about issues affecting the KCKFD,” the lawsuit said.
The Unified Government forbade union representatives from speaking at monthly public safety committee meetings, which the union said violated its members’ First and 14th Amendment rights.
The Unified Government argued the union was subverting its shared collective bargaining agreement, which includes a minimum staffing requirement.
In August 2024, the Unified Government’s board of commissioners approved a revenue-neutral budget for 2025 that reduced staffing on ladder trucks and other equipment from four to three. The National Fire Protection Association’s standard is a minimum of four firefighters. 
About 3:45 a.m. on December 29, 2025, the Kansas City, Kansas, Fire Department responded to a fire at an abandoned house. The house’s first floor collapsed, and four firefighters fell through, into the basement, where the fire had likely been burning for “an extended time,” according to a federal investigation. One firefighter was trapped from the waist down and screamed for help, according to the federal report. The first to fall in tried to radio “mayday” but wasn’t readable, according to the federal report. 
The four were rescued and hospitalized, and they survived with second- and third-degree burns and minor injuries.
The investigation from the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health found that eight factors contributed to the career firefighters’ injuries.
“Responding units faced two of the most dangerous types of structure fires. A below grade fire combined with an abandoned structure significantly raises the life safety risk to firefighters,” a report published in April said.
Among the factors were communication errors, risks associated with fires in abandoned structures and inadequate staffing.
The firefighters union homed in on the inadequate staffing factor in its efforts to persuade the Unified Government to modify its budget and increase fire department staffing levels. The union asked to appear on the public safety committee’s agenda instead of speaking during the designated, time-limited public comment period, which the Unified Government denied. The government’s attorney said union representatives can’t communicate directly with elected officials about topics subject to bargaining. 
Attorneys for the union want a federal judge to grant them a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction, which could force the Unified Government to allow union representatives to speak at public meetings before the Unified Government finalizes its budget in September. 
Jake Miller with Kansas City-based firm Grissom and Miller and Tamara Imam with a Washington, D.C.-based labor law firm are representing the union, and the Unified Government is represented by Ryan Denk. 
U.S. District Court Judge Toby Crouse criticized the union’s attorneys at a hearing Wednesday for failing to notify the Unified Government’s attorney that they were filing a request for a temporary restraining and preliminary injunction, noting that lawyers typically “have the courtesy to pick up the phone and have a conversation.”
Denk said Wednesday the Unified Government would try to get the case dismissed. 
He said in a Tuesday court filing that before the lawsuit, union represented didn’t respond to a written offer to coordinate a private meeting with a designated Unified Government official.
Counsel wrote in a May 12 letter to the union: “If you would like to schedule a formal meet and confer session, please let us know and we will proceed with scheduling the same.”
“The Unified Government never received a response to this letter and the plaintiff never requested to meet and confer relating to the subject of staffing,” the court filing said. “Rather, the plaintiff waited three months and then filed a lawsuit along with a request for an emergency TRO due to the timing of the last Public Works and Safety Subcommittee meeting.”
The timing, Denk said, was driven by the union’s failure to meet and confer with the Unified Government in private.
Crouse said the parties were “throwing” the case at him after they’ve been in conflict for months. 
“I’ve got to deal with it,” he said, and, he added, “I don’t know half of what you know.”

title: Colorado Rep. Mandy Lindsay defends caucus payments during ethics hearing
description: Colorado Rep. Mandy Lindsay told lawmakers on Friday that she did not fully understand the level of financial responsibility involved when she became co-chair of the House Democratic Caucus, and that there was an unset expectation around the accounting and organization of caucus funds. “I did not interpret that role this way. I ran for […]
text:
The Colorado House of Representatives is pictured on the final day of the 2026 legislative session on May 13, 2026, at the Colorado Capitol in Denver. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)Colorado Rep. Mandy Lindsay told lawmakers on Friday that she did not fully understand the level of financial responsibility involved when she became co-chair of the House Democratic Caucus, and that there was an unset expectation around the accounting and organization of caucus funds.
“I did not interpret that role this way. I ran for this role to feed people, to connect us, to host fun events, to plan fun retreats,” she said. “Looking back now, obviously, I did not know what I was undertaking and did not understand the level of responsibility I was undertaking.”
Lindsay, an Aurora Democrat, made the comments during the final day of an evidentiary hearing for an ethics complaint she is facing over alleged mismanagement of caucus funds. She was the last witness to speak with the bipartisan House Ethics Committee. As caucus co-char, Lindsay is in charge of collecting member dues, leading meetings, supplying meals occasionally, and other morale boosters such as birthday cards and flower deliveries.
“We made sure everyone had breakfast and lunch all the time, and sometimes we were being really scrappy to figure out how to do it. To me, that was the end product that mattered,” she said. “I want to nurture and make everyone in the caucus feel that they are a part of something, that we have fun, that we care about each other, and that this workplace can be full of people who have meaningful relationships.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The complaint is based on a series of reimbursements Lindsay made to herself from the caucus bank account. Some of those checks were initially written in error, she said, but the reimbursements were ultimately for thousands of dollars she spent in personal funds for caucus activities over the years.
Colorado ethics panel begins hearing over Rep. Mandy Lindsay’s handling of caucus bank account

“I’m not a bookkeeper,” she said. “But I wasn’t just willy-nilly spending and not knowing how much we had or not knowing how much (dues money) people owed.”
She said it is “abundantly clear” she did not know enough about general accounting practices. Witnesses throughout the two-day hearing said Lindsay’s actions were akin to disorganized bookkeeping, not intentional negligence.
Both Lindsay and co-chair Rep. Junie Joseph, a Boulder Democrat, described a dysfunctional relationship in their partnership. Joseph said it took months for her to access the caucus’s bank account and when she did, she noticed the seemingly suspect transactions. She said she then asked Rep. Bob Marshall, a Democrat from Highlands Ranch, to look over the bank account because of his finance experience.
“I needed a second set of eyes on it,” she said. “Rep. Lindsay and I were not having a lot of conversations, and I didn’t want it to just be me going to her. I wanted to make sure someone else looked at this.”
Marshall ended up filing the complaint against Lindsay early this year.
“I already had big issues with the caucus fund in terms of putting money in and not knowing what the hell it’s doing. I realized it was a big stinking pile of mess, but it wasn’t my mess. But Junie brought this, put it right in front of me,” he said.
Lindsay addressed the largest reimbursement check on Friday, a payment for about $6,000. She said she originally wrote the check when she thought a hotel charge for a caucus retreat in November 2024 would hit her personal card on file. She realized a few weeks later, following what she described as a tumultuous time in her personal life, that the caucus card was the one actually charged.
“I realized that I had foolishly, and crazily, misunderstood what (an email from the hotel) said,” she said. “I was horrified.”
But Lindsay kept the check as a partial reimbursement to herself for accrued costs as co-chair. She hadn’t done the hard math of totaling exactly what she was owed, she said, but she knew it was more than the cost of that hotel charge.
“Once I realized that the charge had not been made to my personal account, I was like ‘OK, well I wrote this check, what should I do?’” she said. “I believe I should have done something different about it, process-wise, but I was also owed about seven grand. And so I’m beginning this process now.”
The committee will make a final determination on the complaint during a meeting on Sept. 4. Members could dismiss it entirely or make a range of recommendations to House leadership about consequences.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: U.S. House candidate Bohannan commits to spend more on cancer research
description: IOWA CITY – Morgan Newman was a 24-year-old dental assistant when she was diagnosed with cervical cancer, a disease that is more common in women ages 35-64.  “I had a metastatic recurrence to my lungs,” Newman, of Norwalk, said as she sat by her mom, Kendra, at an event Friday at Sidekick Coffee & Books […]
text:
Christina Bohannan, Iowa City Democrat running for U.S. House in Iowa’s 1st District, talks with American Cancer Society volunteers and staff at Sidekick Coffee & Books on Aug. 14, 2026 in Iowa City. (Photo by Erin Jordan for Iowa Capital Dispatch)
IOWA CITY – Morgan Newman was a 24-year-old dental assistant when she was diagnosed with cervical cancer, a disease that is more common in women ages 35-64. 
“I had a metastatic recurrence to my lungs,” Newman, of Norwalk, said as she sat by her mom, Kendra, at an event Friday at Sidekick Coffee & Books in Iowa City. “She sat by my side and watched me go through everything I did.” 
Ten years later, Newman is cancer free. But her battle led her to the American Cancer Society, where she now is the Iowa grassroots manager. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Newman and six others talked Friday with Christina Bohannan, an Iowa City Democrat running for Iowa’s 1st Congressional District. The ACS’s Cancer Action Network is asking Iowa candidates for Congress and governor to state their commitment to fighting cancer, a disease that an estimated 2 million Americans will be diagnosed with this year. 
Iowa has the fastest-rising cancer rate in the nation and the state is second, behind Kentucky, in the number of incidences of cancer. The Iowa Cancer Registry expects 21,700 new invasive cancers will be diagnosed this year and 6,400 more Iowans will die from the disease. 
“One of the things that is really alarming to me is not only the number of people I talk with who have cancer, but the number of young people,” Bohannan said. “The age that people are starting to get diagnosed is younger in a way we didn’t hear about in the past.” 
People under 50 are increasingly being diagnosed with some cancers, including colorectal, breast, prostate, uterine and pancreatic cancer, the American Cancer Society reported in 2025. The chances of young people dying from cancer have declined, but the anxiety and expense of fighting the disease take a toll on millions of American families. 
Bohannan, 55, felt some of that anxiety after a recent health screening, she told the group.  
“Recently, I had an abnormal mammogram and it was very, very scary to me,” she said.  
Cancer funding
Bogdan Buzdugan, 23, a cancer researcher at the University of Iowa, said he chose his career path after a friend was diagnosed with glioblastoma, a type of cancerous brain tumor. He wanted to know if Bohannan would support annual increases for cancer research funding to the National Institutes of Health. 
“That is absolutely something we need to support and increase,” Bohannan said. 
Bohannan criticized her opponent, incumbent Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, a Republican from Ottumwa, for voting last year for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which slashed spending on healthcare and is predicted to result in 15 million more people not having health insurance coverage by 2034, according to the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. 
The biggest change under the bill is a requirement that most Medicaid recipients spend at least 80 hours a month working, volunteering or going to school in order to keep their coverage.
Miller-Meeks, an ophthalmologist, recently supported reauthorizing early breast cancer screening. ACS-CAN said it is “in discussions” with Miller-Meeks’ campaign about scheduling her for a similar forum.
Bohannan, whose father died from emphysema after many years of smoking, said she would support continued funding for smoking-cessation programs and oppose efforts to reduce government regulation of tobacco. 
Lung cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer deaths in Iowa. 
“Many people start (using tobacco products) young before they really know the risks and then they get addicted,” Bohannan said. “That’s something I really want to work on.”
Loss of rural health care options
In her travels across Iowa’s 1st District, which covers the southeastern quadrant of the state, Bohannan said she’s heard about Iowans having to drive an hour or more for doctor appointments because some rural hospitals have closed. 
MercyOne closed its health care center in Ottumwa in January and the Southeast Iowa Regional Medical Center in Fort Madison ended birthing and delivery services last December. 
Rural residents also are underrepresented in cancer research trials, Bohannan said. 
“I want to make sure our rural residents are included in some of those studies because there are some issues that affect rural areas sometimes more than other areas,” she said. 
Agricultural risks
Because cancer risk is a mix of genetics, lifestyle and environmental factors, it’s hard to pinpoint exactly why rates are rising in Iowa. But agricultural chemicals have been under increased scrutiny, especially as cities struggle to remove nitrate from public drinking water.
Bohannan said she would like to make more federal money available to incentivize farmers to implement conservation practices, like growing cover crops, that reduce fertilizer runoff. She does not want to tie federal crop insurance to farming practices. 
“We need to keep crop insurance for what it was intended for, which is to make sure that there’s a little bit of a fallback there if things go wrong,” she said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi faith leaders denounce Ag Commissioner Andy Gipson’s comments about Muslims, Sharia
description: Rev. Andy Andrews, of St. Christopher's Church, speaks during a press conference concerning Agriculture Commissioner Andy Gipson’s comments about Islam and Sharia law at the International Museum of Muslim Culture in Jackson on Friday, Aug. 14, 2026.
text:
Mississippi faith leaders on Friday denounced recent comments about Muslims made by state Agriculture Commissioner Andy Gipson, a gubernatorial candidate in next year’s elections.
“This reckless and dangerous rhetoric by an elected official and a candidate for governor has no place in our public discourse,” said Rhoda Yoder of Open Door Mennonite Church, on behalf of Working Together Jackson and Working Together Mississippi, two groups that organized the event. 
The groups invited Gipson to meet with them for “an open and honest dialogue.”
The recent appointment of attorney Assma Ali as municipal judge by the small Mississippi Delta town of Benoit drew social media backlash from internet trolls and a few Mississippi politicians, and even reportedly some threats, because she is Muslim. Her appointment prompted Republican Gipson, a former longtime state lawmaker, to renew his vows to ban “Sharia law and the influence of Islam” if he’s elected governor, even though use of Sharia law in Mississippi courts was already banned by the Legislature in 2015 when Gipson was a lawmaker. 
Leaders from several faith communities gathered at the International Museum of Muslim Culture in downtown Jackson on Friday in response to a social media post Gipson made about the museum and invited Gipson to meet with them.
Gipson has made several social media posts about Islam and Sharia law in recent days, including: “If you are among those who think Sharia law is ‘not an issue in Mississippi,’ you’d better think again. You see what’s happening in Dearborn, Michigan. But did you know that in our own capital city, in Mississippi, there is a center for Muslim Culture at the Planetarium in Jackson?”
The organizations said that one commenter on Gipson’s post called for the museum to be burned down. They said they have historically felt safe in Mississippi but that this has prompted them to take extra security precautions.
Many people and groups have criticized comments by Gipson and others and have come out in support of Ali, saying the U.S. native is a qualified and upstanding member of Mississippi’s legal community. Ali has vowed to uphold the U.S. Constitution and Mississippi law in her role as a city judge, mainly handling traffic violations, misdemeanors and other minor legal issues.
This week, Benoit officials defended Ali and their decision to appoint her as city judge.
“Religion is not listed as a qualification for service as a Municipal Court Judge in the State of Mississippi. Being Muslim is not a lawful basis for denying or terminating the appointment,” the mayor and board wrote, “We are pleased to have her.”
The groups that held the Friday event are nonpartisan civic engagement organizations made of nonprofits, churches and other religious institutions from across Jackson and the state. 
Members of Working Together Jackson and Working Together Mississippi join in prayer during a press conference concerning Agriculture Commissioner Andy Gipson’s comments about Islam and Sharia law at the International Museum of Muslim Culture in Jackson on Friday, Aug. 14, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
In a social media post, Gipson said that on day one if he’s elected governor he would ban Sharia law and Islam’s influence in Mississippi. But the Mississippi Legislature already banned Sharia law in 2015, when Gipson was a member of the state House. He voted in favor of the law that outlaws enforcement of any “foreign law” in Mississippi, which at the time was billed as being an anti-Sharia law measure.
“Sharia law, it’s like the law of Moses. Like the Ten Commandments. It’s just about the laws that govern a just, upright community of people,” said Okolo Rashid, one of the museum’s founders.
In a post, Gipson also included a photo of the museum, which says that it is America’s first Muslim museum, that featured Rashid at an exhibit on the shared heritage of Muslims, Christians and Jews. The museum opened in 2001 and is dedicated to educating the American public on Islamic history, art, and culture.
Members of Working Together Jackson and Working Together Mississippi gather for a press conference concerning Agriculture Commissioner Andy Gipson’s comments about Islam and Sharia law at the International Museum of Muslim Culture in Jackson on Friday, Aug. 14, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“I want to invite Commissoner Gipson to come sit down with us so we can share with him what the museum has to offer,” Rashid said.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Supreme Court shuts door on appeal to use police misconduct findings in murder defense
description:
“The decision to send an ill-equipped, untrained officer into an ongoing chase was a decision that cost her life,” a defense attorney said of law enforcement actions in a deadly pursuit. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Supreme Court shuts door on appeal to use police misconduct findings in murder defense.
text:
The Vermont Supreme Court in Montpelier on Tuesday, June 30, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
The Vermont Supreme Court has dealt a legal setback to the defense team of the driver charged with murder in a police chase that killed a Rutland City officer more than three years ago.
The state’s highest court in a ruling this week denied a bid by attorneys for 23-year-old Tate Rheaume to challenge a Rutland judge’s decision blocking the introduction at trial of a damning internal affairs report that found officer misconduct in the pursuit.
Rheaume’s lawyers had asked to appeal that decision by Rutland Superior Court Judge Cortland Corsones. The judge denied the request, and Rheaume’s attorneys then asked the Supreme Court for permission to appeal. 
The high court, in a unanimous decision, stated it would not grant the appeal request, meaning Corsones’ decision will stand.
The lower court, the ruling stated, “acted within its discretion in denying permission to appeal.”
The Vermont Supreme Court decision is a blow for Rheaume’s defense. He faces several charges, including aggravated murder, in the July 2023 pursuit that led to the death of 19-year-old Jessica Ebbighausen, a Rutland City police trainee.
A great deal of legal wrangling in the case has focused on an internal affairs report, which became public last year. 

READ MORE

That report strongly criticized officers’ actions leading up to and during the chase, finding that officers had committed several policy violations. Those policy violations, according to the report, included conducting a pursuit for something other than a violent felony and not seeking authorization to continue a pursuit.
Then-Rutland City Police Commander Sam Delpha, the author of the internal affairs report, wrote in his conclusion, “The death of Officer Ebbighausen WAS preventable.” Delpha has since retired from the department.
Rheaume, according to charging documents, was allegedly fleeing from authorities after reports that he was inside the home of a former partner in Rutland on July 7, 2023.
Rheaume’s lawyers had sought to introduce testimony regarding the internal affairs report at trial, contending that it was important for jurors to consider officers’ conduct.
However, Corsones rejected that attempt.
“Under these circumstances,” Corsones wrote in the ruling, “any violations by the involved officers of the internal departmental pursuit policy could not be found to be an efficient, intervening cause breaking the chain of causation of the defendant’s actions, in the criminal context.”
David Sleigh, an attorney for Rheaume, said Friday he was disappointed with the Vermont Supreme Court’s decision.
“It seemed to us that the decision to send an ill-equipped, untrained officer into an ongoing chase was a decision that cost her life,” Sleigh said.
“It’s our view that the jury should be able to consider that argument,” he added, “but apparently the view of the Vermont court is that they can’t. That is disappointing to say the least.” 
Rutland County State’s Attorney Ian Sullivan declined to comment Friday.
No trial date has been set. The next hearing in the case is set for Oct. 5. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Supreme Court shuts door on appeal to use police misconduct findings in murder defense.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa nursing home chain faces second lawsuit alleging unpaid bills
description: One of Iowa’s largest nursing home chains is facing new lawsuits alleging nonpayment of bills and wrongful death. Gibbins Advisors, a financial consulting firm based in Tennessee, is suing Accura Healthcare, an Oklahoma company that operates 27 senior-care facilities within Iowa, in Polk County District Court. It is one of two pending lawsuits against Accura[...]
text:
(Photo by David Talukdar/Getty Images)One of Iowa’s largest nursing home chains is facing new lawsuits alleging nonpayment of bills and wrongful death.
Gibbins Advisors, a financial consulting firm based in Tennessee, is suing Accura Healthcare, an Oklahoma company that operates 27 senior-care facilities within Iowa, in Polk County District Court.
It is one of two pending lawsuits against Accura alleging nonpayment of bills. Earlier this week, two of Accura’s former landlords, sued a group of six Iowa nursing homes operated by Accura in federal court, alleging they owe more than $2.1 million in back rent.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As part of that case, Summit Healthcare Operating Partnership and Fantasia Investment allege they are owed a portion of the overall debt — from 8.5% to 10% — that’s consistent with their stake in the group that owns the six Accura facilities.
Accura Healthcare has said it does not respond to the specifics of pending litigation, but says its highest priority is providing “continuous, high-quality care to our residents and fully supporting our dedicated care teams across every community we serve.” The company did not offer a comment Friday regarding the new lawsuits.
The lawsuit filed by Gibbins Advisors alleges that in June 2024, it entered into an agreement with Accura to provide financial and restructuring consulting services, with day-to-day direction provided by Accura’s CEO, Ted LeNeave. Under the contract, Gibbins alleges, it was to provide Accura with assistance in managing cash flow, evaluating any financial restructuring options, and negotiating with Accura’s lenders, landlords and vendors.
As part of that arrangement, the lawsuit asserts, Accura paid a $15,000 retainer to be credited against Gibbins’ billings, which eventually totaled $113,413.
According to the lawsuit, Accura still owes Gibbins $46,546, but has rejected repeated demands for payment. The lawsuit seeks a court judgment against Accura in that amount, plus interest and attorneys’ fees.
In response, Accura has denied any wrongdoing and filed a counterclaim alleging Gibbins employed “unqualified personnel” to work on matters and also failed to provide proper oversight and verification of the work being performed under the contract.
A trial-setting conference in the case is scheduled for Sept. 14, 2026.
New wrongful death lawsuit
Accura is also facing a newly filed wrongful death lawsuit brought by the estate of the late Marcus Leonard, a former resident of the Accura of Cascade nursing home in northeast Iowa.
The lawsuit, filed in July, alleges that on June 27, 2025, Leonard, then 92, was dropped face-first from a mechanical lift while the Accura of Cascade staff transferred him in or out of a bed or chair.  Leonard allegedly suffered facial trauma, head lacerations and broken teeth. The home’s on-call physician was “not notified until a significant period of time after the fall,” the lawsuit alleges.
The home’s initial response to the incident was limited to over-the-counter analgesics delivered on an as-needed basis, the lawsuit claims, and hospice workers had to intervene to obtain adequate pain medication.
Leonard “endured days of conscious pain,” according to the lawsuit, and died on July 4, 2025. The manner of his death was certified as an accident resulting from the fall from the lift, the lawsuit alleges.
During a state inspection after the incident, Accura of Cascade was cited for failing to train its staff on how to properly size the slings that are used in the mechanical lifts, although no fines or penalties were imposed. The lawsuit alleges the staff selected slings by personal preference from an “unsorted supply of mismatched, unlabeled slings that were used interchangeably.”
The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages for negligence, wrongful death and pre-death pain and suffering. In addition to Accura Healthcare, the lawsuit names as defendants Accura of Cascade’s former administrator, Rachel Finn, and former director of nursing, Juanita Bielenberg. Also named as defendants are the unidentified caregivers who handled Leonard’s transfer in the mechanical lift.
The defendants have yet to file a response to the lawsuit.
Previous lawsuit also alleged improper use of lift
In July 2025, the family of Kenneth Willson sued Accura and Shell Rock Senior Living, alleging that on Feb. 19, 2024, the facility staff improperly used a mechanical lift to transfer Willson, causing him to fall to the floor, striking his head.
Willson allegedly sustained a broken leg and head injury in the fall. His family’s lawsuit alleging negligence and dependent adult abuse was stayed after Accura argued Willson’s wife had signed an arbitration agreement stipulating that any claims against the company would be heard by an arbitrator rather than in a court of law.
Court records indicate that in late July, the parties were scheduled to meet with a mediator before proceeding to arbitration.

title: Proceeds from Idaho Women Veterans Medallion to benefit Boise, Blackfoot state veterans cemeteries
description: More than $47,000 in proceeds from the sale of the Idaho Women Veterans Medallion will go toward maintenance and operations of two state veteran cemeteries. A $47,675 check was presented by Idaho State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth to the Idaho State Veterans Cemeteries this week. The funds will be used at the state’s Boise and Blackfoot […]
text:
Idaho State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth, third from left, presents a $47,675 check to the Idaho State Veterans Cemeteries. Proceeds from the sale of the Idaho Women Veterans Medallion will help cover the cost of maintenance and operations at the Blackfoot and Boise state veterans cemeteries. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho State Treasurer's Office)More than $47,000 in proceeds from the sale of the Idaho Women Veterans Medallion will go toward maintenance and operations of two state veteran cemeteries.
A $47,675 check was presented by Idaho State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth to the Idaho State Veterans Cemeteries this week. The funds will be used at the state’s Boise and Blackfoot sites for the “continued care of these places of honor for Idaho veterans and their families,” according to a Wednesday press release from the treasurer’s office.
U.S. Small Business Administration ‘actively working’ to create veterans resource center in Idaho

“As we celebrate America’s 250th birthday this year, we recognize that our veterans have made extraordinary sacrifices to protect the freedoms we enjoy today,” Ellsworth said in the press release. “I am proud that the proceeds from these medallions are helping care for Idaho’s State Veterans Cemeteries and ensuring these sacred places remain a fitting tribute to those who served.”
Since its minting, sales of the medallion have generated over $112,000 for state veterans cemeteries, the press release said. Only 29 medallions remain available for sale, according to the release.
The commemorative silver medallion, released in 2020, honors Idaho’s female veterans during the 100th anniversary of women’s suffrage.
The medallion, which features the motto “Courageous Past, Unlimited Future,” highlights five Idaho women veterans who represent the thousands of Idaho women who have served in the U.S. military. Four stars on the medallion symbolize Idaho’s place as the fourth state to grant women the right to vote — the first to do so by constitutional amendment. The reverse features Idaho’s state seal, designed by Emma Edwards Green.
“It was an honor to represent the incredible women veterans who served during the Vietnam era. This medallion belongs to all women veterans from all branches,” said Judith Eighmy, one of the five Idaho women featured on the medallion, in the press release.
 State Veterans Cemetery Bureau Chief Jake Faulkner said he is grateful to the public for supporting the sale of the medallions.
“The medallion is a lasting tribute to Idaho’s women veterans, and its proceeds are now helping care for the resting places of veterans across our state,” Faulkner said in the press release. “As we celebrate America’s 250th birthday, we are especially grateful for those who have served and sacrificed for our freedoms. We are proud to put these funds to work honoring their service and preserving these sacred spaces for generations to come.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA state House candidate accused of refusing breathalyzer, charged with DUI
description: Authorities charged a Washington state House candidate Thursday with impaired driving that resulted in a five-car crash in Tacoma earlier in the week.  Krista Perez, 40, is accused of driving her pickup truck into a parked car, causing a chain reaction that left three other cars damaged in the 3700 block of South G Street […]
text:
Democratic state House candidate Krista Perez has been charged with impaired driving after a five-car crash in Tacoma. (Photo courtesy of the Krista Perez campaign)Authorities charged a Washington state House candidate Thursday with impaired driving that resulted in a five-car crash in Tacoma earlier in the week. 
Krista Perez, 40, is accused of driving her pickup truck into a parked car, causing a chain reaction that left three other cars damaged in the 3700 block of South G Street in Tacoma near Lincoln High School, according to charging papers filed in Tacoma Municipal Court. She later failed to give an adequate breathalyzer sample, police say.
She was scheduled to be arraigned on the driving under the influence charge Monday afternoon, according to her attorney.
Perez, a Democrat, is in the middle of an election campaign that could see her unseat Rep. Melanie Morgan, D-Parkland. She led Morgan in the primary by about two percentage points, running to the incumbent’s left, with heavy support from organized labor. Her campaign in the 29th Legislative District is one of several tests across Washington of whether a progressive challenger can unseat a more moderate Democrat.
Perez’s defense attorney, Bryan G. Hershman, said Friday that he hopes “we can stay focused on an important campaign.” 
“We’re talking about a DUI,” he said. “It’s not like we’re talking about felony murder here.”
“No matter what happens in this DUI case, there’s still homeless people we need to get off the streets,” Hershman added. “I hope we can stay focused on what’s relevant.”
Hershman said just after noon Friday that he hadn’t yet read the charges filed by the Tacoma city attorney’s office. 
Perez hasn’t responded to direct requests for comment. Morgan couldn’t be reached either.
After the crash Tuesday, an officer noted Perez smelled of alcohol and appeared confused, according to the court documents. She confirmed she was driving, but reported she didn’t know what had happened. Her Chevy Silverado was nearly on top of another car and her driver’s airbag had been deployed. 
Perez told investigators she’d had a glass of wine at a local winery, according to court papers. When they asked how much, the papers said she told them to ask winery staff and appeared offended by the question. She reportedly rated her level of intoxication at a four on a scale of one to 10. She also seemed offended at an officer asking if she believed her drinking had contributed to the crash, according to police. 
An officer asked her to perform field sobriety tests to see how impaired she was, the court documents say. She repeatedly told authorities she didn’t understand, according to the charges. Perez said she wanted to go home before taking the tests, but officers told her that wasn’t an option. She eventually declined to participate in the sobriety tests, police said.
Due to Perez’s odor of alcohol, noticeable mood swings, slurred speech, red eyes and unsteady gait, Tacoma police arrested her, according to the police report. 
At Tacoma police headquarters, she reportedly agreed to provide breath samples after speaking with her attorney. 
But despite several attempts to explain to Perez how to use a breathalyzer, she failed to give a breath sample, according to police. She reportedly tucked her lips in and pulled away from the mouthpiece, resulting in weak breaths that were insufficient. Police labeled her as refusing a breathalyzer test.
If convicted, her sentence could be worsened because of her alleged refusal to take a breath test.
She was booked into Pierce County jail, where she spent six hours before being released.
Perez works for the state as a strategic partnerships manager for the Department of Commerce. She mounted a failed bid for Tacoma City Council last year.
She has repeatedly attacked Morgan, her campaign opponent, for her vote against the state’s income tax on high earners that the Legislature passed earlier this year. She’s backed by several powerful statewide unions, including the Service Employees International Union, Washington Federation of State Employees and Washington Education Association.
The 29th District represents most of south and east Tacoma, Parkland, Spanaway and parts of Lakewood. Morgan has been in office since 2019.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Higher education commissioner stepping down in September
authors: Sam Drysdale | State House News Service
description: Ortega's departure will further shift the state's education leadership, following turnover within the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education and Education Secretary Patrick Tutwiler stepping down earlier this year.
text:
MASSACHUSETTS HIGHER EDUCATION COMMISSIONER Noe Ortega will step down this September, after about four years on the job.
Ortega’s departure will further shift the state’s education leadership, following turnover within the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education and Education Secretary Patrick Tutwiler stepping down earlier this year. Tutwiler was replaced by new Secretary Stephen Zrike Jr., and Commissioner Pedro Martinez began leading DESE last July. 
The Board of Higher Education will meet later this month to consider an interim commissioner, and start the process to secure a permanent replacement for Ortega. 
Ortega is stepping down so “he and his wife can be closer to aging family members,” the Department of Higher Education said.
During his time as commissioner, the state gave approval for the first three-year bachelor degree programs in Massachusetts. Education officials have touted the option as a new strategy to boost affordability for students through limited programs offered by specific universities creating a sub-120 credit “applied” bachelor’s degree. 
Ortega has also overseen a major expansion of early college. The push to give more high school students the chance to take free college classes has been a combined effort of DHE and DESE, funded in large part by the income surtax on high-earners. Gov. Maura Healey has set a goal of having 100,000, or about 40 percent of all high schoolers, participating in early college by 2036. The state expanded the program by 1,692 seats to more than 12,000 high school students this upcoming fall. 
Other major changes in higher education during Ortega’s tenure — including free community college and major financial aid expansions — are also funded by the surtax, which was approved by voters in the same month he took the commissioner job. 
Following these efforts to make higher education more affordable, public higher education enrollment returned to pre-pandemic levels, driven by  community college enrollment growth, which increased 38.5 percent between fall 2022 and fall 2025.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Preliminary 2027 forecast for Alaska’s Bristol Bay fishery predicts more, smaller sockeye
description: With the 2026 commercial salmon harvests winding down in Alaska, the seafood industry is already calculating how to navigate at a profit in 2027, given dynamic biological, economic, climate and market conditions. Their forecast has a far-reaching socio-economic impact across the state — Bristol Bay’s commercial fishery had about $2 billion in economic impact[...]
text:
A spawning male sockeye salmon is seen in July 2010 in the Wood River, part of the Bristol Bay watershed. Bristol Bay is the site of the world's largest sockeye salmon runs. (Photo by Thomas Quinn/University of Washington, provided by the Environmental Protection Agency)With the 2026 commercial salmon harvests winding down in Alaska, the seafood industry is already calculating how to navigate at a profit in 2027, given dynamic biological, economic, climate and market conditions.
Their forecast has a far-reaching socio-economic impact across the state — Bristol Bay’s commercial fishery had about $2 billion in economic impact and supported 15,000 jobs in 2019 according to research from the McKinley Research Group. 
Preliminary forecasts from the University of Washington for the celebrated Bristol Bay wild sockeye fishery are looking at a run of 45 million fish next year, up from the 2026 forecast of 41.5 million. But run size is just one of many factors under consideration.
Fish size is one of those factors: 45 million big fish have more meat — and a bigger economic effect — than 45 million smaller fish. The size of the fish also helps determine which products the processors will produce.
“When we get really big returns the fish are smaller for their age, because they are competing for their food,” said salmon researcher Daniel Schindler of the University of Washington School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences. “We estimate how many fish of each age class are coming back.” 
For 2027 that preliminary estimate is 20 million fish that have spent three years in the ocean — known as three ocean fish — and 30 million fish that have spent two years in the ocean in 2027. Because there are more fish that have spent less time in the ocean, the overall catch will be smaller.
But the climate can affect how much of that forecast becomes a reality.
“The climate factor is baked into the number of fish we see,” Schindler said.  “The fish tell us how well they survived, so if it was a bad climate year we see it early in the numbers of young fish.”
The University of Washington and Alaska Department of Fish & Game both compile data on the Bristol Bay fishery. ADF&G compiles data on Bristol Bay using counting towers. Researchers at the University of Washington go to the spawning grounds and count the fish there. The two methods help inform a more accurate forecast.
The industry would like to increase the amount of domestically-caught fish that Americans consume. According to NOAA Fisheries, the national average consumption of domestically-caught seafood remains relatively flat at 19 pounds per person, with 80% of that seafood coming from foreign imports.  
An ongoing campaign of the Alaska Seafood Marketing Institute focuses on boosting retail consumption of the Alaska catch, including an abundance of salmon, with an eye to how the economy, climate and marketing conditions are evolving. Planning for domestic and overseas markets for the coming year gets underway annually on July 1, with a concentration on harvest information, consumer trends and preferences and numerous other factors, said Greg Smith, communications director for ASMI. 
Smith said the organization’s emphasis is on the wild-caught harvest, the people who catch and process the harvest and the health,nutrition and sustainability of well managed fisheries. ASMI focuses on helping consumers overcome barriers to seafood purchases such as a lack of confidence in preparing seafood, uncertainty on sourcing and sustainability of fisheries, cost of product and convenience, he said. ASMI also focuses on ensuring younger generations become strong seafood consumers.
Harvest forecasts for Alaska’s 2026 salmon fisheries of 125.5 million fish were about 36% lower than a year earlier, resulting in prices per pound in retail shops being higher overall than in 2025. But with fewer fish for sale fewer are likely to be left in inventory for 2027, said fisheries economist Gunner Knapp. Such conditions could keep prices stable in the coming season.  
Long term growth in seafood production is dependent on consumer demand as well as selling fish in product forms that meet consumer demand. Both are important, Knapp said.
As of late July average prices of wild Alaska salmon fillets in the Anchorage area were $13.99 to $26.99 a pound, with sockeye and coho on the lower end and king salmon on the higher end. At Seattle’s Pike Place Fish Market the price of fresh wild Alaska sockeye fillets was holding steady at $29.99 a pound.
The bulk of seafood produced in the U.S. is consumed internationally, so the industry continues to turn its eyes to home — but there is competition from low prices from foreign markets. That fish may not be sustainably sourced with ethical labor practices. “U.S. domestic markets are increasingly important, so in many parts of the U.S. at higher end retail outlets you can find wild Alaska sockeye salmon for sale,” he said.
Knapp characterizes commercial fisheries as a risky business.
“Lots of opportunity and lots of risk, but the resources are so big and so valuable that there will always be a seafood industry in Alaska,” he said. “Only aquaculture has potential to grow.”
Aquaculture is when the fish are not wild caught but cultivated or raised in hatcheries.
“The reason I’ve observed so much more innovation in aquaculture than in wild stocks is that aquaculture is far more able to take advantage of technological innovation than wild fisheries because aquaculture has so much greater control of production,” Knapp said.
“Still because wild fisheries are much older they have stronger cultural traditions, with more dependent communities less receptive to innovation, although they may have more political power,” he said.
Meanwhile, NOAA Fisheries is working to calculate many climate factors affecting the state’s commercial fisheries, from winds and ocean currents to ocean temperatures and precipitation. For salmon, the varying and changing climate impacts winter snowpack, ice cover, growing season lengths and streamflow, said Nate Mantua, a physical scientist at NOAA’s Southwest Fisheries Science Center in La Jolla, California.
“Right now there is a great deal of media attention on the developing El Nino event in the tropical Pacific,” Mantua said. “This is likely to impact Alaska’s winter and spring climate in 2027.” 
El Nino is a climate pattern defined by unusually warming of surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, weakening trade winds and global weather disruptions.  
The current forecast for Alaska’s winter includes increased odds for a warmer than average winter, and increased odds for above average precipitation in Southcentral Alaska and below average precipitation around Norton Sound.
“Another large factor in seasonal forecasts relates back to climate change and the fact that most every winter in the past decade has been warmer than winters before the 2000s,” Mantua said.
“Our ability to predict future climate is limited to about one year in advance and NOAA has an operational forecasting effort provided by the Climate Prediction Center.” 
The rise in greenhouse gas concentrations have caused ocean warming and increased acidification, which is bad for salmon.
University of Washington fisheries researchers have started producing a preliminary report to come out  the third week of August on the 2027 salmon fishery. Its formal preseason river by river forecast will come out in November, after ADF&G finishes collating its data on a river by river forecast.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia officials say new federal Medicaid rules threaten state’s partial expansion program
description: Georgia health officials are asking the Trump administration for more funding for the state’s partial Medicaid expansion program because they say federal changes are expected to increase enrollment by about 100,000 people, raising the costs of the program. The Board of Community Health, which oversees Georgia’s Medicaid program, announced at its Thursday mee[...]
text:
New federal guidelines would make the state’s Medicaid program financially unsustainable, state health officials said at the Board of Community Health meeting in August. the_burtons/Getty ImagesGeorgia health officials are asking the Trump administration for more funding for the state’s partial Medicaid expansion program because they say federal changes are expected to increase enrollment by about 100,000 people, raising the costs of the program.
The Board of Community Health, which oversees Georgia’s Medicaid program, announced at its Thursday meeting that they are once again asking the federal government to increase the federal match from about 67% to 90%, which is what states that have fully expanded Medicaid receive for providing coverage to a larger population. 
The state argued both at the meeting and in its public notice that new federal guidelines for Medicaid eligibility that were included in President Donald Trump’s tax break and spending cuts package that passed last year would make the state’s Medicaid program financially unsustainable. The new federal Medicaid rules take effect next year. 
“The federal government fundamentally reshaped the operational and financial realities of George’s waiver,” Stuart Portman, executive director of the division of medical assistance plans at the Georgia Department of Community Health, said at Thursday’s meeting. “Therefore, we ask that the federal government also provide the enhanced match necessary to make that expansion viable.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Georgia’s current partial Medicaid expansion program, called Pathways to Coverage, requires low-income adults who earn up to 100% of the federal poverty level – or about $15,960 for a single adult – to complete 80 hours of qualifying activity per month, which includes work, school or community service. The current Pathways program doesn’t provide exceptions to the work requirement unless the person is a parent who is a caregiver of a child under the age of 6.
Under the new federal guidelines, Georgia will now provide more exemptions to its work requirements, such as for parents of children under 13 years old, those who were formerly in foster care and those who are considered medically frail. 
Because these exemptions are expected to increase the number of Medicaid enrollees by about 100,000 people, according to the Department of Community Health’s projections, state officials argued in the public notice that “Georgia does not have the financial capacity to fund this expanded scope without additional federal dollars.”
“In turn, the long-term viability of the program serving as the foundation of the community engagement requirements … will be threatened and the state will have no alternative but to make decisions that imperil health policy goals around personal responsibility and healthy choices,” according to the public notice.
The current state’s program was temporarily extended last year until the end of 2026 while a request to continue Pathways through 2030 is still pending.
While the 90% federal match mirrors what is offered to states who fully expand Medicaid, a spokesperson for Gov. Brian Kemp’s administration, Annalise Morning, said “the waiver modification is NOT a Medicaid expansion for Georgia.” 
“Rather, it would preserve the long-term sustainability of Georgia Pathways as a valuable resource for beneficiaries,” Morning said in a statement.
When Georgia Pathways launched in 2023, it made Georgia the only state to require work or the equivalent for its newly covered Medicaid enrollees. The program, which is Kemp’s signature healthcare policy, covers about 20,000 “hard-working Georgians,” according to the public notice. 
Georgia already tried to receive the enhanced 90% match in 2019 under the first Trump administration without fully expanding Medicaid, but the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services at the time said that the enhanced match is provided for states that provide coverage for the income levels up to 138% of the federal poverty line – or about $22,025 for a single adult. 
“Georgia already tried this tactic in 2019 under the Trump administration, and it failed,” said Leah Chan, director of health justice at the left-leaning Georgia Budget and Policy Institute. “But I think what we do know is that the temporary federal approval for Pathways expires in December. So rather than wasting our time pursuing dead ends, we could simply just raise the Pathways income eligibility limit from 100% to 138% of the federal poverty level and pull down the enhanced 90% match authorized under the Affordable Care Act.” 
Georgia is one of 10 states that have not fully expanded Medicaid. Changing course now would require legislative approval and a signature from the governor.
To Whitney Griggs, director of health policy at Georgians for a Healthy Future, a patient advocacy organization that supports full Medicaid expansion, it seems like the state is doubling down on its Pathways program.
“What I’m getting from this is: ‘We’d like to continue Pathways as is,’” Griggs said.
Natalie Crawford, executive director of Georgia First, a bipartisan advocacy group, questioned whether the strategy is the most fiscally responsible in the long-term and whether full Medicaid expansion that “maximizes available federal dollars, further reduces the number of uninsured Georgians and better strengthens our healthcare system” would better serve Georgia.
“Our people are our greatest resource, and healthier Georgians mean a healthier economy,” Crawford said.
Members of the public can comment on the proposed waiver changes through written comments that can be submitted through Sept. 14. There will be a virtual public hearing on Aug. 19 at 11 a.m. and an in-person public hearing at the Department of Community Health’s board room at 12:30 p.m. on Aug. 24.

title: Nearly 1.5 million Floridians have voted in advance of Tuesday’s primary elections
description: As of 2 p.m. Friday, more than 1.47 million Floridians had cast ballots, either at an early voting location or by mail, for the primary elections. More than 950,000 vote-by-mail ballots were yet to be returned, a decrease of about 50,000 the same hour Thursday. Of the 1.47 million votes cast, 665,003 were from Republican […]
text:
A sign directs voters to the polls. (Maya Smith for Kansas Reflector)As of 2 p.m. Friday, more than 1.47 million Floridians had cast ballots, either at an early voting location or by mail, for the primary elections.
More than 950,000 vote-by-mail ballots were yet to be returned, a decrease of about 50,000 the same hour Thursday.
Of the 1.47 million votes cast, 665,003 were from Republican voters. In comparison, 611,882 votes were cast by registered Democrats. Another 172,268 were cast by no party affiliation voters. 
Among outstanding vote-by-mail ballots, Democrats had about 100,000 more, 401,250, to the Republicans’ 302,317. 
As of 8 a.m. Friday, Miami-Dade and Pinellas counties each had more than 100,000 vote-by-mail ballots not yet returned. Palm Beach and Hillsborough had the next highest number of outstanding vote-by-mail ballots with 71,695 and 69,563, respectively.
As of July 31, there were 13.49 million registered voters in Florida. That means as of 2 p.m. Friday, about 10.5% of them had cast a vote. According to the state, in the 2022 primary election 26% of voters turned out. 
That’s significantly lower than presidential cycles, for example, when in 2024 nearly 79% of registered voters turned out. 
Voting ends Tuesday and polls close at 7 p.m. local time. Early voting ends in some counties Saturday. In other counties, it ends Sunday. Check a county’s supervisor of elections’ website for specific information. 
The Florida Phoenix lists voter precincts at the bottom of all of its webpages.

title: Q&A: Thune says Republicans can hold their majority — if they stop fighting each other
description: SIOUX FALLS — U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune’s Republican Party faces midterm elections amid economic anxiety, high gas prices and a war with Iran.  But Thune, of South Dakota, said the biggest threat to the party’s Senate majority might be Republicans themselves. Thune told South Dakota Searchlight and other journalists Friday during an event […]
text:
U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota, left, speaks with attendees including South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden, right, during a groundbreaking on Aug. 14, 2026, for a construction project at Southeast Technical College in Sioux Falls. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)SIOUX FALLS — U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune’s Republican Party faces midterm elections amid economic anxiety, high gas prices and a war with Iran. 
But Thune, of South Dakota, said the biggest threat to the party’s Senate majority might be Republicans themselves.
Thune told South Dakota Searchlight and other journalists Friday during an event at Southeast Technical College that Republicans need to “turn our fire on Democrats, not on each other.”
Thune has been under fire from Republican President Donald Trump for not eliminating the filibuster, the Senate rule that requires the votes of at least 60 senators to end debate. Trump has repeatedly demanded the termination of the filibuster to help pass his SAVE America Act, which would require proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote and a photo ID when casting a ballot.
Republicans hold 53 of the seats in the Senate, and there are 33 seats up for election on Nov. 3. Thune doesn’t face reelection until 2028.
The following question-and-answer session between Thune and several reporters has been edited for length and clarity.
Q: How much is the war with Iran making your job harder?
It’s complicated on a lot of levels and certainly going into an election year with the politics around that. If you look at the things that have been achieved, there have been some great accomplishments there, but ultimately the way people are going to judge this is: How is it affecting the economy, how is it affecting gas prices, is the Strait of Hormuz open?
I think that’s got to be the singular, clear-eyed focus of the White House administration right now — ensuring that we get the shipping lanes open and get the fuel moving again and ensure that our economy here in the U.S. is not suffering as a result of this.
Q: Do you get the sense there’ll be an improvement before the midterms?
I hope so. I think they continue to, or they are trending toward a deal on that to get the strait open. But these are really complicated issues and you’re dealing with a regime that’s dishonest and is not going to play by the rules that the rest of the world community plays by, so you’ve got to be tough. I think the president has leaned into this in ways that puts a lot of pressure on the regime, but the regime is not going to go quietly. I think there are challenges ahead, but I also feel like they’re on a path toward landing something that will at least get things moving again and hopefully lessen some of the pressure on fuel prices here. 
Q: Can the Republican Party maintain its majority in the midterm elections?
I think the headwinds that are there, can it improve? It can. Can it get worse? Maybe. We’re facing typical midterm election political headwinds and some economic headwinds, because people are concerned about the economy and costs and everything else, which they should be since those are pocketbook issues. That’s what most elections are really about. 
Trump urges Thune to hold off on August recess until SAVE America Act passes

I still think in spite of those headwinds, we’ve got really good candidates in the right places at the right time. You look at a state like Michigan, things really broke our way. Minnesota broke our way. The Democrats in both places nominated far-left candidates. We have candidates who are really, really accomplished people with a message I think is really going to resonate with voters in those states. Those are hard states, but we need to be on offense in a few places and we are in Michigan, as we’ll be in Minnesota, New Hampshire, Georgia.
We’re defending some ground too and the places where we’re defending there’s a firewall that if we don’t keep certain states, we’ll lose control of the Senate: Maine, Ohio, Iowa, Alaska — that’s the firewall of the Senate.
If we could win one of those races around the country, that obviously would be a huge success too, but it’s a tough year. These midterms always are. This one’s obviously complicated by some factors that we simply don’t control, but we’re doing everything we can within our control: recruiting a good crop of candidates, raising the resources that are necessary for them to get their messages out, and hopefully succeeding in the ground game, which is the “get out the vote” thing that you have to do come Election Day if you’re going to win elections. That’s harder, especially for low propensity voters who typically don’t vote in a non-presidential year. We’ve got to get a lot of those Trump voters out, so there’s a real effort being made. 
Q: Can you speak to your evolving relationship with President Trump and about him declining to say whether he supports you continuing as Senate majority leader because of your decisions in that role, including retaining the filibuster?
I take all of that with a grain of salt. There is a natural dynamic between any White House and the Senate. Most presidents, in my experience, don’t like the Senate and view it as an obstacle to getting the things they want to get done. But we obviously have a different way of doing things by design, which makes it harder sometimes. The House in a lot of ways is an extension of the White House. It’s a majoritarian body, while the Senate is a non-majoritarian body. It’s designed to give a voice to the minority in this country, so it’s harder to get things done because most things require a supermajority.
Those are the facts I have to live with, and I have very honest conversations with the president. He is entitled to his views about the things that we’re doing in the Senate. I would certainly expect that he has a way of doing things. He’s got a business model that’s full speed ahead, and I know that sometimes in the Senate, just by virtue of the reality on the ground that we have to deal with, we have to pump the brakes occasionally on that. And that’s not something that obviously he probably is good with, but nevertheless we get a lot done and if you look at the record of accomplishment, I think it’s second to none.

We can’t get everything done because it’s a function of votes. I tell people that the math is the math, and the math on the issue that he cares the most about right now isn’t going to change, at least not until after the election. Then we’ll see from there. We get along fine and work together, but if he wants somebody else in the job he’s welcome to that view.
Q: Do you worry that President Trump’s critical view of the body and fellow Republicans right now will be a hindrance ahead of the midterms?
What I’ve said, and I make this point quite regularly, is that we are less than 90 days away from an election. The election ought to be painting a contrast between us and the Democrats and not creating conflicts with fellow Republicans. 
I’ve tried to deliver that message in the work that we’re doing right now, the work we’re focused on keeping, protecting and preserving our majority in the Senate — maybe even expanding it if we could get a win in a state or two. But I am a clear-eyed realist about what we have to do, what’s in front of us and the best way for us to be successful, which is to have everybody pull in the same direction and turn our fire on Democrats, not on each other.
That’s a message I deliver regularly and it seems to be getting across at least on some level, but I think it’s in everybody’s best interest — if you want to have a Republican Senate majority after the election — is not to have us turning fire on each other, but drawing contrasts with Democrats, and there are plenty to draw.
If you want to have a debate about the future of this country, you can really do it because there is a clear division in my view between the two visions of where the parties are headed and where the candidates are headed. I mean, look at Michigan and Minnesota, look at some of these states where you’ve got these far-left, radical Democrats winning elections or winning primaries at least. I think that represents a great opportunity to contrast with them in the fall, and that’s where we ought to be focused.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: After nearly seven months in detention, Maine man granted permanent residency
description: After nearly seven months of being shuffled through detention facilities across three states, during which he faced health problems in unsanitary conditions, Bridgton resident Marcos Gaspar-Da Silva was granted lawful permanent residency and released from a facility in Arizona.  His wife, Alessia Gaspar-Da Silva, was his first call once he got out, sharing t[...]
text:
Portland resident Marcos Gaspar-Da Silva (left) reunited with his wife Alessia Gaspar-Da Silva after he was released from detention in Arizona on Aug. 13, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Elizabeth Lee)After nearly seven months of being shuffled through detention facilities across three states, during which he faced health problems in unsanitary conditions, Bridgton resident Marcos Gaspar-Da Silva was granted lawful permanent residency and released from a facility in Arizona. 
His wife, Alessia Gaspar-Da Silva, was his first call once he got out, sharing the news with her just as she was boarding her final flight to pick him up. He greeted her at the airport Thursday evening with flowers and carried her bags out, taking care of her after she spent months fighting for his release. 
“My mind was thinking, ‘This is a dream,’” he told Maine Morning Star. 
Federal immigration agents detained Marcos, an asylum seeker from Brazil, and another man who he was giving a ride to work on Jan. 20 in Portland, at the start of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s large-scale operation in the state. 
Marcos was on the phone with his wife at the time. She said she heard one of the agents say they were only looking for “extreme criminals” that had outstanding arrest warrants. Her husband responded that he had a pending asylum case and no warrants, she said, but the agents took him and the other man. 
During his months-long detention, he recounted the conditions to his wife, who explained that he was fed meals that resembled dog food and brown water that made him sick. She said he had by far the worst experience at the Arizona Removal Operations Coordination Center, which is supposed to be a short-term holding facility at Phoenix-Mesa Gateway Airport.
There, he was held with dozens of other people in a room with no beds and a toilet that would overflow, spreading fecal matter on the floor, which caused him to develop a rash, his wife said. She said authorities continuously tried to get Marcos to agree to leave the country voluntarily. It was in those conditions at the Mesa detention center where the other man agreed to do so. 
Marcos remained at Mesa, even as his wife feared he would die of sepsis. He was eventually transferred to ICE’s Central Arizona Florence Correctional Complex, where he’d been since February and was released Thursday afternoon. 
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security disputed Marcos’ account of the conditions, calling accusations of overcrowding false and writing that ICE provides all detainees with three meals a day, clean water and showers.
“ICE maintains detention standards that are higher than those of most U.S. prisons holding actual U.S. citizens,” an unnamed spokesperson wrote.
Biddeford protest targets Sen. Collins over ICE funding

ICE and DHS did not respond to requests for comment about why Marcos was detained. 
A lawyer in Brazil who then worked as a general contractor in the U.S., Marcos fled his home country in 2021, after officials there had threatened him during a dispute over the ownership of his clients’ properties, according to written testimony in his asylum interview documents.  
A U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services officer determined that he had credible fear of persecution or torture, allowing his case to move forward. He settled in Maine to live near his child and former spouse. Shortly after, he met his now-wife. They married in 2023, after which she said they filed an I-130 application, the first step to help an eligible family member get a green card.
Fighting for release
Like many people detained in Maine, Marcos was swiftly taken out of state, first held in Massachusetts where his lawyer filed a habeas corpus petition to try to get him released, to no avail. The filing of these petitions across the country have hit a historic high amid President Donald Trump’s push for mass deportations. 
When Marcos eventually landed in Arizona, Alessia sought out the help of local Democratic congressional candidate Elizabeth Lee, after seeing her advocate for another detainee experiencing medical neglect. Lee, who is a nurse, said she was “absolutely astonished” when reviewing Marcos’ medical records from detention, particularly the high level of pain he reported from a tooth abscess, around the same time another detainee in the same facility had died from one. 
Nearly every two weeks for the past several months, Lee has attended Marcos’ hearings and helped with tasks such as picking up his medical clearance for release, which had to be hand delivered. 
“I’m not sure what family members are supposed to do who don’t live within proximity or who don’t have means to drive an hour one way to pick a document up,” Lee said. 
Describing the long stretch of barbed wire outside the Arizona facility and the multiple layers of double-locked doors she passed through to attend his hearings, Lee said, “Walking inside these facilities is chilling — the cruelty of it, but the expense of it is wild to look at.”
Trump and congressional Republicans have passed approximately $240 billion in immigration funding during his second term so far, including a roughly $70 billion package in June following a historic investment of $170 billion last summer in the “One Big Beautiful Bill.”
Federal immigration agents arrested more people in July than in any previous month of Trump’s administration, though more arrests don’t necessarily translate into achieving the president’s goal of mass deportations, as Marcos’ and other cases show.
