Following arrests in Maine and elsewhere, DHS has continued to say they are targeting “the worst of the worst.” But less than a third of current detainees have a criminal conviction and 40% have never been accused of anything but non-criminal immigration violations, according to data through early July reviewed by Maine Morning Star’s sister outlet Stateline.
While immigration agencies are flush with cash, Trump’s firing of immigration judges has at times caused further delays in processing cases. 
“We have been seeing a lot of chaos occurring in immigration processing,” Ruben Torres with the Maine Immigrant Rights Coalition said. “Some cases that have been pending for years are suddenly getting moved up and bundled into a mega master hearing.” 
At Marcos’ latest hearing on Wednesday, Judge Victoria Levin of the Executive Office for Immigration Review adjusted his status to lawful permanent resident, clearing him for release. 
Speaking from the airport mere minutes before getting the call from her husband on Thursday that he was out, his wife remained skeptical he would actually be released until the moment it happened. 
“I’ve planned so much for all the things that could possibly go wrong that I can’t even picture the right things. It’s very surreal,” she said, as strangers, overhearing her story, asked to give her hugs. “Until I can put my hands on my husband, I’m waiting for whatever bomb they’re going to give me.” 
Imprint of detention
Ensuring Marcos’ safety after his release, much like the push for his release, was a group effort. 
Current law does not require ICE to notify family when a detainee is transferred or released.
Staff at the facility dropped him and other immigrants who had been released from detention on Thursday at a local church, which has become known for providing a place to make calls and wait for loved ones to pick them up. Marcos was not given back his phone, passport or driver’s license, he said.
With his wife still en route, Lee picked him up from the church. “He was all smiles,” she said. 
One of the other recently released immigrants carried a large sack filled with paperwork. He had defended his own case while in detention for years without a lawyer, Lee said. Another man kept lifting his hands above his head and shaking them to show he wasn’t in handcuffs. 
But the imprint of detention remains. 
Lee and Marcos stopped for clothes, since he was released in the “Gaspar Contracting” T-shirt he was detained in back in January. But Marcos was nervous being in Walmart, explaining that it’ll still be weeks until he gets his physical green card. 
While they are now back together, his wife is also fearful of the flight home and risks that remain once they are back, given the recent detentions at the Portland airport and outside the courthouse. 
Marcos said he is eager for good meals but he’s cautious about returning to a normal diet too quickly, having been warned by other recently released immigrants of gastrointestinal problems after months of detention food. 
Still, the first thing the New Englander requested was a coffee from Dunkin’ Donuts, accepting the stomach ache that came later.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Lindstrom fails to qualify nonpartisan bid for Nebraska governor; many signatures flagged for fraud
description: LINCOLN — Former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha will not appear on the ballot for Nebraska governor this November after a “significant” number of petition signatures were flagged for fraud. The Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office, which oversees state elections, confirmed Friday that Lindstrom, 45, did not obtain at least 4,000 valid signatures as requ[...]
text:
Former State Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, who has entered the race to be the GOP candidate for Nebraska's 2nd Congressional District. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska News Service)LINCOLN — Former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha will not appear on the ballot for Nebraska governor this November after a “significant” number of petition signatures were flagged for fraud.
The Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office, which oversees state elections, confirmed Friday that Lindstrom, 45, did not obtain at least 4,000 valid signatures as required to appear on the ballot as a registered nonpartisan candidate. At least 750 signatures were needed from each of Nebraska’s three congressional districts.
The office said 3,358 of Lindstrom’s signatures were valid. County election officials were charged with reviewing all 5,765 signatures that Lindstrom turned in by his Aug. 3 deadline. 
About 70% of Lindstrom’s signatures needed to be valid for him to qualify. He had a validation rate of 58.2%.
‘I am deeply disappointed’
Secretary of State Bob Evnen’s office said a “significant” number of signatures were found to be fraudulent. A number of the petitions were circulated by three of the five individuals arrested last week for gathering signatures suspected to be fraudulent on petitions seeking to change Lincoln elections. Those individuals face two felony charges each in Lancaster County.
“Information has been passed along to the Nebraska Attorney General’s Office for further investigation,” Evnen’s office said.
The Nebraska Board of State Canvassers, composed of State Treasurer Joey Spellerberg, Secretary of State Bob Evnen, Gov. Jim Pillen, Attorney General Mike Hilgers and Auditor of Public Accounts Mike Foley, from left, meets to certify Nebraska’s May 12 primary election. June 8, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers’ office had no immediate comment.
Lindstrom’s campaign on Friday said circulators contracted through a professional signature firm “cost the campaign its place” on the ballot and “did not perform their work in good faith.” The campaign said the actions of those circulators directly led to the invalidation of 1,543 signatures.
Lindstrom said in a statement that he was not aware of the activity and that the thousands of Nebraskans who participated “honestly” in the petition campaign were victims of fraud.
“We are pursuing every legal avenue available to us and intend to hold those responsible accountable,” Lindstrom said.
“I am deeply disappointed — not just for myself and our campaign, but for every Nebraskan who signed a petition in good faith, every volunteer who gave their time and every person who believed they were participating in a fair and lawful process,” Lindstrom continued. “They did their part. We did our part. The unlawful actions of a few should not be allowed to erase the voices of thousands.”
County officials verify local signers, checking that at least two of three match records on file across names, addresses and dates of birth. Reviewers then confirm signatures on file. 
Ballot for governor finalized
Friday’s news means the 2026 ballot for Nebraska governor is set: Republican Gov. Jim Pillen for reelection, former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont and Legal Marijuana NOW nominee Rick Beard of Omaha.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen of Columbus, a Republican at center, is running for reelection against former Democratic State Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, left, and Rick Beard of Omaha, the nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW party. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The Republican and Democratic campaigns for Nebraska governor had already sought to portray Lindstrom as either more conservative or more liberal than his nonpartisan label would suggest. Lindstrom had repeatedly said he didn’t want to play “spoiler” in the race, and it wasn’t clear whether his bid, if qualified, would have taken more votes from Walz or Pillen.
In contrast, Beard, the existing third-party candidate, had welcomed Lindstrom to the race.
Lindstrom, a lifelong Republican, left the Republican Party just a couple of months after he dropped out of the GOP primary for Nebraska’s 2nd Congressional District based in Omaha.
Even though Lindstrom will not appear on the November ballot, if he raised or spent more than $5,000 toward his bid for governor, he’ll still need to disclose his campaign finance.
The first general election report for candidates — covering June 17 through Sept. 29 — is due Oct. 5. 
Between Jan. 1, 2025, and June 16 of this year:

Pillen raised $8.6 million and spent $2.7 million. He had $9.5 million on hand by the end.
Walz raised $1.5 million and spent $809,000. She had about $675,000 by the end.
Beard has not exceeded the $5,000 threshold requiring him to report campaign finances.

State law required Lindstrom to name a running mate before petitioning. He chose Mike Picard of Omaha, a Navy veteran and club director and head coach of ENVY Volleyball Club.
Pillen is running again with longtime prosecutor Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly, who led the Lancaster County Attorney’s Office before President Donald Trump appointed him a U.S. attorney. Walz selected Humboldt farmer and agribusinessman Ben Steffen, an ex-Republican. Beard has not announced his pick yet. His deadline is Sept. 1.
Lindstrom turns in signatures, releases ‘Nebraska Doctrine’ for nonpartisan governor bid

Pillen won the GOP nomination over Lindstrom for governor in 2022. In seeking a spot on this year’s ballot, Lindstrom said he wanted a change and released what he termed “The Nebraska Doctrine” with his ideas for the governor’s office. Lindstrom said he thought Walz didn’t have the “math” to win.
Republicans outnumber Democrats nearly 2-to-1 and have held the governor’s seat since 1999.
The last non-Republican Nebraska governor was Ben Nelson, a Democrat who served between 1991 and 1999 and then served two terms in the U.S. Senate from 2001 to 2013. He was the last Democrat elected statewide, too, in his 2006 reelection bid.
Lindstrom considering next steps
Lindstrom said his efforts to “right the ship” for Nebraska and refocus on economic growth and fiscal discipline will not be erased by fraud. He intends to regroup.
“I am open to any and all avenues that allow me to continue doing what I believe is right for Nebraska,” Lindstrom said. “I did not begin this effort simply to run for an office. I began it because I believe our state needs a different direction and because this moment is too important to sit on the sidelines.
“The ballot may have changed. The mission has not.”
The general election is Nov. 3.

title: Arkansas judge grants AG’s motion to dismiss his open-records suit against prison board
description: An Arkansas judge has granted Attorney General Tim Griffin’s motion to dismiss his lawsuit against the Board of Corrections that accused the panel of violating the state’s law on open records and meetings. Pulaski County Circuit Judge Tim Fox’s one-page order Thursday dismissing the case comes less than a month after the state Supreme Court […]
text:
(Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)An Arkansas judge has granted Attorney General Tim Griffin’s motion to dismiss his lawsuit against the Board of Corrections that accused the panel of violating the state’s law on open records and meetings.
Pulaski County Circuit Judge Tim Fox’s one-page order Thursday dismissing the case comes less than a month after the state Supreme Court ordered him to do so. Griffin requested the dismissal after Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders’ four appointees to the seven-member board voted in favor of a settlement agreement.
“Regardless of the parties involved or the issues at stake, transparency and accountability must remain cornerstones of good government,” Griffin said in a statement. “The Freedom of Information Act serves an essential role in preserving public confidence in our institutions, and I will continue to defend it whenever necessary.”
The ruling ends a legal battle that began in late 2023 and was part of a larger fight over who controls the state’s prison system.
The board in March voted to settle the lawsuit, 4-3, after Sanders appointed several new members. Her appointments prior to December did not make up a majority of the seven-member board, which sued her in 2023 over who had the power to fire the Department of Corrections’ top leaders.
Griffin’s lawsuit, filed not long after the board sued Sanders, alleged the board committed several public records and meetings law violations in the process of hiring Abtin Mehdizadegan and his law firm, Hall Booth Smith. 
Mehdizadegan represented the board in both the lawsuit against Sanders and in the lawsuit filed by Griffin until he was fired earlier this year, after the new appointments were made.
Board member Lee Watson and former chairman Benny Magness, whose term expired last year, asked Fox to allow them to intervene and had requested the judge not grant the motion to dismiss. Griffin filed an emergency request with the state Supreme Court, arguing it had the right to request the case’s dismissal.
Watson and Magness said in a statement that while they understood Fox had to follow the Supreme Court’s ruling, they had been looking forward to their day in court. The two said they did not violate the state FOIA.
“Despite the terms of the agreement entered over Watson and Magness’s objections, the attorney general’s dismissal of its suit makes it clear that there was no substance to its suit—which was filed immediately following the board’s challenge to the constitutionality of statues diminishing the board’s authority,” the two said in a statement.
A separate suit challenging laws that gave the governor power to fire the corrections department secretary and the leaders of the corrections and community corrections divisions is pending before a separate judge. Griffin’s office has asked Pulaski County Circuit Judge Patricia James to lift her injunction against the laws.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Health records in GOP race for Oklahoma governor could help sway voters, experts say
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – Gentner Drummond’s push to pressure his opponent into taking a drug test taps into voter concerns over candidates’ health and could tip the outcome of the contentious runoff election for Oklahoma’s Republican nominee for governor, some political observers said. Following questions from moderators during a televised debate, Drummond’s campaign[...]
text:
A sign points voters to the polling place at the Millwood High School Field House on June 16, 2026 in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. (Photo by Courtney Bell/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Gentner Drummond’s push to pressure his opponent into taking a drug test taps into voter concerns over candidates’ health and could tip the outcome of the contentious runoff election for Oklahoma’s Republican nominee for governor, some political observers said.
Following questions from moderators during a televised debate, Drummond’s campaign this week released his health records plus the results of a drug test. Drummond, who has been Oklahoma’s attorney general since 2023, also questioned whether his opponent, Mike Mazzei, would feel “confident in his physical stature” to do the same.
So far, Mazzei – who has picked up the endorsement of President Donald Trump – has not. 
“This appears to be, like, a pretty close race,” said Michael Crespin, director of the Carl Albert Congressional Research and Studies Center and political science professor at the University of Oklahoma. “So, there’s, like, any number of things that can move the needle one way or another.”
Drummond’s release of medical records is also a bit of a political ploy to probably try to draw attention to questions about Mazzei’s health, Crespin  said. But, he added that voters generally are interested in and care about the health of a candidate.
Questions about the health of candidates and elected officials have been in the national spotlight recently. Speculation about the vitality of U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnel, 84 of Kentucky, was rampant online during his recent two-month absence from the Senate. President Donald Trump, 80, has been dogged with questions about his health and cognitive abilities, as was his predecessor, President Joe Biden, who was 82 when he left office.  
Copies of  the 62-year-old Drummond’s health records show a negative drug test and that his doctor wrote that he “is in excellent overall health and remains physically active.”
The physician noted that Drummond has a history of hypertension and elevated cholesterol, which are controlled by medication and monitoring, the letter said.
His blood pressure was elevated, but not high.
“Based on his most recent comprehensive medical evaluation, including appropriate laboratory testing and clinical assessments, he is fully capable of maintaining a rigorous professional, travel and work schedule,” the doctor wrote.
Drummond also has pledged to release his financial records, but the campaign has not done that so far. 
Mazzei told Oklahoma Voice last week he would not discuss releasing his medical and financial records.
He also pointed out that his opponent’s campaign is suggesting that he is unfit to be governor and is “probably on some unhelpful medication.” He said he was “fit as a fiddle.”
Mazzie said he is not on medication and has recovered from a 2008 car accident while he was a state senator that left him with nerve damage to his back. He missed a significant number of votes in the Senate after the crash. 
He said he has not been on pain medication since that car accident.
His campaign did not respond to a request for additional comment.
Having candidates release medical records in Oklahoma races is not unusual nor usual, said Richard Johnson, Oklahoma City University professor of political science.
“When you have a close race, you’re looking to turn over every stone that you possibly can,” he said. “If you feel like your candidate has an open book, you might be able to throw something out there.”
Because a smaller number of voters turnout for runoff elections, “moving a few people at this point does make a difference,” Johnson said.
Melody Huckaby Rowlett, University of Oklahoma political science professor, said fewer people vote in the party primary runoff elections and those who vote in the Republican primary system are more conservative.
She noted that Trump, who was the oldest person elected president in the U.S., has released some of his medical records, but not all of them.
Biden, who dropped out of the 2024 presidential race against Trump amid concerns he had suffered a cognitive decline, released a copy of his physical.
Trump’s endorsement can sway Republican elections.
Since Drummond doesn’t have that, Huckaby Rowlett said, he needs to show something else.
The release of medical records will matter to those who value transparency, she said.
The primary runoff election is Aug. 25.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Treating opioid misuse with mindfulness therapy could save thousands of dollars, new study says
description: A mindfulness treatment created at the University of Utah in recent years has proved to be effective at decreasing opioid misuse. Now, a new economic study found it could also save hundreds of thousands of dollars per patient. That’s if healthcare, criminal justice and lost productivity costs are taken into account. An opioid addiction epidemic […]
text:
The J. Willard Marriott Library on the University of Utah campus in Salt Lake City is pictured on Saturday, Aug. 23, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)A mindfulness treatment created at the University of Utah in recent years has proved to be effective at decreasing opioid misuse. Now, a new economic study found it could also save hundreds of thousands of dollars per patient.
That’s if healthcare, criminal justice and lost productivity costs are taken into account.
An opioid addiction epidemic can cost the United States as much as $4 trillion per year, according to a study by the firm Avalere Health. However, a form of therapy called Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement, or MORE, can save $12 for every dollar spent in those costs, according to a University of Utah health economist’s evaluation.
The treatment, according to the analysis, is two to six times more cost-effective than other addiction treatments and can save more than $324,000 throughout a patient’s life.
University of Utah economics professor Fernando Wilson, who conducted the economic analysis, said in a news release the results suggest that a wide implementation of the MORE therapy could be a potent and cost-effective solution for the opioid crisis.
“At a relatively low cost, MORE has strong potential to reduce opioid misuse and generate substantial economic benefits for patients, health systems and society,” Wilson said. “The cost of implementing MORE is small, and its potential payoff in averting misuse and risk of opioid use disorder is very large.”

The therapy was developed by former University of Utah professor Eric Garland, who also co-wrote the economic evaluation. It aims to teach mindfulness skills to regulate cravings and pain, as well as other tools to manage stress and negative emotions and to “savor pleasant, healthful and life-affirming experiences,” according to a past release about the therapy.
“Rather than getting caught up in the pain or craving, we teach people how to step back and observe that experience from the perspective of an objective witness,” Garland said then. “When they can do that, people begin to recognize that who they truly are is bigger than any one thought or sensation. They are not defined by their experiences of pain or craving; their true nature is something more.”
Opioid overdose deaths have decreased this year in the state, according to data from the Utah Department of Health and Human Services, but remain an issue. This year there have been 172 deaths linked to opioid overdoses in Utah, 10% fewer than in 2025. And, there have been almost 700,000 opioid prescriptions dispensed, also a 10% decrease from last year.
A clinical trial on the therapy following 250 adults with chronic pain on long-term opioid therapy who misused opioids found that the treatment “reduced opioid misuse by 45%, led to improvements in pain symptoms and opioid dosing and strengthened the brain’s responses to positive experiences to reduce cravings,” the university said this month.
“Opioid misuse is a major driver of overdose deaths, hospitalizations, homelessness and economic loss, so substantially reducing opioid misuse could have huge positive consequences for society,” Garland said. “Our study suggests that MORE could be part of a scalable solution that improves outcomes for patients while also reducing burdens on the health care system and society at large.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Tasia Fortune’s troubled life leaves her family grieving, and waiting, as police investigate her death
description: A makeshift memorial for Tasia Fortune is seen in the backyard of a vacant home in the 500 block of Road of Remembrance in Jackson on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. According to authorities, Fortune’s body was found hanging from a tree in the backyard of a vacant home Monday, Aug. 3, 2026.
text:
By her family’s account, Tasia Fortune was a loving, caring woman who led a troubled life. She ran away from foster care when she was 16, leaving western Kentucky and finding her way to Jackson, Mississippi. There was homelessness and addiction. Relationships that didn’t last produced four children.
Then on an August day, the body of the 29-year-old was found hanging from a tree behind a vacant home on the 500 block of Road of Remembrance. The home is in a mostly Black neighborhood in west Jackson strewn with pockets of tall grass, vacant lots and older homes.
“She had a good heart. She just had a hard life,” her mother, Christy Spivey, told Mississippi Today.
Spivey doesn’t know much about Fortune’s life in Jackson, and she fell numb when she learned of her daughter’s fate.
National interest grew in the days following the discovery, primarily because of the manner in which Fortune, a Black woman, was found. Results of an autopsy have not been released. Authorities say they have identified a person of interest, who is being held on an unrelated charge, but have yet to release an explanation of how Fortune died and why. 
Spivey said she is not ruling anything out, but insists her daughter would never take her own life nor does she think race was a factor.
A vacant home in the 500 block of Road of Remembrance is pictured in Jackson on Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026. According to authorities, Tasia Fortune’s body was found hanging from a tree in the backyard of a vacant home Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“I really don’t feel like it was a racial crime. … I think that this was more of a personal crime, but I definitely understand the fears,” she said.
Like many others, Robert Luckett, a professor of history at Jackson State University, has been watching the case unfold. He understands the national attention.
The public’s perception of Mississippi as a dangerous place, particularly for people of color, taps into the state’s history of violence, he said earlier this week.
“It’s a reputation that we’ve earned in the state due to the very real nature of racialized violence whether or not we attribute it to this case or not,” Luckett said.
“It’s an image of this state that lingers and that people from the outside look at Mississippi and say ‘Oh, an incident like this one is obviously a continuation of the history of really intense hate crimes that we witnessed in this nation,’” he said.  
The circumstances surrounding Fortune’s death have evoked the recent case of Trey Reed, a Black student who was found hanging at Delta State University last September. Mississippi authorities concluded he died by suicide amid initial speculation by his family that foul play was involved. 
LaToni Fortune said she last saw her older sister last month when Tasia returned to Kentucky for a family reunion.
“She just comes back to Kentucky and visit us or we’ll go to Jackson and visit her,” she said.
She said her sister had no car and had trouble finding work.
Her mother acknowledged the family’s troubles, describing battles over keeping her family together. 
Fortune and her other two siblings were put into foster care, Spivey said. Fortune grew into a talented student and a cross-country track athlete. Despite being separated from family, she found ways to stay in touch with loved ones.
“They couldn’t keep us apart, one way or another,” Spivey said.
A makeshift memorial for Tasia Fortune is seen in the backyard of a vacant home in the 500 block of Road of Remembrance in Jackson on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. According to authorities, Fortune’s body was found hanging from a tree in the backyard of a vacant home Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Fortune was just 16 when she ran away to Mississippi with someone she met in foster care, her family said. She eventually made her way to Jackson, where she lived for most of the last 13 years of her life. 
She fell on hard times, her family said, spending a lot of her time homeless and wandering the streets.
Spivey was heartbroken to learn her daughter had fallen into addiction. The family tried to help her return to Kentucky and get sober multiple times. She always returned to Jackson to be close to her children. 
The recent reunion in Kentucky is a happy memory for Spivey. It was the last time she would see her daughter. They all went swimming and went out to eat together.
A memorial has risen at the house where Fortune was found, a small mound of flowers, balloons, teddy bears and pinwheels surrounding a framed picture of her.
“We’re going to fight until the end to get justice for her,” Spivey said.
A GoFundMe account has been established to cover burial costs and care for Fortune’s children. 
Candice Wilder and Molly Minta contributed to this reporting.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: U.S. Rep. Russell Fry endorses Sen. Darline Graham in GOP runoff
description: U.S. Rep. Russell Fry is backing Sen. Darline Graham in the runoff to replace her late brother as the GOP's Senate nominee.
text:
U.S. Rep. Russell Fry, pictured Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026, is backing Sen. Darline Graham in the runoff to replace her late brother as the GOP's Senate nominee. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)U.S. Rep. Russell Fry is backing Sen. Darline Graham in the runoff to replace her late brother as the GOP’s Senate nominee.
Fry, who placed third after receiving 20% of the vote in the special primary earlier this week, endorsed Graham Friday as she prepares for a runoff against 5th District Congressman Ralph Norman on Aug. 25.
The winner will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in November. The election marks the first open U.S. Senate race in 22 years in South Carolina.
Graham and Norman advanced to the runoff after receiving 33% and 25% of the 334,880 ballots cast, respectively, according to the state Election Commission.
“President Trump needs fighters and allies in the Senate who will show up every day and get results. I believe Darline Graham will be exactly that,” Fry said in a statement.
Graham already boasts the presidential endorsement.
President Donald Trump surprised political insiders with his “complete and total endorsement” of the political newcomer last month, urging her to run for a full, six-year term.
Fry, too, had been a staunch Trump supporter.
The four-term state House member rose to Congress in the aftermath of the Jan. 6, 2021, storming of the U.S. Capitol.
Then U.S. Rep. Tom Rice voted in favor of impeaching Trump over his role in inciting rioters, who entered the Capitol building in an effort to prevent lawmakers from certifying the results of the 2020 presidential election. Fry criticized Rice for his vote and challenged him in 2022.
Trump endorsed Fry in that race and Fry went on to defeat Rice in the primary by more than 26 percentage points.
On the other hand, Trump and Norman have had a rockier relationship after Norman endorsed former Gov. Nikki Haley over Trump in the 2024 Republican presidential primary.
While Graham was by her brother’s side on the campaign trail in recent years, she was never a candidate herself. Gov. Henry McMaster appointed her to fulfill the remainder of her brother’s term following his unexpected death. The appointment made her South Carolina’s first female U.S. senator.
Ahead of the special election, Norman and Fry, who each have years of experience in the Statehouse and on Capitol Hill, knocked Graham for being an unknown.
However, on Friday, Fry joined other high profile Republicans, including U.S. Sen. Tim Scott, who officially endorsed Graham as she tries to consolidate GOP support.
“Darline knows what it means to struggle, persevere and keep fighting when life deals you a difficult hand,” Fry said in a statement. “Those experiences shaped her, and I believe they give her a real understanding of the challenges families across South Carolina face.”
Scott, who is also the chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, backed Graham the day after the special primary, calling her “the real deal.”
On the other hand, Upstate businessman Mark Lynch, who placed fifth in the Senate race endorsed Norman.
Support from Fry, who lives in Murrells Inlet and won the Grand Strand and the rest of the 7th District he represents in the special primary, could swing those voters in favor of Graham.
Norman took 10 Upstate counties while Graham won the rest of the state.
“I am extremely honored to have earned the endorsement of Congressman Russell Fry,” Graham said in response to the endorsement. “Considering the respect that the Pee Dee has for Russell and his team, I am excited to continue building a conservative force to fight for President Trump’s America First agenda.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: In Idaho, public health officials are trying to curb the rat infestation — with a $250K fund
description: The board that oversees Idaho’s largest public health district on Friday approved a quarter million dollar fund to fight invasive rats.  The Central District Health board approved $250,000 in unspent reserve funds toward a “rodent abatement and prevention project.” The health district is still planning how to spend those funds, but some of it could […]
text:
The two common rat species in Idaho are the non-native Norway rat, pictured, and the roof rat, according to the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare. "Norway rats thrive in environments where food, water, and shelter are readily available, including dumps, sewers, open fields, and residential neighborhoods," according to the Health and Welfare website. (Photo courtesy of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)The board that oversees Idaho’s largest public health district on Friday approved a quarter million dollar fund to fight invasive rats. 
The Central District Health board approved $250,000 in unspent reserve funds toward a “rodent abatement and prevention project.” 
The health district is still planning how to spend those funds, but some of it could go toward free rat traps, finding a way to track rat sightings, and bringing cities together that are affected by the infestation, Central District Health Director Kristin Ryan said in an interview.
Central District Health Director Kristin Ryan. (Courtesy of Central District Health)
Part of why the health district is getting involved, she said, is because rats can pose a public health risk by transmitting diseases. Ryan says she isn’t seeing data to show higher infection rates from rat-spread diseases in the area, but she said officials are trying to be proactive. 
“We’re just trying to be responsive to our community’s needs, and this is a high priority for our communities in Ada County,” Ryan said.
In the spring, bills to curb the state’s rat problem failed to garner enough support in the Legislature. In June, Republican state Sen. Tammy Nichols and Democratic Rep. John Gannon urged local government officials to act on the issue, BoiseDev reported.

name: National
title: Flock Safety tightens safeguards as states, cities question surveillance network
description: Flock Safety is tightening privacy and oversight controls for its nationwide network of automated license plate readers as more communities pull back from the technology and lawmakers across the political spectrum push for new restrictions. The company announced Thursday that it will recommend that police agencies retain license plate reader data for seven d[...]
text:
Flock Safety license plate readers are typically mounted on tall poles, with a camera and solar panel on top. The company says its technology is used in more than 6,000 communities across 49 states in partnership with thousands of law enforcement agencies nationwide. (Photo courtesy of Flock Safety)Flock Safety is tightening privacy and oversight controls for its nationwide network of automated license plate readers as more communities pull back from the technology and lawmakers across the political spectrum push for new restrictions.
The company announced Thursday that it will recommend that police agencies retain license plate reader data for seven days, down from 30, while adding tools to restrict data sharing between agencies and detect potentially abusive searches. Flock also plans to require law enforcement users to associate searches with case codes and automatically suspend users whose activity is flagged as abnormal.
The changes come amid growing scrutiny of a surveillance network that Flock says has more than 120,000 cameras across 49 states and serves thousands of law enforcement agencies and communities.
The cameras photograph passing vehicles and record information including license plates, vehicle characteristics, location and time. Police can search the resulting data during investigations, sometimes across jurisdictional lines.
More than 50 agencies or communities have canceled, suspended or rejected a Flock contract or deactivated their cameras since the beginning of 2026, according to DeFlock, a grassroots group that tracks license plate reader deployments. Cameras have also been vandalized in communities around the country.
Recent incidents involving police officers accused of using Flock to track friends, relatives and romantic partners have added to concerns about how the data can be accessed and shared. The technology also has been criticized after inaccurate license plate information contributed to wrongful police stops, arrests and detentions.
Flock says the new measures will give communities greater control over their data while strengthening safeguards against misuse.
“These changes, like I said, are the next chapter of a long book I hope to write on how we build a better version of America that’s both safer, protects our privacy and holds those who have power accountable,” Flock Safety co-founder and CEO Garrett Langley said in a video statement.
But civil liberties advocates say some of the safeguards have been tried before and question whether the company’s changes address broader concerns about a system that can create a record of people’s movements even when they are not suspected of a crime.
States have taken different approaches to regulating technologies used in policing, including artificial intelligence, facial recognition, drones and automated license plate readers. More than a dozen states have enacted laws governing such technologies, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures, but there is no consistent national framework for their use.
Strengthening privacy and accountability
Flock’s seven-day retention recommendation is one of its most significant changes.
When the company launched nine years ago, it set 30 days as the default recommendation, while allowing communities to choose shorter or longer periods.
For investigations that require older information, Flock is introducing “Evidence Mode,” which will allow detectives to preserve specific license plate data as evidence in an active case.
The change does not automatically apply to existing customers, which can keep their current retention policies. Communities also will continue to choose their own retention periods.
The American Civil Liberties Union called the shorter retention period a potential step forward but said its impact will depend on how the new mode works. In a statement, the group recommended a 48-hour retention period and warned that if searches cause data to be preserved, the new system could allow significant amounts of location information to remain available longer than seven days.
Flock also is giving communities more control over which outside agencies can search their cameras. Under the new “offense filtering” system, a community could allow another agency to search its cameras for specific crimes or offenses and block searches related to immigration enforcement, for example.
Police use of artificial intelligence grows as rules lag behind

Flock also will require all law enforcement customers to adopt its audit assistance tool by the end of the year. The system looks for unusual search activity and flags it for administrator review. Flock plans to automatically suspend users whose activity meets certain criteria for abnormal behavior while their access is reviewed.
The company also will require case codes for law enforcement searches by the end of the year. Officers can bypass the requirement during emergencies, but those searches also will be flagged for review.
Police misuse and erroneous alerts
Flock’s new controls build on safeguards the company has introduced in recent years, including electronic audit logs and requirements that users provide a reason for searches.
The ACLU, in its statement, said some of those earlier safeguards were ineffective. The group pointed to cases in which officers circumvented search-purpose restrictions by entering vague or meaningless explanations before Flock replaced a free-text field with a list of approved search reasons.
The Washington Post reported earlier this month that nearly 50 police officers had been charged or accused of using Flock cameras for unauthorized purposes, many involving attempts to track current or former romantic partners or family members.
In Savannah, Georgia, four police officers and two civilian employees were fired last week after a department investigation found searches involving personal acquaintances and family members, according to a news release. The investigation also found that an officer had allowed an outside law enforcement agency to access Savannah’s Flock system.
The activity was identified using Flock’s audit assistance tool. All six cases were referred to the Georgia Bureau of Investigation for independent criminal investigations.
The technology has also drawn scrutiny when information in the system is inaccurate or outdated.
In Wisconsin, a woman was pulled over at gunpoint earlier this month after a Flock camera incorrectly flagged her vehicle as being involved in a homicide. Brookfield police stopped Amber Newell on Interstate 94 after receiving the alert, but Milwaukee police told officers they no longer needed the vehicle or its occupants. Newell was released.
Milwaukee police later said the incident was caused by an employee’s failure to remove an outdated wanted-vehicle alert from the Flock system, rather than an error by Flock itself. Newell said she had also been stopped at gunpoint earlier that week and was afraid to drive afterward.


In its announcement, Flock said its alerts are intended to be investigative leads rather than conclusions and that officers should visually confirm a vehicle’s license plate before taking action. The company said its system produces fewer than nine human-reported errors for every 1 million alerts.
Bipartisan interest
A bipartisan group of Pennsylvania lawmakers announced Monday that they plan to introduce legislation establishing statewide privacy and accountability requirements for automated license plate readers, including Flock cameras.
The proposal would establish rules governing access to the data, documented reasons for searches, audit trails, data retention and transparency. It also would create civil penalties for unauthorized access, use or disclosure and allow people harmed by misuse to bring civil suits.
“Technology that can help keep our communities safe should never become a tool for stalking or abuse,” Democratic state Rep. Jennifer O’Mara said in a statement announcing the proposal.
Republicans in Congress also have introduced or plan to introduce at least two proposals aimed at restricting automated surveillance technology. One would restrict federal agencies from purchasing or using certain automated surveillance technology, while the other would bar state and local police from using federal funds to acquire automated license plate reader systems.
Last month, 15 Democratic lawmakers in Michigan sent a letter to the state Department of Transportation to end an agreement allowing federal agencies, including U.S. Border Patrol and Homeland Security Investigations, to install surveillance technology on state property. The lawmakers argued that automated license plate readers infringe on residents’ constitutional rights.
The West Virginia House Democratic Caucus also released a statement last month opposing Flock cameras and said it is monitoring canceled contracts and lawsuits involving the technology.
Abandoning the technology
Some local governments are going further by ending their relationships with Flock altogether.
DeFlock’s tracker lists dozens of communities that have canceled contracts, deactivated cameras or rejected proposals since 2021.
More than 50 agencies or communities have taken one of those steps since the beginning of 2026.
Several communities in Rhode Island and Nebraska have acted this month, with city leaders voting to cancel contracts or uninstall cameras.
Earlier this month, the Burnet County Sheriff’s Office in Texas announced that it had removed all fixed Flock cameras after repeated vandalism damaged the equipment. The cameras were provided by the Heart of Texas Auto Theft Task Force, a multi-agency, multijurisdictional task force in Central Texas. The sheriff’s office has initiated criminal cases, but there are currently no suspects, according to a news release.
The debate over this technology is likely to continue through the rest of the year and into 2027, when more state legislatures return to session. That could bring additional proposals to regulate artificial intelligence tools used in policing, as well as how license plate reader data is collected, retained, shared and used.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Klobuchar proposes Minnesota tax credit to assist with rising healthcare premiums
description: If the federal government fails to extend federal subsidies that offset healthcare premiums, Sen. Amy Klobuchar, as governor, would create a state tax credit to help with those skyrocketing costs. Most Republican U.S. senators late last year blocked a Democratic bill to extend Affordable Care Act tax credits, essentially driving up healthcare premiums for mi[...]
text:
Sen. Amy Klobuchar and her running mate Ben Schierer, mayor of Fergus Falls, lay out Klobuchar's plan for housing policy if she wins the governorship alongside first-time homebuyers and housing advocates at a press conference in Columbia Heights Monday, June 8, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)If the federal government fails to extend federal subsidies that offset healthcare premiums, Sen. Amy Klobuchar, as governor, would create a state tax credit to help with those skyrocketing costs.
Most Republican U.S. senators late last year blocked a Democratic bill to extend Affordable Care Act tax credits, essentially driving up healthcare premiums for millions of Americans.
The extra federal subsidies that Republicans blocked are known as “enhanced premium tax credits,” because they raised the income cutoffs at which people can receive subsidies.
The enhanced premium tax credits expired at the end of 2025, hiking up health insurance plan costs by 50% for a projected 89,000 Minnesotans, according to a 2025 release from MNsure — the state’s ACA marketplace.
Klobuchar, the Democratic-Farmer-Labor nominee for governor, standing in front of St. Paul College’s simulation center for healthcare students on Friday, said there’s a strong possibility that the federal subsidies will be extended after the November midterms if Democrats gain more seats in Congress.
But if Congress doesn’t take action, Klobuchar said she would create a state tax credit targeted at small business owners, self-employed workers and farmers who are hit hardest by the expiration of the federal subsidies.
“Millions of Americans have lost their health insurance because they can no longer afford premiums,” Klobuchar said. “Deductibles have risen, too, and prescription drug prices continue to skyrocket. As governor, I will reduce premiums to deliver immediate cost relief and value for Minnesota families, small businesses, farmers and those without employer coverage.”
Ten states offer state-funded healthcare subsidies, including California, Maryland, Washington and New Mexico — the only state to see ACA enrollment growth since Congress allowed the federal subsidies to expire.
Friday was Klobuchar’s first press conference since winning the DFL nomination for governor in Tuesday’s primary election. Klobuchar is running against Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth, who on Friday said that Klobuchar has failed to reform healthcare in the 20 years she’s been a U.S. senator.
Klobuchar’s healthcare plan also includes creating a per-employee tax credit for small employers who fund their workers’ coverage.
Minnesota’s future budget outlook is uncertain, as state spending is expected to continue to outpace revenue in the next few years. Asked how she would deal with the cost of the tax credits, Klobuchar said she expects to find cost-savings in the top-to-bottom audit of state government she will do as soon as she takes office.
Klobuchar said that as Hennepin County attorney, she did the same thing to the state’s largest prosecutor’s office, analyzing the budget and determining areas where it could cut duplicative services or save money by moving employees around.
“If we’re going to spend some money to keep Minnesota growing and strong, we’ve got to look at the health insurance premiums as well as drug prices and things that will bring down the costs overall,” Klobuchar said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Josh Turek urges US Senate Democrats to help advance farm bill
description: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Josh Turek reiterated his support Friday for passing a federal farm bill Friday, saying at the Iowa State Fair that U.S. Senate Democrats should not “let perfection stand in the way of progress” in moving forward a measure. Earlier in August, progress on a farm bill stalled as Senate Democrats were […]
text:
Iowa Rep. Josh Turek, the Democratic nominee for Iowa's U.S. Senate seat, gave remarks at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the Iowa State Fair Aug. 14, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Josh Turek reiterated his support Friday for passing a federal farm bill Friday, saying at the Iowa State Fair that U.S. Senate Democrats should not “let perfection stand in the way of progress” in moving forward a measure.
Earlier in August, progress on a farm bill stalled as Senate Democrats were unwilling to continue negotiations unless Republicans agreed to delay implementation of a law dealing with the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) program.
Democrats are seeking a two-year extension of part of the “One, Big Beautiful Bill” Act requiring states to pay a portion SNAP costs currently covered by the federal government if they have a SNAP payment error rate above 6%.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Turek, a state representative from Council Bluffs, is running against Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson in the U.S. Senate race. He had said in a statement he would have voted in support of the measure, and said Senate Democrats “failed” farmers by not moving forward the bill.
After speaking at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Friday, Turek told reporters this statement does not mean he thinks there aren’t problems with the proposal.
“I think one of the flaws is it benefits far too much the southern farmers, not necessarily the Iowa farmers with with corn and soybeans, but I don’t think that we should let perfection stand in the way of progress,” Turek said. “We’re already three years overdue. Our Iowa farmers are hurting, and so I would be in favor of voting that, moving that along. Because as I’ve been traveling this state, I’m hearing more and more and more, ‘I’m really concerned that we’re going to lose … what remains of our small family farms.'”
He said not passing a farm bill would further hurt rural communities in Iowa, which he said have suffered from losing pharmacies, schools and healthcare clinics. At the same time, Turek said, rural communities are also being hurt by cuts to SNAP.
“To have a functioning rural community, you’ve got to have grocery stores. Well, the SNAP cuts hurt that,” Turek said. “You’ve got to have pharmacies, lack of PBM (pharmacy benefit manager) reform hurts that. You got to have healthcare clinics —  certainly, this is the down ballot effects of Medicaid cuts — and you got to have functioning public schools. I’m seeing rural communities that are absolutely being hollowed out. We got to pass the farm bill.”
While Turek highlighted his disagreement with Senate Democrats on this issue, Republicans speaking at a “Turek’s Too Liberal” press conference at the fair hosted by the Republican Party of Iowa said Turek would side with his party if elected. State Rep. Jon Dunwell, R-Newton, who serves alongside Turek in the Iowa House, claimed Turek “would work with radicals to prevent the passage of the farm bill.”
Chris Perdue, a farmer from Pottawattamie County, said farmers were not able to install terraces for soil conservation because a 43-day federal government shutdown in 2025 happened during the short period between harvest and snowfall when this infrastructure could be built.
“The USDA was shut down, they couldn’t even turn computer on to help us because we needed soil techs to come out and measure the terraces,” Perdue said. ” Congresswoman Ashley Hinson voted for the (continuing resolution) to keep the government open, right? And Josh Turek would vote along party lines to keep the government shut down if that happens again.”
Perdue and the other speakers spoke in support of Hinson’s work on the 2025 “One, Big Beautiful Bill” Act and support for President Donald Trump’s policies, saying Turek would repeal tax cuts made in the legislation.
Turek said he supported some of the tax provisions in the 2025 law.
“I’ve been very open and vocal that I’ll work with anyone, including President Trump, on issues,” Turek said. “I agree with him that we should have no tax on tips and overtime. I agree with him that we need to drive private equity out of housing. I’m willing to work with anyone across the aisle.”
Turek was the first of many candidates scheduled to speak at The Des Moines Register Political Soapbox during the 11 days of the fair. See the schedule here.

name: VTDigger
title: State regulators voice questions and support as Brattleboro hospital aims to revive its ailing finances
description:
“I do think the Brattleboro community is suffering the consequences of mismanagement,” a member of Vermont’s Green Mountain Care Board said Friday of problems recently uncovered at Brattleboro Memorial Hospital.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  State regulators voice questions and support as Brattleboro hospital aims to revive its ailing finances.
text:
A crowd of about 100 people rally July 14 in support of the birthing center at Brattleboro Memorial Hospital. Photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger

State regulators expressed both concern and support as acting administrators at Brattleboro Memorial Hospital outlined plans at a Friday online hearing to curb deficit spending caused by past administrative and accounting problems.
“I do think the Brattleboro community is suffering the consequences of mismanagement at this hospital,” Sara Teachout, one of five members of Vermont’s Green Mountain Care Board, told the facility’s new leaders. “I appreciate what you all are doing to change that.”
The southeastern Vermont healthcare hub, now operating on a $130 million annual budget, is forecasting a $7.1 million shortfall for the coming fiscal year that begins Oct. 1. That would follow operating losses of $33.6 million from fiscal years 2017 through 2025 and an estimated $9.5 million for FY 2026, according to a report discussed by regulators Friday.
To cover the deficit spending, the hospital is tapping its reserves of cash, investments and unrestricted assets, the new leaders said. But that has depleted the facility’s collective accounts from $53.3 million in FY 2021 to a projected $19.7 million for FY 2027.
“The losses have been mounting,” said Elizabeth McLarney, acting co-CEO with fellow doctor Tony Blofson. “We need to recover financially.”
The 61-bed hospital has operated with acting administrators since former president Christopher Dougherty exited without explanation in November and former chief financial officer Laura Bruno departed amid similar silence in December.
In their report to regulators, Blofson and McLarney said consultants had discovered “significant deficiencies” in the hospital’s financial systems. Those, in turn, led to “unhelpful and inaccurate in most cases” accounting assessments and the need to tap into savings to pay staff, taxes and loans.
“It’s kind of death by 1,000 paper cuts — it’s no one thing or one person,” said David Sanville, the hospital’s financial consultant.

READ MORE

The deficit spending has depleted not only the hospital’s savings but also its “days cash on hand,” which is an estimate of how many days it could stay open if it didn’t reap any outside revenue and had to cover expenses strictly with its own reserves.
Regulators consider a figure of 205 days or more to be “very strong” and one of 80 days or less to be “highly vulnerable.” According to its report, the hospital has seen its number decrease from 220 days in FY 2021 to 60 days this summer.
“Our first job is to get back to breaking even,” Sanville told reporters in an interview earlier in the week, “and our second job is to start building up that savings.”
To cut costs, the hospital — one of Brattleboro’s three largest employers — laid off nine support staffers this month to reduce its annual payroll by about $840,000. After eliminating several long-vacant positions, leaders anticipate the number of employees dropping from 528 full-time equivalents in the current budget to 457 in the coming one.
The hospital also plans to save money by closing its birthing center by Dec. 31 if it can’t find a long-term way to cover an estimated annual unit loss of $4.8 million — half of the hospital’s projected overall FY 2026 deficit. Declining the suggestion of a municipal subsidy, leaders are hoping to receive a Rural Health Transformation government grant or approval of a recent clinicians’ call to raise Medicaid obstetric reimbursement rates — both now under review by the state Agency of Human Services.
Even with such measures, the hospital is projecting a seventh consecutive year of deficit spending in FY 2027 and doesn’t anticipate breaking even on an overall annual budget until FY 2028 at the earliest.
“We’ve been making steady progress,” Sanville said, “but there’s a lot to address.”
Brattleboro’s review came on the last day of the care board’s annual budget hearing process for Vermont’s 14 community hospitals. Regulators have spent two weeks listening to administrators from the Burlington-based University of Vermont Health and smaller facilities statewide elaborate on the challenges of balancing rising expenses with revenue.
The care board is expected to rule on whether to approve, modify or deny spending plans by Sept. 15.
This is the second year that regulators have expressed worry about the Brattleboro hospital’s finances.
“Stated as directly as possible, we are deeply concerned about BMH’s solvency,” the care board wrote after last year’s review process.
Regulators last fall ordered the hospital to recalculate its current budget or risk becoming the first to receive a state-appointed monitor under a new law adopted to control costs. After seeing the revisions over the winter, regulators limited their response to a warning, although they can still call for some sort of intervention.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Lawsuit alleges Newaygo County Jail, prison health providers failed to treat inmate’s MS
description: When Shane Veltkamp, now 31, entered the Newaygo County Jail in July 2023, he was fully mobile, independent and able to care for himself, although he would be diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, or MS, while detained, according to a lawsuit filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan against the county […]
text:
Getty ImagesWhen Shane Veltkamp, now 31, entered the Newaygo County Jail in July 2023, he was fully mobile, independent and able to care for himself, although he would be diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, or MS, while detained, according to a lawsuit filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan against the county and healthcare workers at both the county jail and statewide facilities. 
By the time he was released from prison in October 2024, the disease had progressed to a point where he “was confined to a wheelchair, suffered from constant dizziness, altered vision, slurred speech, bowel and bladder incontinence, full body tremors and spasms that were so violent that they caused headaches and made it impossible for him to brush his teeth, feed or bath himself.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The lawsuit was filed in federal court in late July, and Veltkamp’s lawyers are in the process of serving the complaint to Advanced Correctional Healthcare, the provider of jail medical care in Newaygo County, and VitalCore Health Strategies, the provider of jail medical care at Michigan Department of Corrections facilities, both named defendants.
Neither Advanced Correctional Healthcare nor VitalCore Health Strategies responded to multiple requests for comment from the Michigan Advance.
MDOC is not a defendant in the lawsuit.
Newaygo County Administrator Christopher Wren, responding to a request for comment, said that the county does not comment on open lawsuits or litigation matters, but that they are aware of the filing.
The alleges that Veltkamp’s MS, which is a chronic neurological disorder in which lesions develop on the brain, was able to progress so severely because Veltkamp was denied adequate healthcare while incarcerated, both at the Newaygo County Jail and at a series of state-level facilities that he was transferred between.
Veltkamp Complaint
 
“I’m dying in here without proper help … please help me,” Veltkamp wrote in what is known as a kite, a term for an official internal request form submitted to prison administrators, in December 2023, while he was detained at the Central Michigan Correctional Facility in St. Louis, Mich, according to the lawsuit filing. 
He was first diagnosed with MS in September 2023 by a neurologist, who recommended he quickly be prescribed Ocrevus. By March 2024, the neurologist, who had repeatedly reached out to the different facilities where Veltkamp was incarcerated to arrange treatment, closed Veltkamp’s file.
“I have not had luck in reaching healthcare coordinator at facility,” the neurologist wrote, according to the lawsuit. “At this point, I am closing encounter and we will have to wait until patient is released to resume therapy.”
Veltkamp’s attorney, Lisa Esser-Weidenfelle, in an interview with the Advance, emphasized the progressive nature of Veltkamp’s MS.
“It’s one of those things that once you’re diagnosed, the goal is to stop it in its tracks. So this medication that the doctor, the neurologist, wanted him to get, Ocrevus, it’s an infusion treatment, and you get it every six months,” Esser-Weidenfeller said. “What it does is it stops the disease from progressing, it stops new lesions from forming on your brain. As these lesions form, they come with neurological deficits.”
Esser-Weidenfeller said that there was not a significant difference in the standard of care that Veltkamp received when he was in Newaygo County Jail versus state-level facilities that are run by MDOC.



Quotation







These are $100 million contracts in some instances. They should be accountable for providing basic care to an inmate.


– Lisa Esser-Weidenfelle, attorney for Shane Veltkamp


“It was pretty consistent across the board with the same systematic ‘watch and wait’ approach with him, and almost, can we kick the can down the road on every front,” Esser-Weidenfeller said.
Despite the healthcare primarily being delegated to private companies, Esser-Weidenfeller said that the responsibility for the care of those incarcerated at facilities does fall, at least in part, on the institution — whether that be the county or the state.
“They have a non-delegable duty, a constitutional duty for the healthcare of the inmates and prisoners there that are in their jail,” she said. “They don’t get to wash their hands of that by contracting it away to a private healthcare corporation.”
The lawsuit also names multiple other defendants, who are individuals involved in healthcare at the various facilities in which Veltkamp was incarcerated. The complaint alleges those individuals either knew or should have known about Veltkamp’s “deteriorating condition and need for urgent treatment to prevent severe and permanent disabilities,” did not initiate proper or timely treatment of his MS, and “ignored his continuing complaints and deteriorating condition, resulting in permanent and severe disabilities.”
Esser-Weidenfeller further emphasized that those in jail or prison have no other options for receiving medical care and that they “completely, wholly rely on the state, these entities, the providers, and these private corporations to get the care they need.”
“We’re not asking for the best care, we’re not asking for exceptional care. But are we providing basic, ordinary care to our inmates?” she continued. “That is just not happening, and someone needs to take a closer look at the contracts that we’re giving these corporations. These are $100 million contracts in some instances. They should be accountable for providing basic care to an inmate.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Advocates: Public defenders in Hinds County give everything. It’s time to return the favor
description: Public defenders introduce themselves during a press conference advocating for Hinds County to pay its public defenders more on Tuesday, Feb. 24, 2026, in Jackson.
text:
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful Mississippians to share their ideas about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.   

Imagine falling into the hardest of times – caring for a disabled spouse in old age or struggling with a sudden mental health crisis – all while facing something you never expected: a criminal case. For many people, this is a matter of circumstance, of poverty and of a system that shows little mercy to those navigating it alone.
If you were in Hinds County, you might get a lucky break. We, the former client advocates of the Hinds County Public Defender’s Office, could step up to support you.
Client advocates are trained professionals embedded in the defender’s office who, among other things, connect clients with the social services, housing, healthcare and mental health support they need to stabilize their lives – and their cases. Your local defender’s office was using our help to break new ground, implementing cutting-edge methods to increase the wellbeing of our most vulnerable neighbors, while lowering the likelihood of future crime.
We came to Jackson from LSU and Pomona College – drawn by the belief that this work matters and that Mississippi is a place where change is possible. Over two years, we saw this belief proven right. We also saw what happens when public defenders aren’t supported.
Over our two-year fellowship here, we connected 274 clients with 366 services, like local food banks, and leveraged our relationships with community-based providers to help clients find refuge in transitional housing. Our impact meant that residents reclaimed meaningful time in their communities rather than behind bars.
What does this look like in practice? An elderly veteran, devoted to his wife, was on the verge of eviction. They had been through months of unanswered phone calls, endless redirections, and confusing, unsuccessful applications. But with our help, they secured income-adjusted housing that included meals, as well as much-needed dental and medical care that opened the door to a more stable life. This transition marked a stark contrast to the client’s last involvement with the criminal legal system decades earlier.
Hannah Williams Credit: Courtesy photo
Now, our client is making it to his court hearings and has paid off his court fines. He is one step closer to reestablishing stability and working toward independence for his family.
When properly resourced and given the support to innovate, this is the true power of public defense. We were proud to bring our work to Hinds County and for what we accomplished. We have now concluded our fellowship with the public defender, but our work lives on through the efforts of the talented and tireless attorneys, social workers, investigators and office staff at the Hinds County Public Defender’s Office.
That effort, however, needs more support.
Unless the Hinds County Board of Supervisors acts to provide additional funding for fiscal year 2027, the public defender’s office will remain severely under-resourced. Earlier this year, the board of supervisors voted to award $261,000 in surplus funds toward salary increases for the Hinds County Public Defender’s Office.
This is a meaningful start, but it is a far cry from the approximately $1 million needed to fully stabilize the office, achieve more sustained pay parity and let the office keep doing forward-thinking work that lowers future crime, increases community stability and fosters opportunity for low-income families.
The right to effective legal counsel is not a courtesy. It is a constitutional guarantee. But in Hinds County, that guarantee is under serious strain. Caseloads are crushing, and they grew worse in 2025 when a fifth circuit courtroom was added to the county with no corresponding increase in public defenders.
Meanwhile, assistant public defenders earn an average of more than $50,000 less than their prosecutor counterparts, a disparity that makes recruiting qualified attorneys nearly impossible and retaining experienced ones even harder.
When defenders aren’t supported, cycles of harm are perpetuated: defenders burn out and resign, cases linger even longer, courtrooms and jails become even more overburdened and the Raymond Detention Center, already strained beyond humane capacity, grows more crowded.
Consequences spiral: families are separated and both local economies and public health suffer as jails send people home sicker, poorer and less able to thrive. When you consider the research showing that prolonged pretrial detention actually increases future crime, the harm of this backlog is even more evident.
Shanai Watson Credit: Courtesy photo
It doesn’t have to be this way. An up-front investment from our lawmakers can not only move our system faster and reduce harm but turn defense into the incredible service access point we’ve helped create here in Hinds County. 
Instead of derailing lives, we can redirect them. Instead of sapping community health, we can improve it. Instead of leeching dollars out of our neighborhoods, we can restore opportunities and prosperity.
The fix is not complicated. Providing the funding that the defenders need to equalize salaries and stabilize the office, as well as additional positions for attorneys, investigators and legal secretaries to address case backlogs, means that clients will get the care and legal support they need. It is also a sign from supervisors that they are serious about the promise of equal justice and opportunity for all citizens.
By funding public defense, we can address the underlying needs that land people in the legal system in the first place, saving money in the long run.
Over the next month, the Hinds County Board of Supervisors will decide on the public defender’s budget. We encourage the board to approve Chief Defender Gail Wright Lowery’s full budget request.
We came to Jackson believing in public service. We leave having witnessed, firsthand, what it looks like when a community’s most vulnerable people are met with both legal skills and human care. The attorneys, investigators, social workers and staff at the Hinds County Public Defender’s Office give everything they have. They deserve a level of funding that recognizes that dedication.  

Shanai Watson joined the Hinds County Public Defender’s Office in 2024. She graduated from Louisiana State University with a bachelor’s degree in sociology (concentration in criminology, minor in political science) and from Northeastern University with a master’s in public policy. At the conclusion of her fellowship, she will attend Harvard Law School, starting in the fall, where she plans to continue exploring the intersections of public interest law, policy and government.

Hannah Williams joined the Hinds County Public Defender’s Office after graduating from Pomona College with a bachelor’s degree in public policy analysis and sociology. At the conclusion of her fellowship, she will pursue her master’s in public administration at New York University’s Robert F. Wagner School of Public Service as a Georgina and Charlotte Bloomberg Public Service fellow, starting in the fall.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Court of Appeals agrees with order forbidding cross-party nominations, fusion voting
description: Three-judge panel of Kansas Court of Appeals backs lower court's dismissal of lawsuit challenging state's ban on cross-party nomination of candidates.
text:
Jack Curtis, chairman of the United Kansas Party, says the organization will appeal the Kansas Court of Appeals' rejection of a claim the longstanding state ban on multi-party nomination of candidates and fusion voting violates the Kansas Constitution. Curtis says the decision will be appealed to the Kansas Supreme Court. In this April 23, 2024, image, Curtis discusses the state's election system. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The Kansas Court of Appeals affirmed a district court decision Friday dismissing claims that state law forbidding fusion voting and cross-party nomination of candidates violated the Kansas Constitution.
The Court of Appeals acknowledged laws requiring candidates to accept a single political party’s nomination and appear once on a ballot touched upon the plaintiffs’ rights to speech and assembly. The three-judge panel concluded the burden imposed on the United Kansas political party, two candidates and voters in Saline and Reno counties didn’t amount to a constitutional impediment because plaintiffs had other avenues to convey political messages.
United Kansas’ lawsuit was filed against Secretary of State Scott Schwab after his office declared in 2024 that candidates nominated by two or more recognized Kansas political parties would be compelled to renounce all but one of the nominations. That led to lawsuits challenging Schwab’s directive, which were consolidated in Saline County District Court. A judge in that court dismissed the suit based on a view the plaintiffs were unlikely to prevail.
The opinion by the Court of Appeals, written by Chief Judge Sarah Warner, affirmed the district court’s perspective. The appellate court said state law forbidding multiple nominations and fusion voting were constitutional because they served important state interests, including preserving election integrity and preventing voter confusion.
“The ballot restrictions … do not violate the members of a political party’s expression and assembly rights under sections 3 and 11 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights, as they serve important state interests that justify the burdens placed on the party’s desired avenue of communicating its goals,” Warner said in the opinion.
Jack Curtis, chairman of United Kansas, said the Court of Appeals’ decision would be appealed to the Kansas Supreme Court. He said state’s nullification of United Kansas’ candidate nominations was a violation of constitutional rights of speech and association.
“Any law invalidating our nominees undermines the fundamental rights of candidates to associate with the parties of their choice and of parties and voters to choose their preferred nominees,” Curtis said. “We respect the court’s decision, but disagree with the outcome.”
Curtis said the state Supreme Court should have an opportunity to “ensure the rights of our party, our candidates and Kansas voters are respected and the Kansas Constitution is honored.”
The system advocated by United Kansas would allow candidates to be nominated by two or more political parties. Votes for candidates would be tallied separately by party before combined to produce a final result. The plaintiffs say the fusion process would benefit minor parties, especially those aligned on specific public policies.
The state’s current approach to elections made it virtually impossible for candidates to be elected unless affiliated with the Republican or Democratic parties, the plaintiffs said.
For the past 125 years, Kansas has managed elections in a way that blocked fusion voting and required a candidate’s name appear on a ballot only once. Four states — Connecticut, New York, Oregon, and Vermont — enable fusion voting on general election ballots.
The decision of the Court of Appeals signed by Warner and Court of Appeals Judges Thomas Malone and Stephen Hill said the state could select a different ballot method to conduct elections, but the existing “straightforward ballot method” didn’t thwart constitutional rights.
The foundation of the case was built in 2024 by United Kansas when it nominated Lori Blake as its candidate in the 69th district in the Kansas House and Rep. Jason Probst as its candidate in the House’s 102nd District. Blake and Probst were unopposed in the Democratic Party’s primary.
The secretary of state’s office sent a letter to Blake and Probst indicating two Kansas laws required them to choose a single party with whom to affiliate on the general election ballot. The candidates opted to be listed as nominees of the Democratic Party. Both lost to Republicans in the 2024 election.
District Court Judge Jared Johnson, who handled the consolidated lawsuit, dismissed the case after concluding the state had legitimate interests in prohibiting fusion voting.
His reasons included avoiding potential for gamesmanship at the nomination stage and improperly inflating party support, avoiding loss of competition that could come from minor parties selecting already-popular candidates of major parties and avoiding diminished accountability that could result from blurring distinctions between the parties.
