title: Delaware fast-tracks broadband, health projects, raising questions about who gets to skip permitting line
description: JobsFirst promises permitting decisions within 120 business days, but leaves government deciding which projects move first — and which applicants must continue to wait WILMINGTON, Del. — Delaware will fast-track three broadband and health care projects through a state permitting system designed to produce decisions within 120 business days, but the announcem[...]
text:
The accelerator does not simply improve permitting for every business, developer and organization. It creates a priority lane, with the Governor’s Office deciding which applicants receive expedited attention and which remain in the regular bureaucratic process. Image created with AI on 8/14
JobsFirst promises permitting decisions within 120 business days, but leaves government deciding which projects move first — and which applicants must continue to wait
WILMINGTON, Del. — Delaware will fast-track three broadband and health care projects through a state permitting system designed to produce decisions within 120 business days, but the announcement is also raising a broader question: If state government can move quickly for selected applicants, why can’t it do so for everyone?
Gov. Matt Meyer announced Thursday that a rural broadband expansion and two ChristianaCare health campuses have been accepted into the JobsFirst Permitting Accelerator.
The program gives designated projects a single government contact, coordinates reviews across state agencies and creates a process for escalating unresolved problems. Reviews that might otherwise take 18 to 24 months are targeted for completion in about six months.
“JobsFirst is about tackling Delaware’s biggest challenges with urgency, not bureaucracy,” Meyer said. “Whether it’s expanding access to health care, closing the digital divide or building the infrastructure our communities need, Delawareans shouldn’t have to wait years for projects that people need now.”
That argument makes a strong case for faster permitting. It also highlights the unequal treatment built into the program.
The government chooses who moves first
The accelerator does not simply improve permitting for every business, developer and organization. It creates a priority lane, with the Governor’s Office deciding which applicants receive expedited attention and which remain in the regular bureaucratic process.
Executive Order 18 establishes eligibility categories covering housing, broadband, energy, water and sewer, and mixed-use development. However, meeting an eligibility definition does not guarantee admission. The order says the governor or the governor’s designee “may designate” a nominated project as a priority.
The state’s published process says the Governor’s Office considers eligibility, readiness and permitting constraints. It does not provide a public scoring system explaining how competing qualified projects are ranked or why one applicant moves ahead of another.
That distinction matters. Without clearly published selection standards, the accelerator gives state officials significant discretion over who receives a dedicated coordinator, enforced deadlines and direct access to an expedited review.
The administration’s announcement did not say how many projects applied, whether any were rejected or why these three were selected over other potentially eligible projects. It also did not identify the category under which the two ChristianaCare health campuses qualified. Health care is not listed among the program’s five initial project categories.
Projects promise public benefits
The projects themselves promise substantial public benefits.
Talkie Communications plans to install buried fiber within existing roadway rights-of-way, bringing gigabit-speed internet service to 1,448 unserved homes and businesses in Kent and Sussex counties. The project is supported by the Federal Communications Commission’s Rural Digital Opportunity Fund.
ChristianaCare’s planned Georgetown campus would combine a health center and neighborhood hospital. It would provide primary, specialty, behavioral health and outpatient services, along with an eight-bed emergency department and eight inpatient beds.
A similar campus planned for Camden would expand health care and community-based hospital capacity in Kent County.
Accelerating those projects does not mean environmental or public safety requirements will be waived. The administration says JobsFirst changes the speed and coordination of reviews, not the standards applicants must meet. The 120-business-day target also promises a decision, not necessarily an approval.
Those safeguards make the faster process easier to defend. But they also support extending it to other applicants.
Why shouldn’t every applicant receive faster service?
If agencies can review applications simultaneously instead of sequentially, provide applicants with a single checklist and hold employees accountable for missed deadlines, those practices should become the normal permitting system — not a special service reserved for projects selected by the executive branch.
There is also a question of agency capacity. Unless the state has added staff or eliminated unnecessary work, moving priority projects ahead could divert attention from businesses and organizations already waiting.
The administration has not disclosed whether the accelerator is reducing the overall permitting backlog or rearranging the order in which applications are processed.
Small businesses could be especially disadvantaged. Large institutions often have attorneys, engineers and government-relations professionals to help navigate state processes. Smaller applicants are more likely to need the coordination and accountability provided by JobsFirst, but they may be less likely to propose projects large enough to receive priority status.
Transparency should begin with selection
The state has created a public dashboard to track designated projects, participating agencies, required permits and approaching deadlines. That is a meaningful transparency measure once a project is accepted.
Transparency should also cover the selection process. The public should be able to see all applications, the standards used to evaluate them, the reasons projects were accepted or rejected, and whether giving one project priority caused delays for others.
The administration says JobsFirst is being introduced in stages and could eventually lead to a coordinated permitting system covering the full range of state approvals.
That should be the objective.
Everyone should have access to the fast lane
Broadband service and health care facilities should not remain trapped in government bureaucracy. Neither should a housing project, a new employer or a small Delaware business simply because the Governor’s Office did not put it in the priority lane.
The real measure of JobsFirst will not be whether government can move three selected projects faster. It will be whether Delaware uses what it learns to give every qualified applicant a clear, accountable and timely decision.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico senator calls for uranium moratorium amid recent spike in extraction interest
description: A New Mexico state senator is calling for a moratorium on uranium mining, saying the state needs to hold off on new permits until emerging extraction technology is better understood and the state develops a regulatory framework that “reflects the needs of our communities, the needs of our economic base, and not the needs of industry.”
text:
New Mexico Sen. Angel Charley (D-Acoma) on Aug. 13, 2026, called for a statewide moratorium on uranium mining, given the amount of community pushback renewed mining has received all over the state. (Photo by Austin Fisher/Source NM)A New Mexico state senator is calling for a moratorium on uranium mining, saying the state needs to hold off on new permits until emerging extraction technology is better understood and the state develops a regulatory framework that “reflects the needs of our communities, the needs of our economic base, and not the needs of industry.”
State Sen. Angel Charley (D-Acoma) said a temporary ban on all new permits is necessary following a presentation Thursday to the interim legislative Radioactive and Hazardous Materials Committee. The presentation featured anti-mining advocates who described newly invigorated interest by companies seeking to mine uranium from deposits all over the state, including near Church Rock, Canjilon and Pie Town. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Charley likened her push for a moratorium to similar calls from fellow Democrats for a temporary ban on data centers, which state Reps. Micaela Lara Cadena (D-Mesilla) and Angelica Rubio (D-Las Cruces) pitched their colleagues on earlier this week. 
“When we’re putting forward moratoriums for AI centers, I think it is responsible and incumbent on us to put forward a moratorium on uranium mining until we understand the risk of the new technologies,” she said. 
During the presentation, Leona Morgan, a Diné community advocate, described her concerns about in situ recovery mining, also known as in situ leach mining, a process that companies are proposing to use to extract uranium from aquifers. 
NuFuels, Inc., a company seeking to mine uranium in New Mexico, has said the process is safe and less invasive than conventional mining, but the New Mexico Department of Justice recently argued in a Nuclear Regulatory Commission filing that no example exists in the country of groundwater supplies being restored to their pre-mining contamination levels at sites where the process is used. 
Charley pointed to Virginia’s uranium moratorium, which the U.S. Supreme Court upheld in 2020, as proof that states can legally halt uranium production without running afoul of the federal government. 
“It can be done, and it should be done, because we cannot, as New Mexicans, continue to regulate industry after contamination,” she said. 
Anti-uranium advocates wrest control of public hearing on proposed mine near Navajo Nation

Charley told Source NM in a text message Friday that she is still considering whether she’ll introduce moratorium legislation ahead of the upcoming 60-day session, which begins Jan. 19. 
But she’s “open” to the idea, she said, especially given how many mining proposals are gathering momentum all over New Mexico and how many counties are considering their own county-level bans. 
“I would need to meet with the coalition that presented yesterday before moving anything forward,” she said. “What struck me is the diverse counties enacting moratoriums throughout the state.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: In bid to stop Saline Data Center tax break, an attorney argues the township skipped crucial steps
description: Following the Saline Township Board of Trustees’ decision to sign off on a property tax abatement for a controversial hyperscale data center under development by Oracle, OpenAI and Related Digital, one resident and her attorney are calling on the Michigan State Tax Commission to deny the request. In a letter to the commission submitted on […]
text:
Sign for Related Digital's hyperscale data center, known as "The Barn", in Saline Township, Michigan. June 20, 2026. | Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceFollowing the Saline Township Board of Trustees’ decision to sign off on a property tax abatement for a controversial hyperscale data center under development by Oracle, OpenAI and Related Digital, one resident and her attorney are calling on the Michigan State Tax Commission to deny the request.
In a letter to the commission submitted on Wednesday, Kathryn Haushalter of Saline Township and Ellis Boal, an attorney from Charlevoix, said the $43 billion project is ineligible for the tax break, arguing that the township did not take steps needed to ensure the area was eligible for a tax exemption. 
Speaking to reporters at a Thursday press conference, Boal said Saline Township did not hold a public hearing prior to establishing the project site as an “industrial development district,” violating The Plant Rehabilitation and Industrial Development Districts Act.
By missing that crucial step, Boal and Haushalter argued that the community did not actually create an industrial development district, leaving Oracle Cloud Services LLC unable to file for an Industrial Facilities Exemption Certificate requesting the tax exemption.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“They have to go in that order,” Boal said. “The IDD has to be established first, and the IFEC, the exemption certificate, then has to be filed.”
While the township board posted a notice for a public hearing on the matter set for Sept. 10, 2025, they never actually held that hearing, Boal contended, noting it was set for the same date and time as a township board meeting.
Boal also pointed to comments from the township’s attorney, Fred Lucas, from a video of the meeting. 
After the board declined to rezone the property for the data center, Lucas told members there was no longer a need to hold the hearing on the tax abatement, as they had already denied zoning for the project.
When asked for a comment, Lucas directed Michigan Advance to another attorney, Michael Homier of the Foster Swift firm, who is assisting the township with legal matters tied to the data center.
Homier said he was unable to comment, as he had not been provided with a copy of the letter, or any of the exhibits Boal referenced. 
“To my knowledge the township didn’t receive a copy,” Homier said.
A list of recipients at the bottom of the letter did not include any members of the Saline Township Board of Trustees.
Township Supervisor Tom Hammond and Oracle did not respond to requests for comment. This story will be updated if a response is received.
Under threat of legal action, the board agreed to move forward with rezoning. Boal’s letter also noted a provision in the settlement that required the township to complete a public hearing and establish an industrial development district.
On Oct. 15, 2025, the board approved a resolution establishing the Industrial Development District. 
“The next question was: ‘Could they have a public hearing right now?” No, they cannot,” Boal said, adding that Industrial Facilities Exemption Certificate applicants cannot begin construction more than six months prior to filing an application.
A copy of Oracle’s Industrial Facilities Exemption Certificate Application provided by Boal lists the “start date of property improvements” as Feb. 6 2026.

text:
Joe Saunders of Equality Florida addresses a news conference at the Florida Capitol on Jan. 16, 2024. Flanking him, l-r, are Senate members Shevrin Jones and Tracie Davis. (Photo by Michael Moline/Florida Phoenix)Two organizations say they’re investing a quarter of a million dollars to support “pro-equality, pro-academic freedom” school board candidates this election season.
The Equality Florida Political Action Committee and Southern Poverty Law Center Action Fund announced Friday morning that the $250,000 will go toward 300,000 pieces of mail to reach more than 200,000 voters.
The mailers are for “candidates in critical Florida school board races,” which include four in Orange County, three in Sarasota County, two in Seminole County, and one each in Hillsborough, Palm Beach, Pinellas, and Osceola counties.
“The program aims to help voters identify which candidates are committed to getting politics out of the classroom and to recentering schools away from censorship and back toward student success,” a news release announcing the effort reads.
Highlighting Gov. Ron DeSantis’ and Moms for Liberty’s focus on school board races in resent years, the organizations are looking to counter those efforts.
The Florida Trib reported last month that Moms for Liberty, a Florida-born organization with nationwide reach, had not invested in any school board races this cycle.
“Moms for Liberty’s influence has been on a long decline in its home state as the organization faced a wave of resignations, chapter dissolutions and scandals among Moms for Liberty leadership,” the Trib reported.
The Moms for Liberty website does list nine endorsements for school board candidates in Florida, although it seems outdated given that three are not running for reelection and one lost her 2024 race. According to its own count, the organization’s endorsements in Florida in 2022 won at a rate of 80%.
In 2022, most DeSantis backed school board candidates won. In 2024, 11 of his 24 endorsements lost in the primary elections, six won, and seven faced runoffs.
Most DeSantis-backed school board candidates in FL won in the 2022 elections

Joe Saunders, director of Equality Florida’s PAC, said that this year the organization is “bringing an end to the extremism and sideshows.”
“Together, we can fire Moms for Liberty, get politics out of our classrooms, and elect public school champions who believe in our teachers and will fight for the safety and dignity of every student,” Saunders said in the news release.
Another $150,000 is dedicated to digital ads and direct voter contact, the organizations say.
DeSantis’ time in office has been marked by “culture war” issues like more strictly regulating what books students may read in school, punishing teachers who do not stick to pronouns for students according to their gender assigned at birth, and the Florida Board of Education formally adopting a conservative vision for education in the state.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Gender-affirming care for minors will continue in Maine despite latest federal attempt to block it
description: Maine will continue providing gender-affirming care despite an announcement from the Trump administration banning Medicaid from covering hormone therapy and procedures for children under 18. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced the rule on Tuesday, which also prohibits Children’s Health Insurance Program, or CHIP, funds from being used for[...]
text:
Advocates for transgender rights rallied outside the Statehouse in Trenton, New Jersey, on Jan. 5, 2026, to demand lawmakers pass a bill that would protect gender-affirming care in New Jersey. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo / New Jersey Monitor)Maine will continue providing gender-affirming care despite an announcement from the Trump administration banning Medicaid from covering hormone therapy and procedures for children under 18.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced the rule on Tuesday, which also prohibits Children’s Health Insurance Program, or CHIP, funds from being used for this care, typically sought out by people whose gender identity is different from their sex assigned at birth. Under CMS’s definition, gender-affirming care includes puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones and surgical operations. The policy takes effect Oct. 13.
For children on Medicaid and CHIP who currently rely on gender-affirming hormone therapy, state plans may continue to use federal Medicaid funding for up to six months. Funds can still be used for mental health care for kids, the agency said.
“To be clear, gender-affirming care remains legal in Maine and will remain accessible to all patients at Maine Family Planning’s 18 clinics,” said Olivia Penngington, associate vice president of public affairs for the state’s largest reproductive healthcare provider.
“We will do everything in our power to provide this lifesaving care across the state and we will never turn patients away for their inability to pay or their lack of insurance coverage.”
In Maine, between 3,000-4,000 people in Maine receive gender-affirming care and 27% of those people get that funding from MaineCare, according to WMTW. 
The rule is the latest in a series of actions President Donald Trump’s administration has taken to restrict gender-affirming care. Last year, Maine joined a multi-state lawsuit challenging a declaration that called treatments like puberty blockers, hormone therapy and surgeries unsafe and ineffective for children seeking gender-affirming care. That declaration also warned doctors that they could be excluded from federal health programs like Medicare and Medicaid if they provide those types of care. Despite the lawsuit and objections from several national medical associations that advocate for evidence-based care, the proposed Medicaid and CHIP rule has now been finalized.
“The Trump administration knows that access to this care is popular and that they can’t outright ban it,” Pennington said. “So they attack the funding sources as a backdoor ban on peoples’ personal health care decisions.”
Maine law specifically requires MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program, to cover gender- affirming care, which means that even if this rule were to be enacted, children who rely on MaineCare would still be able to have their care covered through state funding, according to Aspen Ruhlin, community engagement manager at the Bangor-based Mabel Wadsworth Center. The Maine Attorney General’s Office declined to comment on whether the state plans to challenge the final rule.
Much like MaineCare can still pay for abortions through state funding despite the Hyde Amendment banning federal Medicaid reimbursements to be used for the procedure, the cost of gender-affirming care for minors will shift to the state. However, because there are a relatively small number of Maine youth seeking such care under MaineCare, Ruhlin said the cost shift would not be a big financial burden. 
“I personally do not have concerns about creating some sort of financial shortfall for the state,” they said. “The concerns there are just that this is normal essential care, and the feds putting those restrictions is just really targeted intentional harm towards a marginalized community.”
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to questions about how much gender-affirming care costs the state currently.
Some Maine providers told Maine Morning Star they’re afraid of being targeted for providing  these services, which then puts this care at risk. Across the country, hospitals in both Democratic and Republican-led states have responded to Trump’s attacks on transgender health care by withdrawing care.
No Maine providers have made such announcements yet. MaineHealth said in a statement that it is “currently seeking additional information and clarification from state and federal officials with respect to this announcement,” while reinforcing its commitment to providing needed care to all patients regardless of insurance status or ability to pay.
However, Ruhlin said some patients who need hormone therapy, puberty blockers or other types of care are foregoing it due to fear. After the announcement, staff at Mabel Wadsworth were preparing for calls from patients seeking to clarify if they could continue their treatment.
“The exceedingly anti-trans sentiments from the federal government has led to a lot of trans folks making the decision to not pursue gender-affirming hormone therapy when they otherwise feel it would be a good fit for them,” Ruhlin said. “Because they are concerned about their safety. Not from the medications themselves — they are very safe — but because the targeting from the government keeps getting worse.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi opioid settlement grantees can seek monthly reimbursement
description: Members of the Mississippi Opioid Settlement Fund Advisory Council meet on August 13.
text:
The Mississippi Opioid Settlement Fund Advisory Council approved monthly reimbursement for all 13 of the attorney general’s office funded grantees that requested the change during its August meeting. 
Under the original model, organizations reported costs and expected to be reimbursed every three months. However, some awardees worried that schedule could negatively impact their finances or require them to take out loans. Their concerns delayed the disbursement of roughly $50 million in settlement funds, awarded earlier this year by the Mississippi Legislature following lawsuit payments from companies that contributed to the opioid crisis.
The Mississippi Administrative Office of Courts and the state Department of Mental Health also requested the shorter repayment timeframe for a portion of their grant-awarded projects.
At a July meeting, the council voted to allow applicants the option to be reimbursed monthly, and asked them to submit an explanation of the proposed change’s benefits.
Out of 28 awardees, the 13 that submitted requests said holding onto costs for three months of staff pay and vendor expenses would create significant cash flow burdens. Some organizations, including the North central Mississippi community mental health center Communicare and the Pontotoc county-based Chase House of Restoration, plan to use their funds to purchase and renovate buildings for substance use recovery programs.
“Advancing three months of contractor payments, construction costs, building materials, inspections, and other capital expenses before reimbursement is simply beyond our financial capacity,” wrote Mason Hester, founder of Chase House, in his request. He added that quarterly reporting would delay access for the individuals and families awaiting treatment. 
Before passing the motion to approve the model change, Joseph Sclafani, a council member and policy adviser to Gov. Tate Reeves, raised concerns about potential fraud from nonprofit organizations without existing track records. 
“It’s harder to fraud on a quarterly basis than it is on a monthly basis,” he said. 
Wendy Bailey, executive director of the Department of Mental Health and co-chair of the advisory council, said her department’s monthly reimbursement process allows them to keep a close eye on how grant funds are being spent. She emphasized the importance of having an option for quicker repayments.
“The majority of our grants go to the community mental health centers, and they all serve individuals regardless of an ability to pay,” she told Mississippi Today. “So it is very important for them to be reimbursed on a monthly basis.”
Plans for the next round
Applications for the 2026 fiscal year will be available to view on Aug. 24 and go live starting Aug. 31, said Deputy Attorney General Doug Miracle, who chaired the meeting. The application will include language stating that awardees can submit financial reports on either a monthly or quarterly basis. 
Applicants will have until October 5 to submit their applications, after which the third-party health consultant Steadman Group will do an initial grading of applications. The consulting group was contracted earlier this year to support the council’s grant approval process.
The advisory council will next meet on Nov. 23 and Nov. 30 to review the applications and Steadman Group’s recommendations. They will recommend applicants to the Legislature in early December, with Mississippi lawmakers making final decisions during the 2027 legislative session. 
Mississippi State Health Officer Dr. Daniel Edney told Mississippi Today having outside help will make the council’s workflow smoother. He said 2025 was an intense year for the council that ran on a tight timeline to create an application process and recommend applicants for Mississippi legislators to fund. Mississippi used the opioid settlement funds specifically earmarked to combat future overdoses. 
“Last year was the best we’ve ever had to push that amount of money out that quickly,” Edney said. “And, and as of today, it’s out serving the people of Mississippi and saving lives.” 
Michelle Williams, chief of staff for Attorney General Lynn Fitch, was positive about the next cycle of applications. 
“We had some great projects funded last year, and we are looking forward to seeing what kind of applications we get this year,” she told Mississippi Today. “There are a lot of really good people out there doing great and innovative things, and we are excited by how it’s going to impact our state.”

title: Congressional approval not needed for White House ballroom, Trump tells high court
text: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump asked the U.S. Supreme Court Thursday to intervene in a lower court decision that halts his $400 million White House ballroom construction unless he receives authorization from Congress.The administration requested the justices grant an immediate stay to a 2-1 federal appeals court decision that sided with historic preservationists who argued Trump doesn’t have the authority to build a 90,000-square-foot ballroom where the White House East Wing stood until Trump ordered its demolition in October 2025.The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit issued the decision on Aug. 7 but delayed the ruling for two weeks to allow the administration time to appeal.U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer, who previously defended Trump before the high court as his personal defense attorney, argued the project was needed to enhance security at the White House.The “updated East Wing complex is absolutely required and should not be enjoined,” he said, citing assassination attempts on the president. Sauer also wrote that Congress has “twice over” already authorized the current project, through a 1916 law governing the National Park Service and a 1978 statute, by empowering the Department of the Interior to embark on major construction projects and delegating powers to the president to use appropriated funds to alter the White House.“Following this tradition, President Trump determined that many factorsurgently required modernizing the old East Wing — most critically, that it no longer performed vital security functions,” according to the appeal.“Compounding those problems were structural defects, such as a degraded foundation, crumbling roof, pervasive mold and mildew, water-related deterioration, obsolete electrical infrastructure, toxic asbestos, and lead paint.”‘Military complex’The Trump administration has asserted publicly the project would serve as a security upgrade. Sauer again made that argument in his 45-page appeal. The ballroom, which is expected to seat 1,000 people, will be incorporated into a “highly integrated military complex” descending several stories underground, he told the court, and would include security features such as drone-proof ceilings, bomb shelters, sniper nests, “military-grade venting,” and “state-of-the-art hospital and medical facilities.”According to Thursday’s appeal, the project is already 65% complete, with a concrete-and-steel “superstructure” reaching five stories underground and 70-feet high, occupying nearly 50,000 square feet. The construction has accelerated over the past four months, with workers on a 250-person crew operating 20 hours a day, seven days a week, “to keep the Project ahead of schedule and under budget,” Sauer wrote, adding that $200 million has been spent or committed to date, and has been “shouldered by private donations.”Court battleIn mid-April, a judge for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia blocked any above-ground construction on the ballroom, allowing underground construction on security facilities to continue. A day later, April 17, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia stayed the lower court ruling and put the case on a fast track. The National Trust for Historic Preservation hailed the split appeals court decision earlier this month as a “great day for our country and for the American people's right to voice their opinions about the historic places they cherish, including the White House.”“From the beginning, our position has been clear and consistent: the law states that only Congress can authorize the construction of a ballroom at the White House,” the trust’s president and CEO Brent Leggs said in a statement Aug. 7.The National Trust for Historic Preservation did not immediately respond to a request for additional comment Friday.The East Wing was originally built in 1902 as a receiving area for visitors, according to the White House Historical Association. A 1942 renovation added a bomb shelter and a second story. From the late 1970s onward, beginning with first lady Roslynn Carter, the wing housed the office of first ladies and their staff.

description: LINCOLN — Former state Sen. Dan McKeon’s criminal case in Lancaster County Court was dismissed after he successfully completed a court diversion program, according to court documents. McKeon, of Amherst, faced a Class III misdemeanor charge stemming from allegations that he inappropriately touched a legislative staff member during an end-of-session party las[...]
text:
State Sen. Dan McKeon of Amherst addresses his decision to resign from Nebraska Legislature hours before doing so. Jan. 13, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Former state Sen. Dan McKeon’s criminal case in Lancaster County Court was dismissed after he successfully completed a court diversion program, according to court documents.
McKeon, of Amherst, faced a Class III misdemeanor charge stemming from allegations that he inappropriately touched a legislative staff member during an end-of-session party last May, according to the Nebraska State Patrol. An Aug. 28 court date has been canceled.
According to court documents filed Thursday, the case was dismissed with prejudice due to successful completion of the diversion program. McKeon was ordered to bear the costs of the case. Dismissal with prejudice means the case cannot be filed again.
McKeon told the Examiner that he was glad the case is behind him and that he recognized it was the path he needed to take to “clear his name.”
“Instead of being negative, I’m trying to turn all of this into a positive,” McKeon said.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
McKeon resigned from the Legislature minutes before debate was set to begin on a resolution to expel him, which if successful, would have been a first in Nebraska.
A State Patrol investigation initially led to McKeon being cited for misdemeanor public indecency in October, a Class II misdemeanor. Prosecutors ultimately charged him with disturbing the peace, a Class III misdemeanor.
McKeon had planned to plead no contest, according to his lawyer Perry Pirsch, but he changed course and pleaded not guilty after the Legislature’s Executive Board recommended expulsion. He has denied any inappropriate conduct.
McKeon’s March 19 bench trial date was postponed after he was accepted into a diversion program, which acts as an alternative to prosecution. Lancaster County Attorney Pat Condon previously told the Examiner that if McKeon completed the program, the case would be dismissed.
According to the Lancaster County website, diversion programs exist to help individuals “overcome their charges, avoid the consequences of having a criminal record, and address the underlying issues impacting criminal behavior.”
Pirsch previously said McKeon completed a “sensitivity training” at the Executive Board’s request before lawmakers pursued a motion to expel him.
McKeon said his diversion program consisted of community service, which he completed by putting up campaign signs for a conservative candidate he declined to name. He said he also completed an eight-hour “victim training” course and attended six counseling sessions.
“My client and I are hopeful that the diversion services completed provided some benefit to Mr. McKeon, and that he doesn’t repeat his past actions,” said Kathleen Neary, the attorney representing the legislative staffer.
The Examiner is not publishing the alleged victim’s name because it is the policy of States Newsroom and the Examiner not to identify people who say they have been abused unless they wish to talk publicly.
While McKeon said he doesn’t have immediate plans to run for public office again, he hasn’t ruled it out. He said he believes there aren’t enough public officials “doing the right thing,” and he called for more mentorship, love and respect “across the board.”
“If the stars align right, maybe,” McKeon said in response to a question about his interest in running for office.

name: VTDigger
title: The future of logging and conservation is one and the same
authors: Jonathan Leibowitz and Robert T. Perschel
description:
Saving Vermont's wild places depends on keeping its logging industry alive.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  The future of logging and conservation is one and the same.
text:
This commentary is by Jonathan Leibowitz, the president and CEO of Montpelier-based Northeast Wilderness Trust, and Robert T. Perschel, author of “Numinosity: A New England Forester’s Search for the Ineffable” and former executive director of the New England Forestry Foundation.
The closure of Finch Paper’s pulp mill in Glens Falls, New York, is a blow that will echo across the Northeast for years. For loggers, truckers, foresters and woodlot landowners, this is not some distant threat to worry about in the future. It is — today — lost income, lost markets for wood and the continuing fraying of a way of life.
One of us has spent a career practicing and advancing forestry; the other leads an organization devoted to wilderness protection. You might expect us to disagree about what comes next. We don’t. Because we both understand a truth that gets lost in moments of crisis like this one: The amount of land we can set aside as wilderness depends wholly on how well we manage the rest of the forest and thus the health of the timber industry. Both wildlands and managed woodlands are needed. Conservation underpins it all.
Wildlands and managed woodlands are not competitors. They are two halves of the same landscape, and the fate of each is bound to the other. When local mills close and markets for timber disappear, landowners lose the income that helps keep forests whole. Land then gets sold, subdivided and paved over. That fragmentation is the true threat to the Northern forest, and it takes everything with it: the logging jobs, the deer camps and a way of life. It also takes away the possibility of conserving wild places.
Put simply, a wilderness advocate who wants more wildlands should be rooting hard for a thriving forest economy. And a logger who wants strong markets and a healthy land base should welcome a network of wildlands that keeps large forest blocks whole, stores abundant carbon, provides the wildlife habitat and ecological processes that are difficult or impossible to maintain in managed forests, and models the full range of what these forests can be. Neither vision succeeds on a landscape carved up, fragmented and developed. Keeping forests as forests is something we ought to all agree on. We all have a responsibility to work together toward that end.
But forests won’t remain forests without conservation. The forces battering the forest products industry are enormous: global commodity markets, consolidation, tariffs, shifting demand for paper, rural development pressure and the rising cost of doing business. These forces are confounding precisely because no logger, landowner or policymaker controls them on their own. And we know that when the ground shifts beneath us, it’s easy to seek a convenient scapegoat. Recently, there has been a lot of finger-pointing at conservation. But the honest answer is harder: The threats to forestry and to forests largely come from the same place, and they are bigger than any of us alone. Vermont has lost more than 5,000 acres of forest per year on average since forest cover peaked in 1997, while the forests that remain shrink into smaller parcels. Conservation is the counterforce to that trend.

READ MORE

Conservation — whether of wilderness or managed woodlands — and a viable logging industry are complementary, not opposed. And the research backs that up. 
In 2024, a team of New England forest scientists laid out exactly how conservation and the logging industry fit together in a report called “Beyond the ‘Illusion of Preservation,’” reviewed by us. Its central insight should be read aloud at every meeting where conservation and forestry are pitted against each other. New England produces only about three-quarters of the wood it consumes, and we make up the difference by importing wood from places with often far weaker environmental and social protections than ours. So when we reduce logging while keeping our own consumption static, we are not saving forests. We are simply exporting the environmental costs of our lifestyle elsewhere. The Finch closure, which will merely send pulp production elsewhere, is the illusion arriving on our doorstep.
The report’s answer is not to choose between conservation and logging or even between wilderness and managed forests. Rather, it is to protect far more of both: 70% of New England permanently protected as a mosaic of both wildlands and actively and responsibly managed woodlands. The report even shows that up to 20% of the region could be permanently conserved as wilderness while still meeting our timber demand. The better we care for the health of managed forests, the more of the landscape can be left wild.
It bears repeating that the overwhelming majority of conserved land in Vermont and across New England remains open to logging. When done well, conservation is not the end of forestry; it is one of the few tools that guarantees a land base for forestry. The path forward for the Northern forest, here in Vermont and beyond, will be built by loggers, foresters, farmers, landowners and conservationists working together with a shared vision for the forest’s future, or it will not be built at all.
The woods have always asked us to take the long view. We argue that the long view says this: Keep the forest whole, keep people working in it, and keep some of it wild. Conserve as much as possible before it disappears. These goals rise and fall together.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Mass. regulators approve new plan to shield solar customers from unexpected price spikes
description: The move, adopted with buy-in from the energy industry, advocates, and state officials, could save thousands of electric customers looking to install solar panels across the state from being saddled with last-minute, seemingly random charges that could stretch past $10,000 per project.
text:
IN THE BATTLE to lower stubbornly-high energy costs for struggling residents, Massachusetts regulators adopted a proposal with buy-in from the energy industry, advocates, and state officials that would wipe away a steep barrier that has squeezed the uptake of solar power.  
The move – which would dramatically reduce solar connection costs for some homeowners and will take effect this fall – was finalized this week by the Department of Public Utilities. It could save thousands of electric customers looking to install solar panels across the state from being saddled with last-minute, seemingly random charges that could stretch past $10,000 per project. 
“We knew we needed to do something about this,” Staci Rubin, a DPU commissioner, said in an interview. “This is an outcome that everybody is going to be supportive of. That’s rare at the DPU.” 
The change is a small win for Gov. Maura Healey’s push to streamline new projects, especially for solar, as part of an “all of the above” approach to energy. It comes at a time when electricity prices in the state are reaching double the national average, power demand is rising, and deadlines for climate commitments are creeping closer. Massachusetts had already been falling behind on new solar installations and a goal to deploy 10 gigawatts of solar by 2028 even before Republicans in Washington eliminated federal incentives for the clean energy source. 
When a resident attempts to add solar to their home, one of the last steps in the wonky process to connect the project to the grid, known as interconnection, is for the utility to determine whether the transformer serving that home can handle the electrical output the home will now be sending back to the grid. A key part of the financial puzzle for a resident to add solar is the ability to sell excess power generated to reduce their electric bill. 
But if the utility determines the transformer can’t handle that influx of power, it needs to upgrade that infrastructure — costs that average thousands of dollars and currently fall on the sole homeowner responsible for triggering that upgrade, even if that transformer serves multiple homes and businesses, like many do. 
That turns the system into a game of chance based on when you happen to get in line: If one neighbor adds solar and eats into the available capacity but doesn’t trigger the upgrade, the next unlucky home to add solar may push the transformer past its limit and get penalized just for going second. Once that homeowner pays for the upgrade, the third homeowner that adds solar will reap the benefits of the new transformer’s expanded capacity without paying for the costs. 
The homeowner often doesn’t know whether or not they will trigger the pricey upgrade until the project is in the permitting process and financing and construction work have been secured. 
That’s exactly what happened to Abe Walters, a homeowner in an environmental justice community in Bellingham who CommonWealth Beacon spotlighted earlier this year. Walters had already secured a loan from the Massachusetts Community Climate Bank, selected an installer after receiving a slew of estimates, and navigated ever-changing tax credits to make his project pencil out through lower utility bills only to then be hit with a transformer upgrade cost of $12,000 — muddying the financial viability of his project. 
The DPU’s approval of the new system eliminates that risk, instead requiring each homeowner looking to install a residential solar project or battery storage to pay a $225 fee to their utility. That fee would more equitably share those upgrade costs that all customers benefit from, covering up to $10,000 of any necessary infrastructure costs for connecting solar to the grid for Eversource and National Grid customers and up to $1,450 for Unitil customers.   
Most other states have a system much like Massachusetts’s current one, but Minnesota, Maine, and Connecticut have adopted solutions similar to the one the DPU just greenlit. 
“People who are eager to help participate and contribute to the clean energy transition can do so without these major cost barriers on the interconnection side,” Rubin said. “When we have more people with solar facilities and more solar on the system, that’s increased supply, and that’s going to drive down costs for all distribution customers.” 
Though only roughly 3 percent of Bay State residents adding small solar projects are hit with the unexpected sticker shock for upgrading transformers, forcing them to either pay the steep price tag, downsize their projects to avoid triggering the upgrade, or cancel them outright, the DPU’s move is being seen as one to bolster project certainty.  
“We joke in the sales team that we get so much practice because we get to sell a project five times,” said James Manzer, regional vice president of the solar company ReVision Energy who led the part of the larger DPU working group focused on this new cost-share plan. “You sell the initial time, and then permitting comes back. You’ve got to resell because maybe you had to change something. And then you have to resell it when interconnection comes back. And you may need to tell the customer, ‘Oh hey, by the way, we need to upgrade your transformer, and that’s $7,500 extra. This is your new return on investment.’ For us, it’s waiting with bated breath to move a project forward, and it’s really clunky and really frustrating for a customer.” 
Plus, the relatively small percentage of customers needing to pay for grid upgrades doesn’t fully capture the scope of the problem. Data from Eversource and National Grid show that many communities across Massachusetts are already at or nearing grid capacity, meaning that the next interconnection request could trigger transformer upgrades that under the current model could stifle solar projects.  
Abe Walters stands outside his Bellingham home. (Jordan Wolman/CommonWealth Beacon)
It’s not entirely clear what the DPU’s move will mean for residents who have already been notified that their proposed solar project will trigger a transformer upgrade. Walters, the Bellingham man, said that he is still assessing what the new policy will mean for his project, which has now been in limbo for five months since he was told about the sudden $12,000 cost. 
Members of the working group that pitched the new cost-share mechanism that the DPU accepted are praising it as a new standard for how to quickly gain consensus among a diverse set of stakeholders who may not always agree.  
The concept, once the group started work on it last summer, took about a year to come to fruition. The plan was submitted to state regulators in March. 
Brendan Moss, a spokesperson for National Grid, said in a statement that the new system will “create a more predictable, transparent, and equitable path to interconnection.” Olessa Stepanova, a spokesperson for Eversource, hailed the “collaboration” that led to agreement on the new approach.  
The utilities worked in good faith to reach agreement — and it’s in their benefit to do so, said Kate Tohme, director of interconnection for Massachusetts-based solar developer New Leaf Energy and co-chair of the DPU working group.  
The utilities worked in good faith to reach agreement, said Kate Tohme, director of interconnection for Massachusetts-based solar developer New Leaf Energy and co-chair of the DPU working group. Connecting more residential solar projects also helps them reach their own state-mandated clean energy targets as fewer customers back out of projects over the upgrade costs. 
“We know that we aren’t going to always come to 100 percent consensus on every issue, and it’s not always easy,” Tohme said. “But this should be the goal and the model for groups across the country. We’re not submitting reports. We are, through a defined process, putting solutions before the DPU and achieving an outcome.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Digital Ad sales tax struck down
description: A first-of-its-kind state tax on some digital ads, worth an estimated $250 million a year to the state, was struck down Friday as a violation of the federal Internet Tax Freedom Act by the Maryland Tax Court. The law had been challenged by Apple, Google and Peacock TV.
text:
The steps of the Maryland State House. (File photo by Danielle E. Gaines/Maryland Matters)A first-of-its-kind state tax on some digital ads has been struck down as a violation of the federal Internet Tax Freedom Act by the Maryland Tax Court.
The decision issued Friday morning related to three challenges to the tax by Apple, Google and Peacock TV, a streaming service.
In its ruling, the court orders the state to refund the taxes collected plus interest. A spokesperson for the Office of the Comptroller said the office was reviewing the ruling.
The law has been the subject of multiple state and federal court challenges since it was enacted.
Portions of the law were struck down last year as a violation of the First Amendment by a federal appeals court.
The 2021 law targets big tech firms including Apple, Meta, and Google.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Under the law, companies reporting gross global annual revenue of at least $100 million are subject to a 2.5% levy. The tax increases in increments of 2.5% to a maximum rate of 10% levied against companies reporting more than $15 billion in gross global revenue.
The state could collect as much as $250 million annually from the digital ad tax, according to a legislative analysis. The funds are earmarked for the state’s education reform program.
In October, the comptroller’s office reported it had collected more than $400 million related to the tax.
Money collected from the tax was supposed to offset costs of the ever expensive Blueprint for Maryland’s Future education program. Costs for that program are responsible for driving billions of dollars in projected state structural budget  gaps. Next year, the state will have to tame a more than $3 billion projected gap as more expensive parts of the program come online.
A spokesperson for Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore), a sponsor of the 2021 bill, was not immediately available for comment.
But Doug Mayer, president of Americans for Digital Opportunity, hailed the decision.
“Today’s ruling validates what every person with the most basic understanding of tax law has been saying for over six years — digital advertising taxes are illegal on multiple levels,” Mayer said. “If elected officials really want to increase revenue, they should be empowering entrepreneurs, not concocting illegal taxes that stifle much of what is powering so much of the economy.”

description: Newark’s Shop Take 15 shows how business coaching and grant support can help entrepreneurs expand DOVER, Del. — Applications are now being accepted for the Business on Main Street Accelerator, an eight-week program designed to help Delaware entrepreneurs strengthen their operations, pursue funding and prepare for growth. The program’s potential impact can be[...]
text:
Newark’s Shop Take 15 shows how business coaching and grant support can help entrepreneurs expand
DOVER, Del. — Applications are now being accepted for the Business on Main Street Accelerator, an eight-week program designed to help Delaware entrepreneurs strengthen their operations, pursue funding and prepare for growth.
The program’s potential impact can be seen in Shop Take 15, a Newark self-care business led by founder and CEO Asia Coleman.
Coleman began working with the Delaware Division of Small Business while Shop Take 15 was primarily an online business. Through the Main Street program, she received help structuring the company, developing marketing ideas and updating its business plan.
The improved plan helped Coleman position the business to pursue funding and qualify for grant support. That grant had a tangible impact: Shop Take 15 grew from a virtual business into one with a physical Newark location.
Coleman also expanded the company’s product offerings and began providing courses. She said the business continues to grow.
Shop Take 15 sells handmade self-care products, including body butters, scrubs, soaps, oils and home fragrances. Its mission encourages people to devote at least 15 minutes each day to their mental and physical well-being.
Coleman’s experience provides a practical example of how technical assistance and access to funding can translate into measurable growth for a small business.
The Business on Main Street Accelerator is a joint initiative of the Delaware Division of Small Business and Launcher. It includes six virtual sessions and two in-person sessions in Dover.
Participants receive assistance with preparing a comprehensive business plan, examining their companies’ financial health, developing compelling pitch decks and using modern marketing strategies. Individualized coaching is also included.
“The feedback that I’ve gotten on the program, which began June 9, 2025, is incredibly positive,” said Anastasia Jackson, coordinator for Delaware on Main Street. “Participants are telling me that the financial reviews and personalized coaching are invaluable to them as business owners.”
The accelerator has graduated 37 small-business owners since it began last year.
Applications for the next class will be accepted through Aug. 31.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Department of Health announces 18th measles case for 2026
description: The New Mexico Department of Health announced this week that an unvaccinated adult in southeastern New Mexico tested positive for measles, marking the state’s 18th case this year as the U.S. sees its highest number of cases in more than three decades.
text:
A nurse readies a measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)The New Mexico Department of Health announced this week that an unvaccinated adult in southeastern New Mexico tested positive for measles, marking the state’s 18th case this year as the U.S. sees its highest number of cases in more than three decades.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a news release, the department said Thursday the person was likely infected out-of-state and began developing symptoms after returning to New Mexico. The person may have exposed others between Aug. 6 and Aug. 10 at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Centers, Walmart and the local emergency room in Artesia.
The state Department of Health advised residents to check their vaccination status and report any measles symptoms to their healthcare provider in the next 21 days if they were at any of those locations during that time period. New Mexicans can also call the state Department of Health hotline for guidance at 1-833-796-8773.
Symptoms typically appear within one to three weeks of exposure, according to NMDOH, and begin with a fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes. A red, spotted rash often appears on the head or face before spreading down the body. Infected patients are contagious from four days before to four days after the rash appears, NMDOH said.
“With measles still active around the country, the New Mexico Department of Health encourages people to check their vaccination status and get the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccination if needed,” Chad Smelser, NMDOH deputy state epidemiologist, said in a statement. “Vaccination is the best tool for protection from measles.”
Earlier this year, a federal report commended New Mexico health officials for their communication and vaccine outreach work during a 2025 measles outbreak. Between February and September of 2025, the state logged 100 reported measles infections, signifying the state’s first outbreak since 1996.
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention report noted that New Mexico saw a more than three-fold increase from 2024 in the number of adults who received the measles vaccine.
The CDC announced in July that measles cases this year have surpassed the entire count for 2025, with the highest number of cases since the disease was declared eliminated in 2000.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Va. school board to appeal federal court order to remove Confederate school names
description: After more than two hours in the second of two closed sessions, the Shenandoah County School Board voted unanimously 6-0 Thursday night to appeal a federal court’s order for the district to remove Confederate names from schools in the county. It may cost millions in taxpayer dollars to contest the decision. Judge: Shenandoah School Board […]
text:
Stonewall Jackson High School in Shenandoah County, Virginia. (Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)After more than two hours in the second of two closed sessions, the Shenandoah County School Board voted unanimously 6-0 Thursday night to appeal a federal court’s order for the district to remove Confederate names from schools in the county. It may cost millions in taxpayer dollars to contest the decision.
Judge: Shenandoah School Board violated students’ civil rights by reinstating Confederate names

On Aug. 6, U.S. District Court Judge Michael F. Urbanski ruled in favor of the Virginia State Conference of the NAACP and families of six students who sued over the school names. Urbanski found the district’s decision to rebrand the schools with the names of Confederate generals violated multiple civil rights laws and ordered the district to remove them immediately.
The board met Thursday for the first time since the verdict was released, hearing from multiple speakers, with some advocating that the board appeal and fight for the names, and others urging them to move on and avoid the potential costs.
Before going into a closed session on Thursday, the board said it wanted to defend what it views as its lawful local authority over school naming and to challenge what it considers legal, procedural, and factual errors in the district court’s ruling. 
“When a federal court’s remedy reaches directly into that local decision-making authority, I believe this board has every right and a responsibility to carefully examine whether that solution is legally justified and whether review by appeals is appropriate,” Board Vice Chair Whitney Pence said at the meeting.
Urbanski wrote that by renaming schools after Gens. Turner Ashby, Robert E. Lee, and Thomas “Stonewall” Jackson in 2024, the school board violated the students’ First Amendment rights, the 14th Amendment, the Civil Rights Act and the Equal Educational Opportunities Act.
AD Carter, a former student and one of the plaintiffs in the case, this week reflected on his time at Stonewall Jackson before deciding to join the case two years ago.
“I thought deeply about this case, not only because I’m a Black student in Shenandoah County, who walked under the name Stonewall Jackson every day, but also because I knew it would affect future students attending the renamed Stonewall Jackson High School,” Carter said in an interview.  “I didn’t want anyone else to have to go through what I experienced. I really wanted future students to have hope for a brighter day.”
The schools had been rebranded in 2021 to strip the names of the Confederates, who seceded from the United States during the Civil War and fought to continue enslaving Black people. But in 2024, the school board argued that its decision to restore the names was necessary to “restore the public’s trust.”
One area the board sought to challenge was the alleged legal error in finding the board liable without a finding of racial intent, members said.
Board members also argued that an appeal is the proper legal remedy to protect taxpayers and the county from a potentially costly settlement and to resist what they perceive as undue external pressure on local governance.
 Plaintiffs proffered remedy that board rejected 

Briana Brown, a former Shenandoah County Public Schools student who is one of six peers and their families to sue the school board over renaming schools after Confederate generals, speaking at the county courthouse on June 11, 2024. Former student AD Carter, another plaintiff (left) listens. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)
A few days before the board meeting, the legal team representing the Virginia State Conference of the NAACP and families of six students sent to the board’s defense counsel a proposal to resolve the issue.
“Where we go from here rests entirely with the school board,” the plaintiffs’ legal team wrote. “We are once again trying to provide an off-ramp to bring a prompt resolution to this litigation … while … ensuring that the school board’s illegal and unconstitutional conduct is quickly remedied and … its schools no longer serve as memorials to the Confederacy and are welcoming institutions for all American school children.”
According to the letter sent to the board’s defense, the plaintiffs’ legal team — The Washington Lawyers’ Committee, Covington & Burling LLP, and Holland & Knight LLP — wrote that their clients are offering to fund a private mediator to establish a “community-driven” renaming process and resolve legal fees.
Under the proposed terms, the board would agree to stop using the Confederate names by Monday, choose a mediator both sides accept by Aug. 31, and finish mediation by Sept. 30.
“Should the school board once again elect to continue this litigation by pursuing an appeal, we are respectfully putting you and the school board on notice that we will not agree to any discounting of the amount of costs and fees following such an appeal,” the legal team wrote.
The cost to the school board for this case could be substantial and is expected to rise if the board decides to appeal, including the plaintiffs’ additional costs and fees for opposing the appeal. 
The letter says the board has incurred about $500,000 in actual costs related to the litigation, while total attorneys’ fees have exceeded $15 million. 
The plaintiffs plan to file a petition for approximately $7 to 10 million in legal fees. This request reflects a voluntary reduction of approximately $6 to 8 million from the total fees incurred, intended to ensure the rates and scope of work are consistent with what a court would likely deem reasonable, the legal team said.
They have reminded the board multiple times about its liability for attorneys’ fees, the plaintiffs’ lawyers said, dating back to last September.
If the board chooses to appeal, the attorneys stated the cost will be “significantly higher,” largely because the final award would then include the “enormous additional costs and fees” required for the plaintiffs to oppose the appeal.
In response, board member Lewis Michael Scheibe said Thursday, “We may be a small county and a small school board, but we should not be bullied by strong-arm tactics by an organization that is claiming to want to protect the kids.”
“Appeals are there for a reason. It is part of the legal process,” Scheibe added.

description: Gov. Patrick Morrisey has extended the state of emergency for 12 counties that were hit hard by the deadly storms and flooding on July 21 and 22.  The state of emergency will be extended through Sept. 12 in Barbour, Doddridge, Harrison, Lewis, Pendleton, Pleasants, Randolph, Ritchie, Tucker, Tyler, Upshur and Wetzel counties. In the state’s […]
text:
Maj. Gen. Jim Seward, Adjutant General of the West Virginia National Guard, visits troops from the West Virginia National Guard as they continue to conduct flood response and debris removal operations in Weston and Buckhannon, West Virginia, on July 25, 2026. (Photo by Edwin L. Wriston/U.S. Army National Guard)Gov. Patrick Morrisey has extended the state of emergency for 12 counties that were hit hard by the deadly storms and flooding on July 21 and 22. 
The state of emergency will be extended through Sept. 12 in Barbour, Doddridge, Harrison, Lewis, Pendleton, Pleasants, Randolph, Ritchie, Tucker, Tyler, Upshur and Wetzel counties. In the state’s remaining 43 counties, the state of emergency will end Aug. 20.
“West Virginians have made tremendous progress cleaning up and recovering from these storms, but there is still a lot of work ahead in some of our hardest-hit communities,” Morrisey said in a news release Friday. “This extension ensures our state and local partners have the flexibility and resources they need to rebuild and recover.” 
Storms on July 21 and 22 brought 9 tornadoes and up to about 7 inches of rain in some areas of the state, leading to flash flooding. Central West Virginia was among the hardest hit. Flooding killed two people in Upshur County. 
The federal government has so far approved individual assistance for Ritchie, Pleasants, Upshur and Lewis counties. The assistance will help eligible homeowners and renters with the costs of recovering and rebuilding. 
The extension allows state and local agencies to continue coordinating personnel, equipment, and other resources necessary to support relief and recovery operations in the affected counties, Morrisey’s office said in the news release.
