name: Kansas Reflector
title: How the air conditioning of Kansas homes is like an old-timey carnival trinket
description: I don’t remember many epiphanies that I had as a fourth grader. But I remember one. I was standing in the tiled hallway of my suburban elementary school while other kids squealed and raced past the open classroom doors. On this day, the entire campus — the gymnasium, the parking lot, the playground and the […]
text:
Memories of old-time carnival gave Friday columnist Eric Thomas a striking insight into the world's climate crisis. (Illustration by Eric Thomas for Kansas Reflector)I don’t remember many epiphanies that I had as a fourth grader. But I remember one.
I was standing in the tiled hallway of my suburban elementary school while other kids squealed and raced past the open classroom doors. On this day, the entire campus — the gymnasium, the parking lot, the playground and the classrooms — transformed into our annual carnival.
The parent-teacher association provided all of the classic games. There was a cake walk (always choose the red velvet). The music room had a contest in which lucky students went home with live goldfish (sorry, parents). And then there were dozens of games with penny trinkets as the prize.
My epiphany came from the finger trap.
Perhaps you remember these from your childhood, too. Or maybe your kids brought one home this summer from a friend’s birthday party. I won mine by flipping over the lucky rubber ducky floating in a kiddie pool that stretched out on the floor of the first grade classroom.
The finger trap was a green-and-pink woven tube, about 6 inches long. Slide a finger into each end — so innocent, simple and safe.
But try to escape by pulling your fingers away from one another and you will discover the trap. The harder you try to escape, the more stuck you become.
This truism came to me, a 10-year-old, as an epiphany. It was a physical logic puzzle with a counterintuitive solution. (In part, that is how the gimmick became known by another name that rests on stereotypes.)
The finger trap remains memorable because of its metaphorical lesson: Forcing things can make them worse.
That’s why I was thinking about finger traps last week — four decades later — on a summer vacation to Europe.
The continent has descended into a hot and stewy fever. The Swiss and Italians that we met spent equal time welcoming us and apologizing for the heat. The oppressive weather has triggered wildfires, likely killing more than 10,000 people and rewiring daily life.
As a Kansan, you’re nodding along. We have been baking too — just look at our run of 100-plus degree heat index readings.
What’s different for the Europeans is air conditioning — or rather, the lack of it.
In Kansas, more than 9 in 10 homes have air conditioning, according to 2000 data from the U.S. Energy Information Association. According to that data, 85% of Kansans have central air, while about 15% rely on individual window-style units. A more recent study from the U.S. Census Bureau estimates 98.6% of occupied homes in Kansas have air conditioning.
Almost every business provides AC, as well. When I visited the local Costco warehouse store today, enormous garage doors at the front of the store yawned wide open, sharing the football fields of cold air with the sizzling sidewalk outside.
The Shawnee Mission school district this week showed off its air-conditioned buses.
Also this week, I sat in the passenger seat with a fellow Kansan at the wheel. She explained how she loves setting the car’s air-conditioning to 58 degrees while opening the sun roof to let in the sun and fresh air.
“It’s the perfect mix,” she said.
I stared back blankly.
Then — being the ultimate buzz kill that I am — I described the suffering in Europe. During our days as tourists, our group discovered how draining the non-stop heat can be. Outdoor restaurants thirsted for more shade. Rolling AC units snaked through small boutiques. One winery became a de facto sauna. Climate change is transforming the quaint cobbled streets into skillets and clay houses into ovens.
As Kansas tourists, we realized how much we take for granted each day in America with our customary intermittent reprieves: when we step into a chilled shop or rest in an air-conditioned restaurant.
With high temps outside and no AC, there’s no relief in Europe.
As the New York Times reported during the heat wave, many Europeans resist air conditioning for both cultural and environmental reasons. Some balk at making air conditioning part of daily life. Others correctly worry that more air conditioning and its required energy use will further accelerate climate change.
Here in Kansas, we wrap our loving arms around AC. Our state uses almost 30% of our household energy consumption on air conditioning and the air handlers that are part of air conditioning units. This consumption ranks eighth in the nation out of the 50 states plus the District of Columbia, according to the Energy Information Association.
Besides air conditioning, other forms of household energy consumption in Kansas place us near the national average. For instance, we rank near the middle in energy use on TVs and related equipment and 40th in energy spent on clothes washers. But air conditioning is a Kansas household priority.
Kansas and Oklahoma expend essentially the same amount of energy on air conditioning as a part of their whole energy budget. Every other state bordering Kansas uses at least 12% less. Just to the north, Iowa uses more than 36% less on air conditioning. It’s clear that we Kansans could use less by dialing up the thermostat a few degrees.
To be fair, our summer temperatures on the plains likely fuel this consumption. Only southern states such as Texas, Nevada and Florida spend more of their household energy dollars on AC than Kansas. Arizona, for instance, spends a staggering 46.75% of household energy on air conditioning.
(Yes, I acknowledge my AC complicity in this. After all, while we were in Europe, our son was back in the Kansas suburbs in a five-bedroom house cooled just for him — and our dog.)
Why does the tug of war between climate change and air conditioning remind me of the carnival novelty finger trap?
As we Kansans struggle to escape the heat, we dial down the temps in our houses. But that air conditioning demands fossil fuel and accelerates the rise in global temperatures. Escaping this week’s heat makes it less likely that we will escape the larger, global heat wave of climate change.
Europe is heating more quickly than the rest of the world. The continent relies on the cooling effect of the Arctic ice sheet. The reflective white of the arctic is melting away day by day during the summer, replaced by the dark blue hue of the ocean, which absorbs heat.
As my friend and I hiked through a valley in Switzerland, we gawked at the color of the river surging past our gravel path. Even after years of hiking in the Colorado mountains, I had never seen a mountain stream so frothy and white. The river appeared almost chemically treated, like the slurry of detergent and water from a washing machine.
The milky appearance results from rapid glacial thaw, we learned. The glaciers in the surrounding mountain store rock “flour,” tiny bits of rock that eventually cloud the rivers.  This summer has been particularly damaging to glaciers, which have been melting at unprecedented rates and thereby making the rivers murky.
In short, Europe is disproportionately warmed by our Kansas air conditioning.
To make my tortured finger trap metaphor hold for worldwide climate change and air conditioning, we must add another wrinkle.
As I stood in the hallway, fourth-grade me realized that he only needed to relax to escape the finger trap. Expend less energy? A quick escape.
However, the collective action problem of climate change demands that everyone work together to escape together. We must have a coordinated effort that relaxes our habits, dials down our thermostats and burns less fossil fuel.
The alternative: that we end up stranded in a trap of our own making.
Eric Thomas teaches visual journalism and photojournalism at the William Allen White School of Journalism and Mass Communication at the University of Kansas in Lawrence. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Federal grants to Indiana fell last year by more than $700M
description: When Medicaid is excluded from the results, the percentage drop in competitive federal grants grows to double digits.
text:
The U.S. Capitol building in Washington, D.C., amid fog on Tuesday, Dec. 10, 2024. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)The state of Indiana took in $733 million less from the federal government last year compared to the previous year, according to an analysis by award indexer Granted.
The grand total in the previous federal fiscal year — which ran from Oct. 1, 2024 through Sep. 30, 2025 — was $22.6 billion, down 3%.
That’s although Medicaid grants increased to $15.9 billion, up from $14.7 billion, according to the July analysis. Money for the low-income health insurance program made up 70% of federal receipts.
But when Medicaid is excluded from the results, the percentage drop grows to double digits. Competitive grants to Indiana fell to $6.7 billion, down 22% from the previous $8.6 billion subtotal.
‘Powerless’: Indiana families describe the toll of losing Medicaid access

The Biden-era Broadband Equity, Access and Deployment program represents the largest share of the $1.9 million drop, according to Granted founder Nathan Eagle, who tapped the federal government’s spending database for net financial assistance awards.
Indiana received $868 million in federal fiscal year 2024 to bring high-speed internet to every Hoosier. The line item for the one-time program then fell to zero in the 2025 fiscal year.
The Indiana Broadband Office, meanwhile, is busy putting the money to work. It has received approval to allocate about 40% to internet service providers in the first round of awards, according to a January newsletter, but there’s plenty left to do.
Funding for New Empowering Rural America also decreased to zero, from nearly $679 million. The program, another initiative of former President Joe Biden’s administration, offered loans and grants to rural electric cooperatives transition for renewable energy projects.
President Donald Trump’s administration has introduced a similar effort, Powering Affordable Reliable Technology, which will furnish partially forgivable loans for investment in biomass, geothermal or hydroelectricity, as well as energy storage systems. The program will begin accepting letter of interest next month, according to its website.
Indiana additionally netted $292 million less for the Epidemiology and Laboratory Capacity program, which is meant to strengthen the nation’s ability to detect, prevent and respond to infectious diseases.
That line item, Eagle cautioned, “is a net deobligation rather than a thin award year, so it reads as money coming back rather than money not arriving.”
The state chose not to participate in the Summer Electronic Benefit Transfer program to feed hungry schoolchildren, so that award dropped to zero, down from nearly $164 million. 	


Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



Indiana has only participated once, in the first year of the initiative. The state passed $120 monthly onto 669,000 children in the summer of 2024, while schools and their cafeterias were closed. Officials opted out last summer, and have said they’ll do so again next summer, Fox59 reported.
Additionally, funding for the Drinking Water State Revolving Fund also decreased to about $77 million, down from $214 million.
There were some increases beyond Medicaid, however, including three transportation infrastructure program.
Nationally Significant Freight and Highway Projects grew to $143 million from zero, Federal Transit Capital Investment nearly cracked $142 million compared to just $8 million and Highway Planning and Construction landed at $1.4 billion, up from about $1.3 billion.
Grid Infrastructure Deployment and Resilience rounds out the top five, increasing to nearly $103 million from under $5 million.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Measles outbreak in Southwest Wisconsin grows; most taken ill weren’t vaccinated
description: A report earlier this week of a couple of measles cases in Southwest Wisconsin has turned into an outbreak, with 13 more confirmed cases and six probable cases of the viral illness, the state health department reported Thursday. The outbreak, in Iowa and Lafayette counties, highlights the importance of getting vaccinated for measles, considered the […]
text:
Wisconsin's top doctor says a new outbreak shows measles is spreading in the state. (Photo by Getty Images Plus)A report earlier this week of a couple of measles cases in Southwest Wisconsin has turned into an outbreak, with 13 more confirmed cases and six probable cases of the viral illness, the state health department reported Thursday.
The outbreak, in Iowa and Lafayette counties, highlights the importance of getting vaccinated for measles, considered the safest and most effective way to prevent the spread of the virus, said Dr. Ryan Westergaard, the chief medical officer in the communicable disease bureau of the Wisconsin Department of Health Services.
Ryan Westergaard, M.D., Wisconsin Dept. of Health Services
The new group of measles patients who have been diagnosed are in Iowa County, Westergaard told reporters at a DHS briefing on the findings. Most of them were not vaccinated for measles, he said.
DHS announced two measles cases Tuesday, one in Iowa County and one in Lafayette County, that were confirmed through tests at the Wisconsin State Lab of Hygiene. 
Those were the third and fourth measles cases in Wisconsin in 2026, and were not related to the first two this year, which were linked to out-of-state travel.
Subsequent investigation by the local public health departments in the two counties turned up the 13 confirmed and six suspected cases that DHS announced Thursday. None of the current cases have been tied to travel. 
“The rapid emergence of these cases, particularly among people who have not traveled outside of Wisconsin, indicates that there is active local transmission, and it’s very likely that additional cases exist in the community that have not yet been identified or reported to public health,” Westergaard said.
State tracks 23 cases so far
Westergaard said DHS would not release the ages or age range for any of the people with confirmed measles cases in the current outbreak in order to protect their privacy.
The department maintains a state registry for all measles cases that includes age ranges and vaccination status. Thursday evening, that record showed that of the 23 confirmed or suspected cases identified in Wisconsin in 2026, three were in children age 4 or younger, 11 were in children ages 5 to 17, and nine were in adults ages 18 or older.
Westergaard said that it’s likely that there are more people with measles whose cases haven’t been identified and therefore aren’t on the state’s dashboard.
With one exception, the patients identified in 2026 were not vaccinated for the measles virus, according to DHS. One has been hospitalized.
Vaccine is ‘single best tool’ to stop outbreaks
DHS is asking people to verify whether they’ve had the MMR vaccine — the shot that includes protection against measles, mumps and rubella. That information is probably available from a person’s regular health provider, if they have one, or from the Wisconsin immunization registry.
The MMR vaccine is usually given in a two-shot sequence: the first dose when a child is 12 to 15 months old, and the second when the child is 4 to 6 years old.
“Having received two doses of MMR vaccine provides exceptional, long-lasting protection, and this vaccine remains our single best tool to stop this and future outbreaks,” Westergaard said.
For an adult without a record of the shot or who is uncertain about having had it, it is safe to get an additional shot, he said.  
DHS is also asking people to be familiar with measles symptoms. Westergaard said those include a high fever, a red rash that starts at the head and spreads down and covers the whole body, a cough, a runny nose and red or bloodshot eyes.
A person who develops those symptoms, or whose family member experiences them, should call their regular healthcare provider, Westergaard said.
People with the symptoms should call ahead before visiting a clinic, urgent care or the emergency room, he said, so that medical personnel can take precautions to prevent airborne spread of the virus before a patient arrives to protect other patients in the facility’s waiting room.
Easily spread virus
“Measles is known to be one of the most contagious viruses,” Westergaard said, “and we treat every case very seriously, because our goal is to completely stop measles transmission in the community anytime we have a case or a cluster of cases.”
Measles can cause serious health problems, according to DHS — pneumonia, deafness, and brain damage as a result of swelling from the disease.
Local public health agencies in the two counties haven’t identified specific public places where the virus might have spread, Westergaard said.
One of the jobs of local public health departments is to track contagious illnesses such as measles in their communities or counties, he said. DHS supports local agencies as they work to trace who else has been exposed to the virus.
Trump urges shift in childhood vaccine recommendations, calls for splitting up MMR vaccine

When a person who’s been exposed has been identified, they’re monitored for symptoms “to make sure that if any new cases pop up, we can get them isolated right away,” Westergaard said.
While the current outbreak is still small, “it’s a dynamic situation,” he added. With help from DHS, local health departments are tracing the spread of the virus and watching for more people who develop symptoms, “because that would be a sign that it’s getting larger.”
New Trump order ‘contradicts the best available science’
Thursday’s announcement follows an order Monday from President Donald Trump. Wisconsin’s top health official said Thursday that Trump’s order goes against the best scientific recommendations for measles prevention.
Trump’s order calls for separating the MMR vaccine into separate shots for each illness.
“There is no new scientific evidence that justifies changing recommendations that have, and continue to, protect children across the United States,” said Kirsten Johnson, secretary-designee of Wisconsin DHS, in a statement released Thursday.
“The executive order does not square at all with our recommendations on how to prevent measles or other vaccine-preventable diseases,” Westergaard said. “It was not science-based. It actually contradicts the best available science about how to prevent disease and keep kids healthy.”
DHS early this year turned from the Trump administration’s Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s vaccine recommendations after the agency cast aside previous longstanding vaccine guidance.
DHS instead has endorsed the childhood vaccine recommendations from the American Academy of Pediatrics and the American Academy of Family Physicians.  
Westergaard said vaccinations in Wisconsin have fallen below the 95% rate that helps ensure widespread protection from illnesses that vaccines can prevent, and are even below 90%. That has happened for many complex reasons, he said — including misinformation, sometimes spread deliberately.
Wisconsin has so far avoided the “massive outbreaks” of measles that have occurred in states such as Utah, Texas and North Carolina, Westergaard said. Public health officials can contain the illness if they learn early of cases and are able to move quickly to identify and quarantine patients. But that’s more challenging because the state’s vaccination rate is lower than it should be, he said.
In addition to encouraging more vaccination, cooperation with public health measures is “a second layer of defense,” Westergaard said. “Let’s work together as a community, as a team, when an outbreak happens — be willing to share information, be willing to stay home when any symptoms happen, and allow us to identify the extent of an outbreak and to stop it.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Haitians in Springfield are required to report to Ohio’s ICE offices and wear ankle monitors

text:
Mural in downtown Springfield, Ohio. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal). Haitians living in Springfield, Ohio are being required to wear ankle monitors and turn their passports over to United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement. 
Haitians in Springfield are getting letters telling them to report to the ICE office in either Blue Ash (near Cincinnati) or Westerville (near Columbus). 
“When they do, their passports are collected,” said Carl Ruby, pastor of Springfield’s Central Christian Church.

“They’re fitted with ankle (monitors); I call them ankle shackles.” 
This is happening after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in June that President Donald Trump can end temporary protected status for the 330,000 Haitians who’ve fled the violence in their home country.
TPS officially ended for Haitians on July 27 and a court lifted an injunction last week.
About 15,000 Haitians live in Springfield, with a mixture of temporary protected status, citizenship, and other legal status.
Even though about 30,000 Haitians with temporary status live in central Ohio, only Haitians in Springfield are being asked to wear the ankle monitors as of now, Ruby said.
“What you’re seeing in Ohio is a Springfield focused effort,” he said.
He has gone down to ICE’s Blue Ash office with some Haitians to receive their ankle monitors, which can track where people are at any given moment and have about a 75 mile radius, Ruby said.
“The ICE officers indicated, ‘If you keep coming back every time we call you, that may help your immigration case,’ which I don’t believe,” he said. 
“I think it’s a means to round up people quickly, and that when they’re ready, they have the logistics in place to deport them. I think that’s what’s going to happen.” 
The Haitians are then told to report back to the ICE office when they are summoned, which is expected to be every three to four weeks, Ruby said. 
“It’s inciting a lot of fear,” Ruby said. “I think (ICE’s) real goal is for them to self-deport. … I think it boils down to they want to have complete control over them, so (ICE) can easily deport them as soon as they’re ready.”
Ruby is unaware of any Haitians from Springfield who have self-deported back to Haiti. 
The U.S. Department of State currently has a Level 4 “Do Not Travel” advisory for Haiti “due to the risk of crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest, and limited health care,” according to the state department. A top security official and chief of staff to the nation’s defense minister was kidnapped in June. 
“It just makes me sick thinking of the sexual violence that is the norm in Haiti,” Ruby said. “There there are kids who sat next to our kids in Springfield City Schools who are going to be raped if they’re sent back, and that’s just the truth.”
More than 1,000 children born in Springfield with American citizenship have Haitian parents. Springfield City Schools declined to comment for the story.
ICE detained 35 people — including four Haitians — in central Ohio between Aug. 5 through Aug. 10, said Maqueli Eldredge, a paralegal at Legal Immigration Services in Dublin. Ruby said he has not noticed an increased ICE presence in Springfield. 
“They say they would come for the Haitians on this special task force, but they take any collateral damage people,” Eldredge said in a text message. 
The ICE office in Westerville was full of Haitians coming out with ankle monitors when Eldredge was there last week.
Many of their Brazilian clients in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia were asked to start wearing ankle monitors in July 2025. She said they have a 16-year-old client wearing an ankle monitor in Pittsburgh. 
“It is very embarrassing to wear them,” Eldredge said in a text message. “(The) devices cause lesions, rashes and blisters, bleeding on their ankles.” 
She said it can be hard for their clients to sleep with the ankle monitors. 
“It beeps in the middle of the night and (it’s) hard to get comfortable,” Eldredge said in a text message.
The ankle monitors will start beeping if the battery is not functioning well, Eldredge said. 
“They break all the time and batteries malfunction and get very hot, some caught on fire when charging,” she said in a text message. 
Some people are afraid of going back to the ICE office, so Eldredge knows folks who have cut off the ankle monitors and leave the state or self-deport. 
“(Officials) follow up where they leave that monitor and sometimes just take some collaterals,” she said.

title: SC students statewide now eligible for scholarship allowing a debt-free degree
description: COLUMBIA — High school seniors across South Carolina are newly eligible for scholarships enabling them to earn a college degree with little-to-no debt under a partnership approved in the state budget. An $18.7 million commitment by the Legislature will expand Meeting Street Scholarships to 32 counties, promising low-income students statewide with above-avera[...]
text:
College of Charleston student Brianna Ramirez talks Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026, during a virtual news conference from the college's Center for Intentionality about what the Meeting Street Scholarship has meant for her family. Beside her are Josh Bell, president of Beemok Education (left), and Ben Navarro, founder of the scholarships and other education programs run by Beemok. (Photo courtesy of Beemok Education) COLUMBIA — High school seniors across South Carolina are newly eligible for scholarships enabling them to earn a college degree with little-to-no debt under a partnership approved in the state budget.
An $18.7 million commitment by the Legislature will expand Meeting Street Scholarships to 32 counties, promising low-income students statewide with above-average grades up to $40,000 each toward their college education.
Nearly 3,000 students in the Class of 2027 could attend college with the scholarship that fills gaps not covered by other aid — up to $10,000 annually for four years for students who keep at least a B average. State funding will pay for an estimated 2,300 of the scholarships awarded next year.


The 14 “legacy” counties
The following is a county breakdown of students awarded scholarships between 2021, when the program launched in Charleston County, and 2025:

Allendale: 11
Bamberg: 10
Barnwell: 24
Charleston: 755
Clarendon: 22
Darlington: 96
Dillon: 89
Florence: 248
Jasper: 19
Lee: 11
Marion: 52
Marlboro: 25
Spartanburg: 195
Williamsburg: 42

Source: Beemok Education


“It’s an unbelievable thing,” said Ben Navarro, the Charleston businessman and philanthropist who founded the scholarship program.
“It’s not limited to numbers. It’s not a beauty contest. It’s none of those things,” he said Thursday during a virtual news conference from the Center for Intentionality student center that he provided to the College of Charleston.
The scholarship offers a path to success, he said, for any student who demonstrates financial need by qualifying for a federal Pell Grant and the ability to do well in school by receiving a lottery-funded LIFE or Palmetto Fellows scholarship: “That’s basically it.”
What began as a scholarship for Charleston County high school students, starting with the Class of 2021, has spread to 14 counties with private donations from Navarro and his wife, Kelly, and other philanthropists. They include Darla Moore of Lake City, whose donation first expanded the program into the Pee Dee. Donors have collectively committed roughly $88 million so far.
Once the statewide expansion is fully implemented in 2030, when today’s eighth graders become eligible, roughly 10,000 students annually will be attending college with a Meeting Street Scholarship. That is, if the Legislature fulfills the commitment. Funded this year through lottery profits, the state’s share of the aid will need to increase to nearly $60 million yearly, Navarro said.
“I feel super confident this scholarship is here to stay,” he said.
As evidence, he referenced statements from legislative leaders.
The expansion “gives thousands of hardworking students an opportunity they’ve earned and strengthens the future of South Carolina,” House Speaker Murrell Smith, R-Sumter, said in a news release. “This is an investment worth making, and I look forward to working with my colleagues to secure the support necessary to continue this opportunity for the Class of 2027 and future classes.”
Of the nearly 2,220 students awarded a scholarship since 2021, 88% of them have either graduated or remain in college, according to Navarro’s nonprofit Beemok Education, which runs the Meeting Street Scholarship Fund and other education programs he founded.

(Left to right) Meeting Street Scholarship recipients Sy’Mone Miles and Priya Frazier walk along the Horseshoe at the University of South Carolina campus in Columbia. (Photo courtesy of Beemok Education)

On average, the scholarships fill a $7,900 gap in the cost of tuition, housing, meals and other fees not covered by other aid.
Brianna Ramirez, entering her second year at the College of Charleston, is among the nearly half of scholarship recipients who are the first of their family to attend college.
“This is more than just a scholarship to me,” Ramirez, a graduate of Charleston County’s Academic Magnet High School, said during a virtual news conference. “It represents hope and opportunity not just for me but the rest of my family.”
She recalled seeing “pure joy and hope” on her father’s face at the Celebration Summit, held annually for first-year recipients, and she hopes to “show the power of getting an education” to her three younger sisters, so they enter the program too. A business major, she has a GPA of 3.66.
“That’s what I mean about investing in our future,” Navarro said. “We want Brianna here, in South Carolina, attending one of our colleges. We want her to stay here after that, and that’s what a scholarship like this can do.”
Scholarship program that enables debt-free college now available in 13 SC counties

Of the program’s graduates so far, 70% left college with zero debt, and 80% stayed in South Carolina to work, according to Beemok.
The $15 billion state spending plan that legislators sent Tuesday to Gov. Henry McMaster’s desk included the public-private partnership. In the 32-county expansion, 20% of the scholarships will be privately funded, while state lottery profits fund 80%. In the 14 “legacy” counties, private donations will continue to fully fund scholarships.
The state budget isn’t finalized yet. It takes effect with McMaster’s line-item vetoes, expected to be issued Monday. But the governor is guaranteed not to veto spending he recommended. The Legislature ultimately funded $3.7 million more than he put in his executive proposal.
That’s due to one big change in the eligibility rules: Previously, only graduates of public high schools qualified for the program.
The estimates increased when legislative leaders asked that graduates of private schools and homeschools qualify as well, said Josh Bell, president of Beemok Education.
Asked what happens if the numbers exceed estimates, Navarro made clear no qualifying student will be turned down.
“One way or another, we will fund every one of them,” he said of private donations. “If we exceed the state dollars, we’ll find a way. Anyone that qualifies will be in.”

(Left to right) Meeting Street Scholarship recipients Shondrea Enoch, Christia Holland, Maria Medrano, Lacie Straley and Zann Chandler pose for a selfie on the University of South Carolina campus in Columbia. (Photo courtesy of Beemok Education)

The program also has a work component.
Starting this school year, students in their second and third years of college must work 250 hours to keep their scholarship next year, which can include a part-time job on or off campus, internship, or research.
More than 80% of recipients were doing that anyway. The new requirement, announced in May, aims to ensure students get the work experience they need to get a job after graduation, Bell said.
Scholarship recipient Sy’Mone Miles, who’s entering her senior year at the University of South Carolina, said she sees it as more of a needed nudge than a requirement.
“It’s just really a great push in the right direction to ensure that we have the best future after college,” said Miles, a graduate of Early College High School in Charleston County, whose leadership roles at USC include organizing networking events for other scholarship recipients.
For her, she said, the scholarship means “being able to not put any financial burden on my parents at all for the cost of college, which has been really liberating.”
Navarro stressed that none of the state aid goes to administrative costs. “Every single dollar” provided through the state budget goes to scholarships, he said, as all overhead expenses are fully covered by the Meeting Street Scholarship Fund run by Beemok.
“This isn’t giving out money,” he said. “You have to earn this scholarship. Not every kid is supposed to be in college, but if you meet these criteria, if you work hard in school, you should go to college. This allows it to happen and allows it to be affordable.”



Eligible colleges
Students can attend any of the following colleges with a Meeting Street Scholarship, which meet the program’s graduation rate criteria. The number beside each college reflects its percentage of students graduating within six years on average:

Clemson University: 86%
Furman University: 83%
Wofford College: 81%
*University of South Carolina’s Columbia campus: 78%
The Citadel: 72%
Bob Jones University: 68%
College of Charleston: 66%
Columbia International University: 65%
Anderson University: 64%
Winthrop University: 60%
Presbyterian College: 59%
North Greenville University: 55%
Southern Wesleyan University: 55%
Columbia College: 54%
Converse College: 54%
Claflin University: 50%

*There is an exception for one USC campus. Students graduating from a Spartanburg County high school can use the scholarship at USC Upstate, as per the request of the private donor for scholarships in that county.
Most popular colleges
The following are the top five colleges students select. The following numbers do not include students starting this fall:

University of South Carolina in Columbia: 553
Clemson University: 390
College of Charleston: 190
Winthrop University: 126
Claflin University: 94

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Bookman: Years of low-key ‘grunt work’ are paying off for Ossoff
description: “We the people of the United States of America ….” That phrase from the preamble to the Constitution seems a quaint, almost archaic notion in these divisive times, times in which we’ve lost faith in ourselves and in each other. We the people, acting together, toward a shared purpose, a more perfect union? Do we […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff at a rally for him and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, who is running for governor, in Atlanta on May 31, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder“We the people of the United States of America ….”
That phrase from the preamble to the Constitution seems a quaint, almost archaic notion in these divisive times, times in which we’ve lost faith in ourselves and in each other.
We the people, acting together, toward a shared purpose, a more perfect union? Do we still share enough common ground to make that possible, despite our differences?
One place to start in revitalizing that shared purpose would be at the most basic level of public service. Senators and House members are elected to be our representatives to the federal government. They are our intermediaries between ourselves and Washington. If we have a problem with obtaining a passport, getting a response from a far-off federal agency or an answer about Social Security benefits, your local congressman is supposed to be there to help you, to help all of us, regardless of party.
For many years, the gold standard for constituent service in Georgia was the office of the late U.S. Rep. John Lewis. Even Georgians who didn’t live in Lewis’s 5th District would call his office for help, and in most cases would receive it. Set aside what you thought of his politics, Lewis took the idea of public service seriously, and his office reflected it.
That kind of grunt work isn’t for show ponies. It doesn’t get you an appearance on CNN or Fox News. It’s not something that you can easily put into a campaign ad, or use to impress donors. Yet it’s how the system is supposed to work, for all of us.
U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff, who interned with Lewis and views him as a mentor, has picked up that mantle of constituent service. I doubt Ossoff did it in hopes of political gain, but if so, fine. Good work deserves reward. But Ossoff has gained a reputation, among Republicans as well as Democrats, as someone who is reachable and effective. And people have noticed.
Take Scott James Matheson, a self-described “hard-core conservative” who serves as mayor of Valdosta, in deep-red south Georgia. Matheson has endorsed Ossoff for re-election, citing Ossoff’s willingness to work to help the people of Valdosta even though few likely voted for him.
“I will take heat for this endorsement, and it doesn’t matter,” Matheson told the Atlanta Journal-Constitution. “There’s no way I can turn my back on this relationship.
“The voters put me in here to do a job, and that man has been absolutely incredible.”
Another south Georgia mayor, Julie Smith of Tifton, tells a similar story.
“I don’t have to track him down. He tracks me down,” Smith said. “He’s been very good to south Georgia, and in my nonpartisan role as mayor I have to look to someone who takes care of their constituents. I’m a Republican, but there are times when a person exceeds the party. They go above and beyond.”
Of course, not every politician takes that approach. In recent court filings, Trump administration officials were forced to admit that they had canceled $7.5 billion in federal grants to blue states, based solely on how those states had voted in the 2024 elections. Grants to red states were left untouched; grants to blue states were canceled. Administration lawyers acknowledged that none of the grants were canceled “based on any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction or performance-based factor.” It was pure politics.
Disaster grants show a similar pattern. Blue states applying for emergency relief through FEMA have been far more likely to be rejected under Donald Trump, even when they meet every statutory and regulatory requirement for disaster assistance. Red states have had no such problem.
Is that how it’s going to be? Are government benefits going to be parceled out depending on loyalty to one particular party, to one particular person?
This goes beyond partisan politics. It’s about who we are as a people, as a nation. It’s about whether we still function as a nation in the first place.
“We the people … in order to form a more perfect union ….”
That’s still the goal, right? We have plenty of things to fight about, and seem to invent new ones out of thin air all the time. But we are all still Americans, equal under the law and Constitution, what John Lewis referred to as “the beloved community.”
Right?

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio Supreme Court allows Ashville referendum against data center project to move forward
description: Ohio’s local governments cannot fast-track new data centers without giving specific reasons, the Ohio Supreme Court ruled last week. The decision put an Ashville referendum, which would strike down the village council’s approval of a local data center project, back on track to make Ashville’s ballot. It also makes municipalities that pass future emergency re[...]
text:
The Gavel outside the Supreme Court of the State of Ohio, September 20, 2023, at 65 S. Front Street, Columbus, Ohio. (Photo by Graham Stokes for Ohio Capital Journal. Republish photo only with original article.)Ohio’s local governments cannot fast-track new data centers without giving specific reasons, the Ohio Supreme Court ruled last week.
The decision put an Ashville referendum, which would strike down the village council’s approval of a local data center project, back on track to make Ashville’s ballot. It also makes municipalities that pass future emergency resolutions — which waive a 30-day grace period for standard resolutions — explain why they need to take effect immediately.
Brian Meyers, a plaintiff supporting the referendum and a bus technician for over 20 years, said the court’s decision felt like a statement against those who have tried to block their efforts, even if the referendum fails in November.
“If it goes on the ballot, and folks vote for [the data center project], then so be it,” he said. “That’s the will of the people, and that’s how it’s supposed to play out.”
The case started in April, when the Ashville Village Council approved a term summary for Virginia-based developer EdgeConneX to build two data center buildings and an 800-megawatt natural gas plant.
Ashville allowed EdgeConneX to start plans immediately by declaring an emergency, stating it was necessary for “the public peace, health, and safety” and adding that the council “needs to accept these terms as soon as possible so that this project is not unnecessarily delayed.”
Meyers said he learned about the new data center from an announcement on the back of his water bill. Alongside other Ashville residents, he helped gather enough signatures to petition for a referendum overturning the emergency resolution.
State law bars referendums from overturning emergency resolutions, and Ashville’s fiscal auditor blocked the petition. The petition’s supporters appealed to the state’s highest court in July.
“This is blatantly not an emergency,” Meyers said, “and luckily, the Supreme Court felt the same way.”
In a near-unanimous decision, the court ruled that the village’s stated reasons were not enough to be a valid emergency. The first reason “merely parrots” state law on emergency resolutions, and the second reason could apply to almost any emergency measure, the court wrote.
“All emergency measures are presumably designated as such because commencement of the underlying matter should not be delayed,” the majority said. “But Resolution No. 06-2026 does not explain why waiting 30 days for the resolution to take effect … would unnecessarily delay the EdgeConneX project.”
The village resolution is still in effect, and EdgeConneX’s plans are in motion. The natural gas plant portion of the project sits in front of the Ohio Power Siting Board for approval.
Meanwhile, the Pickaway County Board of Elections will now decide whether to validate the petition. At the end of its opinion, the court cautioned that the board of elections could deny the petition if it finds that the resolution was an administrative action that cannot be struck down by referendum. The board of elections is consulting the county prosecutor’s office on the issue.

On deck: A large-scale data center ban in Trenton heads to the Ohio Supreme Court
Another group trying to get data centers on their local ballot is also appealing to the Ohio Supreme Court, this time out of Trenton.
Organizers for Woodsdale and Trenton Environmental Resistance gathered 336 valid signatures for a local ban on new data centers that use over 25 megawatts of power, largely in response to an 880,000 square foot data center project in the city proposed by California-based developer Prologis.
From Cleveland to Clearcreek Township, dozens of Ohio municipalities have passed temporary bans on new data centers. City councils in Pataskala, Sunbury, Hubbard, and Urbana have approved ballot initiatives for permanent bans similar to the one proposed in Trenton.
Plaintiff and Trenton resident Barry Blankenship said the ban is meant to address hyperscale data centers, which are increasingly being used to train and power artificial intelligence models. He referenced low water pressure near data centers in Georgia and extreme pollution from a massive xAI data center in Tennessee as test cases against them.
“That’s not what we need in our communities at all,” he said.
Trenton City Council rejected their petition at an Aug. 4 meeting and passed an ordinance that set 10% of the city’s registered voters, or 820 people, as the required threshold for petition signatures.
The resistance group organizers filed a lawsuit against the city in the Ohio Supreme Court on Thursday. They argue that the city’s ordinance is overruled by a 1996 Ohio Supreme Court case that set 10% of voters in the last general municipal election, or 128 people in Trenton’s case, as the bar to clear.
Blankenship said the fight against his city council has left him with little faith in his local government.
“We knew we were in an uphill battle with them, but you still have to at the end of the day stand for something,” he added. “You’ve got to try to protect your community, one way or the other.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Why all the flack about Flock
authors: Bill Stevens, Robin Gilmartin, Scott Gamester and Arman Haidari.
description: West Hartford is asking us to trust ALPR companies like Flock Safety, an $8.4 billion private artificial intelligence company.  Many of us simply don’t.
text:
West Hartford’s police chief raised a good question in the town’s recent Public Safety Committee meeting.  The meeting was focused on Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs), cameras used by law enforcement to catch suspected criminals, recover stolen vehicles and locate missing persons.  
Given that the town had installed ALPRs, through a vendor called Flock Safety in 2022, why all the flack now, four years later?
The chief addressed his own question thoughtfully. He talked about erosion of public trust due to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) abuses. And, he cited cases in which out-of-state law enforcement officers have misused ALPRs to locate women seeking reproductive care in jurisdictions like Connecticut where abortion is legal. 
The chief also cited the country’s darker episodes of trampling on civil liberties, such as the internment of Japanese-Americans during the Second World War and the infamous Tuskegee experiments in which Black “subjects” were misled and denied healthcare resulting in painful deaths.


We’re suggesting some additional reasons for the current flack about Flock. First, when  Flock Safety ALPRs were installed in West Hartford there was no prior public input. While the state requires public engagement before the installation of red light cameras and speed cameras, there is no such requirement for ALPRs. The upshot is that many of us in West Hartford were unaware that ALPRs had been installed. 
It’s clear from conversations with neighbors and on Facebook, that many of us conflate ALPRs with red light and speed cameras. The confusion about license plate readers appears widespread,  which makes sense as we’re only now becoming aware and trying to learn about them.
Second, Americans are increasingly distrustful of corporations, especially those in the artificial intelligence (AI) sector. Flock Safety uses AI technology to read plate numbers along with characteristics of the vehicle and establishes patterns of movement over time. The 2025 “Edelman Trust Barometer” reveals extremely low public trust in corporations. They report fear of corporate misconduct at an all-time high and cite three reasons for that fear: high-profile corporate scandals, the perception that companies prioritize profits over people, and a growing concern about use of AI.
West Hartford along with other municipal governments are asking us to trust ALPR companies like Flock Safety, an $8.4 billion private artificial intelligence company.  Many of us simply don’t.
Flock Safety’s “Director of Public Trust and Technology,”  Max Weinstein, participated in  West Hartford’s August 4 Public Safety Committee meeting and answered questions from Town Council members, the Mayor, Town Manager, Police Chief, Deputy Chief and police Lieutenant. The meeting was virtual, with the public able to watch but not participate. 
Weinstein provided assurances that the town “owns the data” and that Flock Safety does not sell data. The next day, Ken Barone, Associate Director at the University of Connecticut’s Institute for Municipal and Regional Policy told WFSB, the local CBS affiliate, that standard Flock Safety contract language states “that the customer, the community, the police agency, grants FLOCK a limited, non-exclusive, royalty-free, irrevocable, perpetual, worldwide license to use and disclose the customer’s data.”  
We do not understand the full implications of that sentence, but it does not sound good. We need more than the company’s word that our data is safe and our privacy protected. Public trust requires public engagement.
It’s worth asking:  What builds public trust in government? Public trust is built on transparency and democratic engagement. As residents, we have submitted three Freedom of Information (FOIA) requests to the town in order to learn how our ALPR data is being accessed, for what purposes and by whom. We’ve been waiting for results for over four months. Democratic engagement includes a forum for public discussion, education and input. It is not too late for that: We are asking West Hartford for a public hearing on ALPRs following the release of information requested through the FOIA process.
Data shows that people in Connecticut have greater trust in local government than in federal or even state government. This is also true nationally. It makes sense because local leaders are our neighbors, teachers, business owners and serve our shared community, often in a volunteer capacity.  We trust the West Hartford Police and town leaders and believe they have public safety and our best interests at heart. But this new technology raises questions.
Community is where democracy starts. We can, and should, have the hard conversations at the local level about how to balance privacy and public safety with respect to ALPRs. But first we need to know what we’re dealing with and not just take a company’s word for it. This means understanding what happens with our data and hearing from subject matter experts in the fields of AI technology, civil liberties and privacy.
Then, as a community we can debate, inquire and deliberate and ultimately make an informed collective decision about this technology going forward. In doing so, we strengthen democracy and our trust in each other.
Bill Stevens, Robin Gilmartin, Scott Gamester and Arman Haidari are all West Hartford residents.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho judge ruling allows abortion if it protects mother’s health, prevents self-harm
description: Pregnant women may receive abortions in many cases if there are serious risks to their health or if there’s a high risk she will harm herself, an Idaho federal judge has ruled.  The decision, released Thursday, marks a major change to the Idaho abortion ban’s exemptions. The judge determined U.S. constitutional protections under the Due […]
text:
An Idaho federal judge blocked the Idaho attorney general and Ada County prosecutor from enforcing Idaho's abortion ban in cases where women face severe health risks or there's a high risk she may harm herself. (Getty Images)Pregnant women may receive abortions in many cases if there are serious risks to their health or if there’s a high risk she will harm herself, an Idaho federal judge has ruled. 
The decision, released Thursday, marks a major change to the Idaho abortion ban’s exemptions. The judge determined U.S. constitutional protections under the Due Process and Equal Protection clauses of the 14th Amendment “establish a narrow but fundamental right to abortion when a pregnancy threatens the woman’s life or health.” 
U.S. District Court of Idaho Judge B. Lynn Winmill in his 81-page decision blocked the Idaho attorney general or Ada County prosecutor from enforcing Idaho’s criminal laws that prohibit providing abortions in narrow cases to protect the mother’s health. 
Initiative to end Idaho’s strict abortion ban qualifies for November’s general election ballot

“By banning health-preserving abortion, Idaho attempts to deny this fundamental right on the basis that the threat of harm comes from a fetus, which depends on the woman for survival,” Winmill wrote. “But a pregnant woman’s health is not a state resource to be allocated at the legislature’s whim. The Fourteenth Amendment exists precisely to prevent subjugation like this.” 
His ruling largely favored the protections sought by Dr. Stacy Seyb, a Boise maternal-fetal medicine specialist, who challenged the state’s laws. 
The Idaho Family Policy Center, a Christian political advocacy group that opposes abortion, denounced the decision in a press release Thursday. The policy center helped author Idaho’s civil enforcement abortion law, which allows family members of an aborted fetus to sue the abortion provider for a minimum of $20,000. 
“It’s important to recognize that the civil cause of action in the Heartbeat law still remains in effect — meaning that any physician who performs an abortion that is prohibited by the Heartbeat law can still be liable for breaking the law,” policy center President Blaine Conzatti wrote in the press release. “And doctors should take note: The IFPC Legal Center stands ready to hold doctors accountable who illegally perform abortions.” 
Conzatti wrote that he expects the decision to be overturned, arguing that the U.S. Constitution does not protect abortions for mental health reasons. 
Idaho’s criminal abortion ban allows abortion to prevent the death of the mother, to treat ectopic or molar pregnancies, and in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester, if there’s been a police report filed. Doctors who provide abortions that don’t fall within those exceptions face two to five years in prison and revocation of their medical license. 
A voter-led initiative will appear on November ballots this year that, if approved, would overturn Idaho’s abortion ban and enumerate protections to women’s reproductive healthcare and privacy into law.  
Winmill wrote in his decision that Idaho may still ban abortion in some cases that may be “troubling,” but that did not violate the Constitution. 
“For Idahoans who oppose this law, the solution lies at the ballot box rather than the courthouse,” he said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 How does the ruling affect abortions related to mental health? 

Idaho’s criminal ban states that abortions are not allowed to “prevent the death of the pregnant woman because the physician believes that the woman may or will take action to harm herself.” 
Winmill said the state’s law treated people with severe mental health risks differently than those with physical health complications. 
“The brain is an organ of the body, and healthcare providers use empirical tools to reliably assess the risk of suicidality and the most effective treatments,” he wrote. “It is an affront to human dignity to bar pregnant women from receiving life-saving care on the basis that the threat comes from a mental health condition rather than a physical health condition.” 
 How does the ruling affect fetal diagnoses? 

Under his ruling, pregnant mothers who receive a diagnosis that their fetus is unlikely to survive to term or unlikely to survive long after birth may only receive an abortion if that diagnosis also puts the mother’s health at risk. 
Women who receive a life-limiting fetal diagnosis that does not threaten their health, are still prohibited from receiving an abortion in Idaho, the judge ruled. Abortion would also still not be allowed in cases where there is a diagnosis of a significant disability, he wrote.
“Some may find the law cruel,” the judge wrote. “And the Court fully understands and appreciates that sentiment. Pregnant women faced with a devastating fetal diagnosis must either bear the challenges of pregnancy while waiting to watch their child die or flee the state to receive appropriate medical care.”
“Although some women may certainly wish to continue the pregnancy,” he continued. “And one might conclude that Idaho regards women in this latter category more as incubators for a fetus who will not survive than as human beings with the capacity to make an extraordinarily difficult decision about their bodies and their families. But the Court’s role here is not to express its personal judgment of the wisdom of the legislature’s decision.” 
Winmill decision 8-13-26

title: North Dakota governor lifts ban on TikTok from state devices
description: North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong this week lifted a ban on TikTok for state-owned devices, citing a change in ownership for the social media company. The TikTok ban for state government devices had been in place since a 2022 executive order from then-Gov. Doug Burgum. The prohibition aimed to safeguard the state’s cyber infrastructure and […]
text:
In this 2020 photo illustration, the TikTok app is displayed on an Apple iPhone. (Photo Illustration by Drew Angerer/Getty Images)North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong this week lifted a ban on TikTok for state-owned devices, citing a change in ownership for the social media company.
The TikTok ban for state government devices had been in place since a 2022 executive order from then-Gov. Doug Burgum. The prohibition aimed to safeguard the state’s cyber infrastructure and citizen data from the China-based technology company ByteDance, which owned TikTok.
Armstrong’s office announced he is rescinding that order because the app has come under the control of a majority-owned, American-led consortium. TikTok announced the U.S. operations joint venture in January, including company ownership stakes and members of its majority-American board of directors. Armstrong’s executive order also cites a July U.S. Department of Justice’s Office of Legal Counsel opinion that related to federal government employees using TikTok.
Requests to access TikTok on state-owned devices must go through the North Dakota Information Technology’s review process, but the department has determined the app “no longer presents an unmitigated or unique cybersecurity threat to state operations,” according to Armstrong’s office.
Separately, the North Dakota University System has its own policy that blocks TikTok from being accessed from public college and university networks or devices. Students, staff and faculty are able to access the app through personal devices not connected to a college or university network.
Armstrong’s order will not affect the TikTok policy for state colleges and universities.
The State Board of Higher Education could consider changes to the policy at a future meeting, said Billie Jo Lorius, a spokesperson for the North Dakota University System.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Washington poised to elect its first openly trans legislator
description: Jaelynn Scott is set to become Washington’s first openly transgender legislator after sailing through last week’s primary. She also could be one of only two members of the Democratic Socialists of America in the Legislature. “I think it’s important that people see themselves in me, and the fact that they can run and they can […]
text:
Jaelynn Scott is likely to represent the 37th District in the Washington state Legislature. (Photo courtesy of the Jaelynn Scott campaign)
Jaelynn Scott is set to become Washington’s first openly transgender legislator after sailing through last week’s primary.
She also could be one of only two members of the Democratic Socialists of America in the Legislature.
“I think it’s important that people see themselves in me, and the fact that they can run and they can win,” Scott said.
Scott, who leads the Black trans advocacy organization the Lavender Rights Project, will represent the 37th Legislative District in south Seattle. She’s received over 88% of the primary vote, facing only a college student running as an independent.
She feels being the first is a “heavy burden.”
“You sometimes feel like you have a weight on your shoulder because you’re carrying the sort of hopes, dreams, wishes, concerns,” Scott said.
“I don’t want to do it alone for long, and so I need people to join me,” she added.
Scott will also be the first Black openly trans state lawmaker elected in the country. In Massachusetts, Althea Garrison served one term in the 1990s, but was outed while in office and didn’t publicly confirm she was transgender until years later.
Scott is an ordained Buddhist minister, but isn’t practicing currently. She moved to the Central District in the 37th in late 2024, and has worked in the district for nearly a decade. She grew up in Mississippi.
The seat opened up with Rep. Chipalo Street seeking the state Senate position Rebecca Saldaña is vacating to run for King County Council.
Scott will be on the ballot in November alongside a conservative-backed initiative to bar transgender girls from competing in girls’ school sports. She recently spoke at the rally launching the “No Hate in WA State” campaign to defeat the Let’s Go Washington initiative.
The Trump administration has also tried through various means to restrict the ways transgender Americans can participate in society.
Scott says the Legislature has taken an “incrementalist approach and one that is too moderate.”
“This urgency of this moment actually kind of demanded that I try at least to go in to be a voice for the community,” she told the Standard this week.
Rep. Shaun Scott, the Legislature’s other democratic socialist, hopes Jaelynn Scott’s presence on the House floor can “change the ways issues related to the LGBTQ+ and the trans community are discussed.”
Some recent debates over parental rights have spiraled into diatribes about transgender people from conservative lawmakers. Let’s Go Washington also has a parental rights measure on the November ballot.
Shaun Scott also believes Jaelynn Scott will be an ally in his push to tax major corporations.
“When there are two different Rep. Scotts making that point, it helps,” he said, noting the two are not related.
The first-term Democrat from the 43rd District proposed a payroll tax on large employers, but it didn’t go anywhere this year as progressives instead forged a successful effort to pass an income tax on high earners.
Jaelynn Scott’s top focus is raising more revenue for state services via taxes.
“It’s a matter of life and death at this point and the moment for a very careful strategy is well beyond that,” she said.
She’d like that money to go toward investing in housing construction, education and healthcare. The Legislature’s cuts this year to state childcare funding troubled her. Scott’s Lavender Rights Project helped lead the charge to recently open a new supportive housing complex. She wants the state to build more public-owned housing.
She has also expressed support for legislation considered this year to bar law enforcement in the state from employing former federal immigration agents hired under President Donald Trump.
The 37th district’s other state House member faces a tough reelection campaign. Rep. Sharon Tomiko Santos, D-Seattle, trails in a two-candidate primary to Kelabe Tewolde, who is running to her left. Santos is the longest-serving active member of the Legislature. Jaelynn Scott supports Tewolde, despite having a “lot of love and respect” for Santos.
The district covers diverse south Seattle communities like Beacon Hill, Rainier Valley, Columbia City and the Central District.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Sen. Mark Kelly calls for Iowans to elect Democrats so Congress can investigate Trump ‘corruption’
description: CLEAR LAKE — Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona told Iowa Democrats Thursday their state plays a vital role in combating the “corruption” of President Donald Trump by helping decide control of Congress in 2026 through competitive elections for the U.S. Senate and House. Kelly, a former astronaut and naval officer, delivered the keynote address for […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Mark Kelly, an Arizona Democrat, delivered the keynote address at the Iowa Wing Ding Aug. 13, 2026 at the Surf Ballroom in Clear Lake. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)CLEAR LAKE — Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona told Iowa Democrats Thursday their state plays a vital role in combating the “corruption” of President Donald Trump by helping decide control of Congress in 2026 through competitive elections for the U.S. Senate and House.
Kelly, a former astronaut and naval officer, delivered the keynote address for the Iowa Wing Ding, an annual Democratic fundraiser hosted at the Surf Ballroom in Clear Lake. He asked the crowd of more the 750 people who gathered at the event who they wanted to represent them in Congress and the state government, joking, “This isn’t rocket science, and I should know.”
He said Republicans also know the importance Iowa plays in the 2026 midterms.
“Republicans, you know, they understand how important these races are, and they’re spending hundreds of millions of dollars right here, right now,” Kelly said. “They’re flooding the state with everything they have, and they’re going to fight for the system that is working for them. And that’s why we have to fight too.”
Kelly first took office in December 2020, winning an Arizona special election to fill the state’s U.S. Senate seat left vacant with former U.S. Sen. John McCain’s death. He won reelection to serve a full six-year term in 2022.
The Arizona Democrat made national headlines when President Donald Trump and U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth accused him and other Democratic lawmakers of sedition after releasing a video in November 2025 calling for members of the U.S. military and intelligence officers to refuse to carry out illegal orders.
“I know what happens when you speak truth to this administration,” he told the crowd. He said the statement was something “everybody, including Pete Hegseth, should agree with — that our troops should not follow illegal orders.”
Hegseth sought to reduce Kelly’s retirement military rank as a naval officer because of his comments in the video, but a federal judge blocked this move in February. A grand jury also declined to indict Kelly and Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who also spoke in the video, on charges of seditious conspiracy.
Kelly said, “really, all this bullsh** — it is not about me. It is about silencing people who are willing to speak up, to stand up for what’s right.”
He called for Iowans to elect Democrats in order to be able to protect Americans’ freedom to speak and vote — and to help create an economy that better serves working class Americans. Kelly shared a story in which he told his daughter, “the system is still working, it’s just not working for you.
“It’s working for the same people who are writing the rules — the rich, the powerful, the predators in the Epstein files,” he said.
Kelly also criticized Trump for committing “unimaginable corruption” during his second term as president, saying that a Democratic Congress would be able to investigate Trump and his family, “and how he’s trying to enrich himself and his family and his friends.”
The Wing Ding is not the only stop on Kelly’s trip to Iowa. He also plans to go to the Iowa State Fair, which kicked off Thursday.
While Iowa did not make the list of states the Democratic National Committee’s rules panel has put forward as part of the 2028 nominating calendar early window, the state has long been an important place for presidential hopefuls to visit. Kelly told the BBC in February he would “seriously consider” a presidential run in 2028.
Turek finishes 99-county tour, Republicans criticize his voting record
Before the Wing Ding, a group of conservatives called for Iowans to reject Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Josh Turek at the ballot box in November, saying he was “too liberal” for Iowa.
John Latham, center, a farmer from Sheffield, alongside John Rosefeld, right, chair of the Cerro Gordo County GOP, and state Rep. Charley Thomson, left, criticized Iowa Rep. Josh Turek outside the Surf Ballroom in Clear Lake Aug. 13, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Four Republicans spoke as part of the Iowa Republican Party’s “Turek’s Too Liberal” tour outside the Surf Ballroom before the event began, calling for voters to instead support his opponent, U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson.
The speakers said Turek, who currently represents Council Bluffs in the Iowa House, did not represent Iowans’ values through his votes in the state Legislature. They said his positions like a call to repeal the 2025 “One, Big Beautiful Bill” Act if elected to the Senate would hurt Iowa families.
John Latham, a farmer from Sheffield, criticized Turek for not voting on the “Iowa Farm Act” introduced by state Agriculture Secretary Mike Naig, a Republican, in the 2026 legislative session. Latham said the measure “delivered tax relief for for producers, helped support young and beginning farmers, and included provisions to keep Iowa farmland with the next generation, not big corporations or foreign countries.”
Additionally, he said Turek opposes Hinson’s “Save Our Bacon” Act — federal legislation that would ban states from enacting specific laws, like California’s Proposition 12, that regulate growing conditions for agricultural products. While Turek has opposed Hinson’s proposal, he also said he does not support California’s Proposition 12.
“Iowa agriculture needs a strong voice in the Senate, not an activist who will vote like every other liberal in Congress,” Latham said. “Josh Turek would be bad for farmers, bad for agriculture, and bad for small family businesses.”
Before speaking at the Wing Ding, Turek held a campaign event in Northwood, the final stop of his 99-county tour. He joked he intentionally held the final event of the tour in Worth County, “so we could say that this trip was ‘worth’ it,” as he introduced himself to the crowd as a former Paralympian and the first permanently disabled member elected to the state Legislature.
Iowa Rep. Josh Turek, left, spoke to Sheri Miszewska and Jan Miszewski at a campaign event in Northwood Aug. 13, 2026, the final stop on Turek’s 99-county tour as he runs for the U.S. Senate in 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
He told those gathered at the event about his first election in 2022, winning his Iowa House seat by a margin of six votes — and his reelection in 2024 by a margin of 5 percentage points.
“It has taught me the right candidate with the right message (can win), and I believe that message is common-sense prairie populism,” Turek said.
After giving brief remarks, Turek visited with voters — including Sheri Miszewska, a former teacher, who criticized Iowa’s all-GOP federal delegation for supporting cuts to medical research funding and education. Miszewska said she believed Turek’s campaign had a good chance of succeeding in Iowa in the 2026 election.
“Looking at his past record — he’s fighting for the average person, fighting for veterans, school districts,” Miszewska said.
As Turek spoke later at the Wing Ding, he reflected on what he heard from Iowans after spending a year on the campaign trail.
“I got in this race a year ago yesterday, and it’s been interesting, because I’ve been traveling this state all 99 counties,” Turek said. “I keep engaging with people (who) say the same things — ‘Josh, I’m struggling. I’m struggling just to keep food on the table, pay my electric bill, keep gas on my table.’ And I think we’re all feeling that, that struggle, right now. We’re looking at a state that has really hit the bottom. … This is not the Iowa we know, this is not the Iowa we grew up in. But Iowans are ready for change.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Juneau neighborhoods spared major damage in glacial outburst flood
authors: Alix Soliman, KTOO, Clarise Larson, KTOO, Corinne Smith
description: Mendenhall Valley residents in the flood zone celebrated Thursday afternoon as the Mendenhall River crested at a level well below initial predictions. The event was much less destructive than disastrous floods that struck over the past three years. The flood crested at 14.7 feet on the Mendenhall Lake gauge at 2:15 p.m., according to the […]
text:
The Mendenhall River as it crests on Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. (Photo by Clarise Larson/KTOO)Mendenhall Valley residents in the flood zone celebrated Thursday afternoon as the Mendenhall River crested at a level well below initial predictions. The event was much less destructive than disastrous floods that struck over the past three years.
The flood crested at 14.7 feet on the Mendenhall Lake gauge at 2:15 p.m., according to the National Weather Service. As floodwaters started to recede Thursday afternoon, only a handful of residents reported damage.
“We have crested officially, and we are now on the way back down — we did it, Juneau,” said Zoe Kaplan, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service, during a livestream just before 3 p.m.

Ann Lind lives in the flood zone on Marion Drive. She said she had been anxiously waiting for the flood all spring and summer. Last year, her home flooded when drainage pipes failed and water leaked through the floodwall.
“For months it was like this slow-moving bullet coming straight at me, and didn’t know if it was going to be a hit or a miss,” she said. “And today, it’s a miss.”
Lind said the water didn’t even touch the HESCO barriers that make up the flood wall in her backyard.
“This flood this year is the scenario we all wanted — we all hoped for,” she said.

A pump pipes water over the flood wall on Killewich Drive as the flood crests on Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. (Photo by Clarise Larson/KTOO)
A couple of riverfront homeowners on Killewich Drive said their crawl spaces flooded this year due to seepage, but they were able to pump out the water.
 
Riverfront homeowners on Killewich Drive pump water out of their crawl spaces on Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. (Photo by Clarise Larson/KTOO)    

View Drive residents saw the worst flooding, as they have every year. This is the second year in a row they were left without the protection of the flood wall constructed by the City and Borough of Juneau and the Army Corps.
Mandy Mallott lives at the end of the street. Last year, she and her neighbors set up their own flood wall made of HESCO barriers and an earthen berm in an attempt to protect their homes. She said her home was spared, but there was still a lot of damage throughout the neighborhood.
On Thursday afternoon, she said she and others who put up barriers on the street didn’t see flooding in their homes.
A man walks across the top of HESCO barriers as the Mendenhall River rises on Thursday morning, Aug. 13, 2026. (Photo by Clarise Larson/KTOO)
“The emotions that are running through us are a big sense of relief and thankfulness to our friends and our neighbors that we got through the night and this gorgeous day together,” Mallott said.
Malachi Thorington also lives on View Drive, where he said his house and his next-door neighbors’ flooded this year, but not as badly as in the past.
Downstream on Meadow Lane, near Juneau International Airport and the mouth of the river, Bob Jacobson watched the flood from his son’s deck overlooking the river.
He described watching a tree strike the barriers across the river — just minutes before — to two U.S. Army Corps officials who had just arrived at the barrier.

Army Corps crews chainsaw a log that struck a HESCO barrier across from Meadown Lane on Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
Within minutes, Army Corps crews chainsawed the log away from the barrier. Pumps were stationed along Meadow Lane but did not need to be turned on as the flood peaked.
The HESCO barriers below Brotherhood Bridge are new. There was some seepage, but neighbors said it was nothing compared to last year when water rose up the bank and into yards and some driveways, just feet from homes.
 
An industrial-sized pump pipes water over the flood wall on Meander Way as the flood crests on Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. (Photo by Clarise Larson/KTOO)    

Jeff Garmon is the meteorologist in charge at the Weather Service in Juneau, and he lives on Meander Way — a street that’s been hit hard by flooding in the past. As the flood peaked, he had minor pooling in his backyard, which was piped back over the HESCO flood wall by pumps provided by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers.

Jeff Garmon walks to his backyard, where an industrial-sized pump pipes water over the flood wall on Meander Way as the flood crests on Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. (Photo by Clarise Larson/KTOO)
“We’re fortunate this year we didn’t have an atmospheric river going into this,” Garmon said. “I think that was our saving grace.”
Garmon said he’s proud of how the city, Army Corps, U.S. Geological Survey, University of Alaska Southeast researchers, the Central Council of the Tlingit and Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska, flood advocacy groups and countless others worked collaboratively to support residents in the flood zone.
“It’s something Juneau should be proud of — that as a community we came together,” he said.
